I really enjoyed Kurt Vile's previous album, "Smoke Ring for My Halo," so I was looking forward to this new offering. I like it, but I feel like I should have been blown away more than I actually was. I keep waffling: one day I think it's brilliant, a timeless work of musical genius. And the next time I play it, I find it hard to stay awake, thinking perhaps this is nothing more than a bunch of over-hyped aimless jams.I've played this CD a full 20 times now, and I'm still not QUITE sure what to think of it all. Certainly, Vile is a great guitar player, and the seeds for some memorable music are lurking in there, but too many of these tracks drag on for far too long. It's great that you get nearly 70 minutes of music on this CD, but I think this is one of those cases where less might have equaled more. At least I wouldn't nod off so often if the songs were shorter!So, is this a great album or an overrated one? I'm still sitting on the fence. But I'll keep playing it --- that alone should serve as some sort of endorsement --- and think about it all again 3 months from now.
summary: One day I love it, the next day I don't

reviewText: When i heard there was a new ICE CUBE album on the very near horizon afew months back i was counting down the days til it dropped. After getting every album he's ever released i knew what kinda "CUBE" i was looking for and for the MOST part on this cd i got him. Apart from the truely disasterous moments that are all 3 LIL'JON tracks "go to church", "holla @cha'boy" and "you gotta lotta that", the remainder of the album is particularly tight. Admittedly there are moments where he reverts back into "don mega" mode which i was never a huge fan of but the majority of the time its the blistering return to form that got me hooked. On tracks like "smoke some weed", "child support", "laugh now, cry later", "growin'up", "click clack-get back" its like we stepped back in time to get some vintage CUBE over futuristic beats!!! Then with other highlights such as "spittin' pollaseeds", "why we thugs", "doin'what it pose 2do", "the game lord", "the nigga trap" and "steal the show" you cant help but be impressed by the return of the gangsta rap creator. reviewText: I love Saves the Day.  I really do.  The music they've made over the years has helped me through some of the worst times, and have made some of the best times even better.  Chris's lyrics are etched onto my heart and into my mind, I'll never forget "Blindfolded" or "the Choke".  Saves the Day is a band that introduced me to the underground and indie music that I never knew exsisted, and that I now can't live without.Having to write this review really does in a way break my heart.  This album had so much potential, Stay What You Are was a spectacular album even though the shock of the change in style almost convinced me to never give the album a chance.  Well, I've given In Reverie more than enough chances.  I listened to it before its release, I bought it the it was released, and I've listened to it since.  And I must say, that this is a very poor effort.  The music is very uninspired, the lyrics are very childish and simple, and the production doesn't even sound good.  Chris said that this was a natural progression and that every album was going to sound different.  In Reverie is indeed a progresion, but one in the wrong direction.  I'll say it again, I love this band, always will, but this album is a huge dissapointment.  It sounds like it was written and recorded in maple syryp.  It's just so thick and slugish.  If you want a good Saves the Day CD, then buy any of the older ones.  I reccomend Can't Slow Down for the fast punkier side, Stay What You Are for straight rock and roll, and Throught Being Cool for a more popier punk version of the band.  And of course there's the all acoustic CD, I'm Sorry I'm leaving, which is very beautiful and very overpriced.

This was a phenomenal follow up for Men at Work. After the huge success of '82's Business as Usual, they come up with this solid rock album of no nonsense songs in 1983. Overkill is adventurous as well as mainstream when you hear it, and I feel like I'm on some beach when I hear it. It's A Mistake has such a superb midtempo groove with some funk beds inside of it. The funny Settle Down and Colin Hay's chirpy singing in it is also unique. It sounds like something Sting would do. The last song rocks like nothing else Men at Work would do. After this album, they had Two Hearts in 1985, then just vanished. Why didn't they continue that momentum? They'd be at 10 or 12 albums right now and be just as large as U2 is at this moment. They were on such a roll at this point after album #2. Sorry if the band had some conflicts, but not at the expense of all that great music that they made. This music business is tough to some artists, since record companies like to keep up with the changing music trends. The band has reunited now, but just imagine what might have been if they stayed on the course. Cargo is really the best of those albums that they made.

I have grown to love Steely Dan's eclectic music.  When I was 20 years younger, and mainly buying and listening to hard rock outfits like Aerosmith, Rush, Led Zeppelin, etc., the only Dan music I was familier with was the few "hits" being played on the local Rock radio.  They played Rikki Don't Lose that Number and Peg.  And I remember Josie off the Aja album.The first Steely Dan cd I bought was the debut, Can't Buy a Thrill. I must have bought it because my favorite song is Do It Again.  Later, in the heyday of original compact disc releases (vs. re-issues of former vinyl albums) Steely Dan's A Decade of Steely Dan came out.  It was a popular cd.  Great songs and great sound.Years went by.  I was still just a casual fan.  Had maybe purchased just a couple of other titles on MCA records.  They were a bargain in price, but not in quality.  So-so sound quality, No liner notes. etc.  Finally, in the last few years, major musical acts of any "significance" have had their early albums/cd's remastered and re-released.  All this at a very reasonable price!  That's when I started replacing old discs and buying some that I did not own before by the Dan.  Wow, did I discover some great music that I had never heard on the radio!Night By Night is one of my all-time favorite Dan songs.  Really smooth and jazzy.  The title track, Pretzel logic is also one I had never heard.  Great stuff.  I have now purchased all of their early albums.  One at a time.If you are just starting out. Try either their first album or the great Aja from 1977.  If you like what you hear (and you will) then just keep picking them up.  Some are only $8 apeice.  You can't go wrong.

They played some original pieces together, while also playing a cover of some Bob Marley  tunes. When you combine the two, they deliver an unmistakable performance - bringing people together - who listen to their music as a "unified-whole." This duo of "highly-talented" guitarists, "kicks butt." There's not a whole lot I can say about this particular album other than to say, there's not very many good songs on it. Ben's enigmatic-style voice goes from being soulful - to sounding nasally and high-pitched (which really gets to be annoying somtimes), and a little breathy. Ben's good at guitar - don't get me wrong - but with his voice and some of the inconsitancy (the title of the CD "Diamonds On The Inside," explains it all) of some of the songs is the reason why I give this album ***3-stars***.

Albums like this don't come along every year (or if they do, I have a heck of a time finding them). From start to finish, this is an album full of masterful pop songwriting and awesome production combined into a lush tapestry of harmonious synth vocal awesomeness.One of my favorite songs is the first, Lisztomania. It starts strong, uses varied silence and dynamics (gasp!) and excellent musicality to actually develop the song through its choruses ending up at a truly gorgeous lush drop away and a build-up to another power-pop verse straight to the end, which in itself leads into (gasp!) the next song!The whole album essentially goes that way. In the middle, it drops into something more dynamic -- something more mysterious -- in Love Like a Sunset, both parts of which are great on their own merit. Then the catchiness hits again with Lasso. It doesn't stop - every song after that has a hook, to catch you line and sinker into liking it and being interested in it, and loving it as much as the last one. No track gives you a reason to dislike it, even as hard as you try to find something wrong; nope, there's the chorus and I'll be darned if it doesn't perfectly match the personality of the song.The only thing wrong with the album may be the last track, which isn't quite as unique as some of the others, and not quite a thoughtful ending either; it doesn't exactly know what to be. I'd like to think it should have gone somewhere in the middle instead, for those of us who still listen to albums in order.Anyway, the simplest way to put it is that I've been addicted to this album for... hmm... 3 weeks straight. It's definitely one of those. Don't miss it.

reviewText: Norma Jean Bless the Martyr Kiss the Child...can't make music like this.  Can they?!  This follow-up to their first album (when they were known as Lutikriss) is LIGHT YEARS ahead of most other bands on the scene today.  Norma Jean's first release under that moniker is a ground breaking effort compared to the likes of Botch and Every Time I die.  The ferocity of the riffs, the unabashed live feel the album has and the singer's guttural screams and growls are so well done that I'm hard pressed to find any flaws with this record what-so-ever.Norma Jean take the cake with this album as the kings of noisecore.  The high pitched dissonant notes backing almost every song make you want to start a circle pit in your own house.  Turn this album up to max volume, clear a spot in your living room and prepare to break things.For fans of Botch, Every Time I Die and The Chariot (former Norma Jean singers new band)

I maintain a certain distance with bands like the old 'Bends' Radiohead days and Augie March, and whilst I pull out their albums occasionally, I can't get too pumped about listening to them..they often lack a certain backbone that I desire.I find Travis a little similar to the old Radiohead (before they got weird on us) but I find this album an absolute delight.It reminds me of the light lovely steps of faeries, and thatshow it works; slowly seeping into your every crevice. You find yourself singing it on the bus, and realise that you absolutely adore it!It is an easy going bunch of tunes which may be critised for being lightweight, but there is a gentle kind simplicity in the sound and a fabulous freshness to this album.Complications are zero, and this is one that doesn't need deeply considered, though of course, it does allow for some thought in there.Have a listen to #5..Or another gem, # 8 (you may have to check out the song titles above, I have misplaced the album cover...) has this lovely liltng sound, and some hearfelt lyrics..'The mistake we made..was never having planned to fall in love...' Additionally, the first three tracks strike a chord..but then I am in love with all of Travis..If you are expecting Tool or Smashing Pumpkins, you can forget it. If you are even expecting another 'Why does it always rain on me', you can forget it. I was least impressed with that track on the album, but cannot recommend the entire album enough.

Black Gives Way To Blue is a CD that takes me back about 15 years or so to the height of grunge music.  While Alice in Chains is more complicated than a single label, there has been a musical void since the grunge movement ended in the 90's.  As I listen to this CD, I find it every bit as dark and brooding as the music that marked that period.It is also a bold move by the remaining members of the band after lead singer Layne Staley's passing in 2002, and it is their first studio recording with new vocalist William DuVall.  While the sound of Black Gives Way To Blue is true to Alice in Chains, I have to give DuVall credit for not falling into the trap of trying to sound like another Staley.  However he and Jerry Cantrell manage to blend their vocals in a way that longtime fans will find familiar yet fresh.  The differences start out subtle on the opener "All Secrets Known" and "Check My Brain", but DuVall takes center stage on "Last Of My Kind".  The good news is that DuVall is no slouch whatsoever, and he is a big part of making this CD great.  It may sound odd to say this about an Alice in Chains song, but the harmonies on the second verse of "Black Gives Way To Blue" are a thing of beauty.The instrumentation on Black Gives Way To Blue is very tight.  Most songs are driven by the three pronged attack of drums, bass, and rhythm guitar to a pace that is moderate.  Alice in Chains was never a thrash or punk band, and the slower tempos helped create the brooding vibe.  At the same time, though, there are a couple of acoustic heavy tracks in "Your Decision" and "When The Sun Rose Again".  The latter also features tablas, an Indian percussion instrument, that adds a unique vibe.  I found the structure of "Acid Bubble" to be very interesting as the verses are fairly slow and driven by the base line while the chorus takes the tempo up briefly before giving way to the second verse.  This pattern repeats after the second verse and then the song ends.  As a final note, the piano on "Black Gives Way To Blue" is courtesy of none other than Elton John.  That has to be pretty far up the list of unexpected collaborations!I'm not sure how much of the lyrical content is supposed to be about Staley's drug use and its affect on the band, but you can certainly read that into a number of the songs.  "All Secrets Known" seems to be about moving on from the past as it opens "Hope/A new beginning".  However "Your Decision" seems to be the most pointed with lines like "Time to change has come and gone/Watched your fears become your God" or later in the song "You feed the fire that burned us all/When you lied/To feel the pain that spurs you on/Black inside".  One could argue, though, that "When The Sun Rose Again" is just as strong with "Pray/Squeal when your caught/Cry/It's not my fault" and "Time to trade in never befores/Selling out for the score".  Yet on the closer, "Black Gives Way To Blue" to tone is more conciliatory "Lay down, black gives way to blue/Lay down, I'll remember you".  This brought things full circle for me as it hints at the night passing into a new day but with a touch of sentimentality.Overall, it is hard to call Black Gives Way To Blue anything short of a triumph.  I highly recommend it to fans of Alice in Chains' previous work or the 90's grunge music.  I've had a hard time keeping this out of the CD player in my car.Download this:  Your Decision
summary: "No One Plans To Take The Path That Brings You Lower..."

reviewText: "Worldwide Underground" is an intriguing, fascinating mess of a record.  Delayed for at least a year, it lacks some of the cohesion and focus of Erykah Badu's last two studio albums, particularly 2000's "Mama's Gun," an underrated classic that literally turned the whole boho soul genre upside down on its head.  Badu hasn't made lightning strike again on "Worldwide Underground," but there are some solid touches that are worth a listen.  The free-flowing groove of "Back in the Day," the catchy and memorable "Danger," the playful "Love of My Life (with Queen Latifah and Angie Stone)," as well as "Bump" pass along nicely and all invite repeat listens.  They're all good slices of the laid back soul we've come to expect, but the EP, as a whole, is as unstructured as Badu's afro wig.  And not everything holds together, especially "I Want You."  That song has an interesting hook, but when stretched over 10 minutes in length, it overstays its welcome way too soon.  Warts and all, I like and recommend "Worldwide Underground."  Did she record another "Tyrone" or "On & On?"  Nope.  Did she release a flawed yet solid EP?  Yes.  This is one of those records that may throw you in for a loop on the first listen, but it will ultimately grow on you.  Grade: B.

This once punk "policeman" just keeps getting more mellow with age. But that's ok. I like his newer stuff too, even if some of it does approach "Phil Collins" territory. His first solo album sounds closest to "The Police" of course, especially in the excellent song "Fortress around your Heart". For ABC "Lexicon of Love", was the million dollar album.All the pretty dancegirls and all the men, danced the nightaway in the nightclubs around Sheffield, England. It was ahuge funship boosted by lager and lime, loud music and rollinghome at 2AM. After everyone had tired of "The Look of Love", theeuphoric trip died a quick death."Beauty Stab",never would re-enact those days. Nightclub life inEngland is very fickle. People move on, some get married. Others"hang around" waiting for the next surge. {Depeche Mode really keptthem alive.} It is unfortunate for "Beauty Stab" contains many tracksto entertain the mind. Such as "S.O.S.", "United KIngdom", and "Designby Default."Martin Fry really did not change the key of the songsvery often, and the orchestrations needed more attention...but therewas more to come...."How to be a Millionaire" was for many the bestalbum ABC recorded. Some might disagree, because it was still not"The Look of Love." and that really is the whole point, there neverwill be any replacement for that mammoth record. Meanwhile "Beauty Stab"deserves hours of listening because it is ABC, and worthwhile.
summary: Let's get to know our ABC's

Now don't get me wrong, that would have been fine with me, but he displayed an all-round entertainer. D danced, sang, cooked, smoked, ran around, slowed it down and the whole nine. Vandenberg, the Dutch hard rock/heavy metal bands featuring young guitar wizard Adrian Vandenberg (in his pre-Whitesnake days) debut in 1982 with this self-titled album. The early Vandenberg sound walked the line between melodic rock and heavy metal, and was clearly influenced by bands like The Scorpions and MSG.Vandenberg is a really rockin' album, and one that's fairly fast-paced throughout. It's wall-to-wall with catchy riffs and blazing solos, and there's plenty of melody and polish to make it, if not quite AOR, then at least radio friendly. MSG seems like the obvious point of comparison, but there are also similarities to Uriah Heep's early `80s albums as well. The lyrics tend to be a bit silly, and Bert Heerink's vocals aren't as strong as most, but the songs are well-written and there's just a great early `80s hard rock vibe throughout the album. You hear it especially on songs like "Burning Heart," "Nothing to Lose" and "Out in the Streets," but the whole album is rock solid.It doesn't have the same metal edge ofHeading for StormandAlibi, but Vandenberg is probably the strongest overall album of the three. If you're a fan of guitar-driven early `80s hard rock along the lines of Rail, Grand Prix and especially MSG, you'll definitely want to check out Vandenberg. The Best of collection is probably enough for casual fans, but if you like what you hear, come back around to the debut.Edition Notes: Wounded Bird reissued Vandenberg (along with the rest of the Vandenberg catalog) in 2002. It's a typical Wounded Bird reissue - no remastering, no bonus material and almost non-existent liner notes. This is an album that's practically begging for a full-on remastered Rock Candy reissue.
summary: Hard rocking debut from the future Whitesnake guitarist

reviewText: Simon And Garfunkel's third album was released on Monday, October 10, 1966 and remains my favorite of their albums. The album opens with the sweet traditonal song Scarborough Fair/Canticle as arranged by the two. Patterns is a nice song about figuring out life's mysteries and never being able to completely unravel them. Cloudy is a sweet upbeat song that comes in at just the right point with it's cheerful and upbeat attitude. Homeward Bound is a sweet sad song about being stuck a long way from home while The Big Bright Green Pleasure Machine is a commentary on mass marketing, advertising and popular culture. The first half of the album ends on a happy note with 59th Street Bridge Song (Feelin' Groovy).The second half begins with the moving The Dangling Conversation which is a sad commentary on a dying relationship with nothing left in common. Flowers Never Bend With the Rainfall is more upbeat and can get your toe tapping. A Simple Desultory Philippic (or How I Was Robert McNamara'd into Submission) is a Dylan send up with Paul telling us he's been Rolling Stoned and Beatled till he's blind with a serious message in there too. On top of all that, he loses his harmonica. Laughs. For Emily, Whenever I May Find Her is a sweet song sung by Art Garfunkel. A Poem On The Underground Wall which was inspired by the cover shoot forWednesday Morning 3am. The album ends with 7 O'Clock News/Silent Night which finds the two singing a sweet version of Silent Night while the song becomes quieter, the "News Broadcast" becomes louder with with it's very real reporting on disputes of the Civil Rights Bill, the murder of 9 Nurses and the death of Lenny Bruce among other things which is positively mournful. The two bonus demos are nice and give a good feel for what would actually happen with the songs. All in all, a very moving album filled with much joy and sadness.
summary: Everyday's an endless stream of cigarettes and magazines

reviewText: Having been a member of Groove Theory and the onetime vocalist of Sweetback, Amel Larrieux branches out into her own with this delectable solo debut.  Offering laid-back beats with uplifting messages, "Infinite Possibilities" is as soothing as iced tea in July.  "Get Up" gets the mood right with its deep bass and Larrieux's seductive vocals.  There's no denying the jazzy vibes of the ultra-classy "Down," but Larriux doesn't really cut loose vocally until we get to the excellent closer, the mellowed "Make Me Whole."  This stellar debut, which was unjustly ignored upon release, is an effective and atmospheric hodgepodge of street-savvy r&b and jazz that was one of the better releases I've heard.  "Infinite Possibilities" is a CD that certainly lives up to the promise of its title.
I've been a big fan of The National from the get-go, but I must admit that though I love the vocals on this album, the music is just too low energy for my tastes.

As a Toriphile, I love almost everything Tori Amos has released in her career, only her project with Y Kant Tori Read and the dance remixes from some of the songs from Boys For Pele and From The Choirgirl Hotel don't do it for me. When this album came out, I really had the feeling that Tori drifted a bit to far from her "old" musical approach. Twelve covers written by men and on this album seen from the female perspective. I liked the album then but it paled in comparison with her first five albums. No original lyrics, a very dark atmosphere and Tori's voice sounds "different", compared to her other albums.On the SLT in Europe I visited her (beautiful) performance in Amsterdam, and that show was a complete thrill. After that show, I really started to listen to the album and finally found the beauty of SLG.1. New Age opens the album rather quietly, but the lyrics really form a picture about a nude woman wearing only a necklace and thinking about her future. At the end the song gets more aggresive and louder.2. '97 Bonnie & Clyde is really a frighting song and Tori succeeds in her concept of how lyrics can creep up to you.3. Strange Little Girl was the first (and only single!) released from SLG, and it was a pity that Alantic didn't promote the song more; it's catchy and could have been a hit.4. Enjoy The Silence is rather quietly with only Tori and her piano and some strings. The lyrics really shine on this song, written by Martin Gore from Depeche Mode.5. I'm Not In Love is one of the highlights on SLG. There is a dark atmosphere (created by the bass paiting and drill guitar) and this song also has something from Massive Attack. I would love to hear Tori collaborate with them. Tori's vocals are really flat and monotonous. Again, the lyrics shine because of this vocal approach.6. Rattlesnakes is another winner. A lovely melody and it sounds like Tori could have written this song. A gorgeous song.7. Time is only Tori and her piano. This song really creeped up in me with all the terrible events in the USA last year. Another beautiful song, originally written by Tom Waits.8. Neil Young's Heart Of Gold gets a complete makeover. The song is really uptempo and noisy, with Tori singing like a twin banshee over all the dissorted sounds. Love this one.9. I Don't Like Mondays is about the murders that happened at a school some years ago, but this theme is very recent because of the more recent events at schools around the world.10. The Beatles' Happiness Is A Warm Gun also gets a complete makeover and this song is the longest on SLG. A lot of voices about the murdering of John Lennon and the weapon constitution. The song seems to drag on a bit, but after almost two minutes Tori begins to sing. A very difficult song to get into, but rewarding.11. Raining Blood is my personal favourite from this album. The incredible dark lyrics from Slayer, the omnimous bass painting and Tori's solo piano make this song really creepy. Tori also shows of her incredible voice, soaring from very low to operatic high. Definetly the winner on SLG.12. The last song is Real Men, written by Joe Jackson. The lyrics are very funny. (What is a real men anyway?) and Tori sings them with lots of compassion. This song is almost the same as Jackson's version.Strange Little Girls is another winner from Tori Amos. I still prefer her original work but this strange little album is the perfect addition to Tori's catalogue.I can't wait for Scarlet's Walk!...(Release: oktober 29.)

ABC's the Lexicon of Love is the ultimate Valentine's Day album, a pop masterpiece, a thinking (and pretty funny) man's disco party. That man is lead singer Martin Fry -- a silver-tongued devil in a gold lame suit.What makes the CD so great is the juxtaposition of the glittering sheen of the music with Fry's head-spinningly witty, sarcastic, and self-aware lyrics. "More puns and allusions than Elvis Costello had managed in a career," says Spin Magazine in its Alternative Record Guide, and it's no overstatement.Here's some of the best quotes on a CD full of em:1. "If you judge a book by its cover/then you judge the look by the lover."2. "Look but don't touch in paradise/Don't let them catch you damaging the merchandise."3. "Everything is temporary, written on that stand/Looking for the girl who meets supply with demand."4. "I stuck a marriage proposal in the waste disposal."5. "No I won't be told, there's a crock of gold/at the end of the rainbow. All the pleasure and pain, sunshine and rain/might make this love grow."6. "Skip the hearts and flowers, skip the ivory towers."7. "I get sales talk from sales assistants/When all I want to do, girl, is lower your resistance."8. "When she's gone all I've got to learn/is the law of diminishing returns."9. "The 12 disciples might kiss and tell/But you can tell me much more than they can."10. "Then I say I love you, foul the situation/Hey, girl, I thought we were the right combination."Woo-hoo!At first blush, the thing that stands out is the music, specifically Trevor Horn's impeccable production. Xylophones, glockenspiels, synths, a string section, cash registers, and probably a couple of kitchen sinks, are the order of the day.The smooth production is probably what got ABC (mistakenly) lumped in with Spandau Ballet and Wang Chung back in the day, which was maybe part of the joke. Fry's bitchy Vegas-singer-with-a-brain shtick points to satire, but it says something about the quality of the writing that these songs also pack an emotional wallop.The big hits here are the Look of Love and Poison Arrow, great songs both, but for my money the overblown orchestrations on All of My Heart, the happy ca-ching of the cash registers on Date Stamp, the opening fanfare of Show Me, and (of course) the Mr. Roboto intro ("Evil!") on 4 Ever 2 Gether" make these tracks equally deserving of your time.ABC has never had an album as good as this one, but fans should check out Be Near Me, Between You and Me, Ocean Blue, How to be a Millionaire, and 15-Storey Halo (on the underrated How to be a Zillionaire CD), When Smokey Sings (the band's tribute to Smokey Robinson from the Alphabet City CD), and That Was Then, but This is Now (from the otherwise awful Beauty Stab CD).If you like this CD, I also recommend the Divine Comedy's "Casanova" and the Magnetic Fields' "69 Love Songs."
summary: If you judge a book by its cover, then you judge the look by the lover

reviewText: Indeed, the whole thing was a gimmick from the start (albeit a gimmick that succeeds), but the American series of albums have done more than anything else to bring Johnny Cash back to the forefront of popular music. With producer Rick Rubin, Cash hab elevated the art of the cover version, choosing seemingly incongruous songs and making them work.Well, mostly. The tracks on American IV: The Man Comes Around are a mixed bag, but extra points are given for the pure imagination it took to pair The Man in Black with such dissimilar artists as Fiona Apple (on Simon and Garfunkel's "Bridge Over Troubled Water") and Nick Cave (on Hank Williams' "I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry," which the Cowboy Junkies performed so beautifully on The Trinity Session) with apparently minimal regard for the success of the recording.The high points of American IV: The Man Comes Around come from varied spots. Opener "The Man Comes Around" is an original Cash composition that inspires with quotes from the Book of Revelation. Christian songs usually turn me off with their heavyhandedness, but Cash's sincerity and understatement make this one soar. In fact, he seems to have a knack for making other writers' songs sound more genuine coming from his lips than their own. During Depeche Mode's "Personal Jesus" (from their Violator album), I always felt that lead singer Dave Gahan was just paying lip service to a good idea, but Johnny Cash makes us believe that he really would be there if you needed him.And who would have thought that anyone could make a Nine Inch Nails song even more depressing? Trent Reznor's version of "Hurt" (on The Downward Spiral) would occasionally descend into whining, but Cash speaks from a long life of struggle. Benmont Tench's dramatic keyboard work underscores every emotion, assisting them through a crescendo all the way to the end, showing why Tench is our greatest modern ivory-tickler.Coming as the closer, "We'll Meet Again" carries even more emotional weight than originally, now that the two stars of the song -- Johnny and June Carter Cash -- have passed on. But their legacy remains to entertain us evermore. The fact that Rubin -- best known for producing hip-hop records of the 1980s -- allows Cash's artistry on American IV: The Man Comes Around (and its predecessors: American Recordings, Unchained, and American 3: Solitary Man) to flow unimpeded by unnecessary bells and whistles, in a time when even Cash himself didn't think that possible, shows his confidence in the simple truth of his work and his soul. All music fans owe a debt to Johnny Cash and we will all feel his absence, even indirectly.

Here's some solid evidence that we've nearly reached the end of the wagon trail. Before long, music will be pumped straight into our veins calibrated to our particular mood, taste or ambition -- and still, we will gravitate toward the dizzying spectacle, the flab of the gab.Question: Are we living in such excessive and/or inattentive times that our rock musicians have to clutter all their tunes with mixers, pedals, effects, filters, trinkets, various other whoop-de-doos, and then truck in the whole fricken high school band room? "Golden Age" is particularly unsettling, mixing Thomas Magnum's theme bassline with a sickly attempt at a "Thriller" medley. Dear lord, I thought-gasped as my earhairs recoiled at the audible tragedy that is "Family Tree," a tune that I figure would get regular airplay on an FM radio version of the Hallmark Channel.There's this point at the end of "The Last Waltz" (a film I obviously intend to trash at a later date) where all the guest musicians gather for the last hurrah. Everyone is playing along and singing, some four-wide at the mikes. And it sounds absolutely horrible. All these beautiful, distinctive voices just battering, blistering the air -- and formless clatter lathered by too many instruments vying for attention.

After the vibrant energy of their debut ("In the City"), their second album ("This is the Modern World") was something of a disappointment. One had to wonder if Paul Weller really only had one good  album in him. This third LP put that wonder firmly to rest.On "All  Mod Cons" Paul Weller finds a truly original lyrical voice, based  heavily on the English storytelling tradition well-worn by the likes of Ray  Davies, and the band kicks in with a tremendous jump in sophistication. The  love/hate of "To Be Someone" and miserable circumstance of  "Down in the Tube Station at Midnight" capture the emotion of  20-something London with a closeness, a personalness, that few achieved  before or after.  Weller would go on to even greater brilliance (e.g., the  "Sound Affects" LP), but many of his gems are here.The band's  musical muscle may have been born on their debut, but "All Mod  Cons" in the genesis of Paul Weller's songwriting genius.
summary: Third album finds an original rock 'n' roll voice

reviewText: Madonna has graced my life in some interesting ways and this is one of them. I was never a huge Madonna fan, just an undercover one, one of my best friends had this CD and she made me listen it to it during our long bus rides to our "in the boonies" middle school, and sure enough I fell in love with this album and three years later I bought it.It's a very poetic album, lush and sophisticated and it hits some grounds that only Madonna could reach.The album starts with the major hit, "Like A Prayer" I remember this song, even though I was four when it came out, it has that gospel tinged feel to it with some pretty strong lyrics, it feels like Madonna has had the holy ghost! lol"Express Yourself", my personal fave, Madonna has described as her Sly and The Family Stone tribute song. She channels some major funk with this song and the lyrics are great for singing at the top of your lungs. The Purple One (Prince) appears on "Love Song", it's pretty quirky (duh! It's Prince!) but it's lacking something, probably my least favorite song on here, still it's Prince & Madonna what more could you ask for? The remains of a broken marriage are evident on "Till Death Do Us Part" a very dancy, soft rock song that sounds a little to happy for a "breakup song" but it still gets you moving."Promise To Try", everytime I hear this song I think of my grandmother, I find this song comforting, Madonna does a wonderful job singing with only a piano backing her up, though she didn't have a wonderful, Whitney like voice she still made this song special. I love "Cherish" it's such a beautiful song, lush, poppy and happy. It has a bit of 50's doo woop flavor to it and it's a great song to blast on a sunny day. "Dear Jessie" is pretty odd for Madonna to do, it sounds psycadelic and "pink elephants and lemonade"? What famous pop singer talks about that kinda stuff? Madonna of course. A very enchanting song, the music video is cute too, it features Madonna as a cartoon fairy. On a serious note,"Oh, Father" is another special Madonna song, it's haunting with a sense of hurt and betryal. It really touches you to know what it felt like for Madonna being abused by her father. Another song that Madonna doesn't have to belt out, the words carry her through. "Keep It Together" has a jazzy/blusey feel too it with a strong message, staying together with family is important. It's not totally dancable but it livens up things. "Spanish Eyes" is another beautiful song, Madonna, like on "La Isla Bonita", samples some Latin flavors to this song. I love the litte horn and guitar parts in the song. Beautifully done Madonna. "Act of Contriction" is just a little "remix" of "Like A Prayer" with Madonna praying and then screaming at the end, don't get it much...lolThis is one of Madonna's shining moments, it hits alot of ground and proves that Madonna had something to offer, more than just frilly dresses and boy toy belts. This is one album to own and "cherish" for life. A true masterpiece.

reviewText: This was truly the first album by The Moody Blues at least the verison we've come to know. Justin Hayward replaced Denny Laine as frontman and John Lodge came on board as bassist adding two singing/composing talents to the band. Their new album was done on the sly--Decca wanted them to record a rock/orchestration version of "Picutres at an Exhibition" to test the new Decca stereo system. The Moodies agree provided they had no interference from the suits. They met with their producer Tony Clarke and stated that they wanted to do an album of original songs--a song cycle about the passing of the day with orchestrations by Peter Knight."Days of Future Passed" (named by the label NOT by the band themselves) resulted form this unusual collaboration featuring songs the band had been trying on the road using their new acquisition-a mellotron that Mike Pinder had obtained.This remaster done in 2008 with Justin Hayward has a number of merits and flaws; As with all the previous versions since the original issue of the album this features the remix tha Tony Clarke and the band prepared in the early 1970's replacing the original mix which they felt wasn't quite as good as it could have been. The master is compressed and loud compared to all previous editions but not uncomfortably so (at least for me)--be aware however that means that there isn't much dynamic range here and that peak limiting has been applied.The best sounding versions of this album are still 1) the Mobile Fidelity CD 2) the Decca first pressing on CD (the vinyl, of course is another matter entirely)with this third. The bonus tracks are the reason to pick this up (unless you want the multi-track SACD which does sound quite nice).We get (for this edition) a BBC radio session of the band performing "Don't Let Me Be Misunderstood". We also get the singles "Fly Me High"/I Really Haven't Got The Time" (the latter has been avaiable on CD before), "Love and Beauty"/"Leave This Man Alone" and the b-side "Cities" all presented in mono (none of these were ever remixed for stereo to the best of my knowledge).We also get four alternate mixes/outtakes:"Tuesday Afternoon"-an alternate mix"Dawn is a Feeling"-an alternate version"The Sun set"-an alternate version without orchestraand "Twilight Time" with an alternate vocal mix.There's an excellent, comprehensive 20 page book that covers the recording sessions.While this isn't the optimal presentation of the album in terms of the mastering, the bonus tracks make this reissue an essential addition for Moody fans AND, if you can find the two disc SACD set, snatch that up as it has a multi-track mix for 5.1Recommended but be aware of the limitations of this reissue.
summary: Seminal remaster deserves five stars for the material the mastering, not so much so--3 stars

reviewText: I don't "get" squarepusher.Having bought 'budakhan mindphone' and only liking two tracks on it, I was skeptical about buying this release.  However, after reading the rave reviews on this page, having the guy at the music store rant and rave on and on about this CD and the fact that squarepusher is touring with plaid, one of my favorite IDM/electronica artists whom I plan on seeing live, I bought this CD.Now, I love IDM/jungle/drum'n'bass/experimental type of stuff (like industrial pioneers throbbing gristle or the analog sonic assaults of add N to (X) ) and autechre is my all time favorite electronic artist but squarepusher baffles me.  Don't get me wrong, there are moments of brilliance here i.e. 'my red hot car' is an awesome track that lives up to all of the accolades on this page (and is he saying what i think he's saying?).  I love the spastic shouted vocals backed with manic drum beats on 'the exploding pscyhology'.  'i wish you could talk' is dreamy perfection and the one track I really like a lot and 'plaistow flex out' is a laidback analog close to the  disc. However the other tracks sound like random electric screeches, squelches and jarring beats haphazardly thrown together.  I could do the same thing on my music generator for playstation ... and I have.I guess to really appreciate squarepusher you must be under the influence of some mind altering consciousness raising hallucinogenic ... whatever.  I gave this CD three stars because it's average.  Not really bad but not really good. For me (and those are the key words here:  FOR ME) I like music that is challenging but I couldn't find the challenge here.  Perhaps as I get older my music tastes are slowly changing or perhaps the state of electronic music is becoming so stagnant and tired that now the challenge is to find the music amongst the chaos and debris (check out autechre's new release ... yeesch).  I think I'll stick to the softer, more organic sounds of plaid.Buy 'go plastic' only if you're a tried and true squarepusher fan as all of the reviewers on this page are. I'm just trying to add a little diversity to the reviews so those out there who haven't heard squarepusher before can get both sides of the coin before making a decision.

First, I DO NOT THINK THIS ALBUM DESERVES 1 STAR, I AM ONLY GIVING IT 1 TO BALANCE OUT ALL OF THE LIARS THAT ARE GIVING THIS 5 STARS!I'm going to do something few others are, I'm giving an honest criticism of "Hypnotize" because there are few of those here. I say it deserves 3 1/2 stars, but that would still keep it up really high so I knocked it down to one."Hypnotize" is by far inferior to SOAD's other albums (I'm including "Steal This Album!", by the way). Now, many people complain and say that it and "Mezmerize" are a double-album and should have been sold as one. Looking at how long each one is:"Mezmerize" 36:17"Hypnotize" 39:41other SOAD albums are about 42:00 minutes longBecause of this, I am considering these two as separate albums. Here's a song by song for "Hypnotize"1.Attack: Gets kinda annoying and repetitive, but it is one of the better ones.  7/102.Dreaming: I forgot what this one sounds like, so it obviously isn't very impressive. 0/103.Kill Rock N' Roll: Everyone complains about Daron's vocals on the majority of "Mezmerize" and "Hypnotize", but I feel that his voice sometimes works ok with their songs. Granted, Serj is much much better, but there's really nothing we can do but complain about it. Daron's voice works ok here and I felt this was a stand-out track.  9/104.Hypnotize: Pretty impressive. I didn't immediately like it like some people but it's grown on me after a couple of listens. 9/105.Stealing Society: Decent at best. 5/106.Tentative: This song's a mess IMO. Here would be good place to point out Daron's bad singing. 3/107.U-Fig: I like Serj's screaming parts, but this is one of SOAD's worst choruses ever. 4/108.Holy Mountains: This song takes for ever to get fast. The fast part is damn good, but the slow part is a big hurdle IMO. 6/109.Vicinity of Obscenity: A new candidate for SOAD's most nonsensical crazy song! This is fun SOAD having fun with their songs like they used to! This one is filled with many silly sexual innuendos and Serj screaming the craziest line ever, "BANANA BANANA BANANA TERRACOTTA BANANA TERRACOTTA TERRACOTTA PIE!!!" Love this song and all it's craziness! 10/1010.She's Like Heroin: Took me a couple of listens to like this one; it's another one where Daron sings a lot. Pretty catchy. 8/1011.Lonely Day: No no no, this is so over-rated. If you loved Aerials from "Toxicity," you'll love this one (I didn't). 1/1012.Soldier Song: The best song on the album. Not much else to say really. 10/10

Sarah McLachlan did it again, without really doing something.This record contained all the tracks she recorded for soundtracks, other artists' records or performed during special live performances since the first Rarities, B-Sides and Other Stuff (1996).It's gotta be said that this is a great album with many highlights. Especially when you consider that most artists don't even release rarities records at all.It starts out with 'Ordinary Miracle' from the movie Charlotte's Web. And this is not the only soundtrack recording represented on this compilation. Sarah's version of The Beatles' 'Blackbird' from I am Sam is beautiful and stays very true to the original and 'When She Loved Me' (Toy Story 2) is very touching. The absolute highight of this cd for me is 'The Rainbow Connection' (from The Muppets), this song goes straight to the bottom of my heart everytime I listen to it.There are also some very interesting duets on this album. 'Just Like Me' with DMC or 'Time after Time' with Cyndi Lauper are very nice additions to Sarah's catalogue. 'Angel' (live) with the amazing Emmmylou Harris and 'Pills' met The perishers are simply wonderful. But the outstanding duet has got to be 'Don't Let Go' with Bryan Adams (from the animation movie Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron).'Prayer of St. Francis' and 'Unchained Melody' (in a totally onrecognizable version!) are two very interesting recordings and show how many different sides and styles there are to miss McLachlan.And just like on Rarities, B-Sides and Other Stuff volume 1, there's another Joni Mitchell cover on this volume; 'River'.Yes she recorded River for her 2006 season album Wintersong, but the nice thing is that this version is a different one.I'm a big Joni Mitchell fan myself and don't really like it when people cover her songs, but Sarah's versions of Blue and River make me wish she will one day release a record full of Joni Mitchell covers.One can always dream, right?And dream is something this cd will surely let you do. The voice, the words, the music... Sarah goes straight into the heart of her listeners.If you don't already have this cd, get it now. You won't regret it!
summary: A great gift to the fans

reviewText: With a guitar riff that traces straight back to Heartbreaker by the Rolling Stones, Nikka Costa gets out to a fast start on the first track, Like A Feather, and then shows her range as a songwriter/vocalist throughout this excellent CD.She reaches deep into her soul for real interpretations of R&B;, blues and gospel, with a variety of mixes in the production. Though I am not a fan of layered vocals, Costa is able to do an admirable job because of her range of expressions in delivering the parts.She sings it like she's lived it in Push & Pull and Corners Of My Mind, with Tug Of War and the title track compelling enough to make you stop what you're doing and listen intently.A dynamite CD likes this one means that the artist has refined the material over a period of years and may struggle to reach the same peak or is starting one of those magical runs of quality releases. Costa has set a solid foundation and Everybody Got Their Something will stand on its own no matter what the future brings.

In the fall of 1979, I had just turned 11 years old, and had not only just been given one record for my birthday, but also had received money which I then used to buy the first vinyl LP I ever bought.  (I had only seriously begun to pay attention to the top 40 that spring, and had only bought 45s up to that point; I owned a grand total of 3 LPs, all of which had been given to me as presents, and maybe a couple of cassettes.)  It was the very beginning of my long history (27 years now) as a collector.That first LP was ELO's Discovery.  All that spring and summer, I had been hearing the various singles from that album ("Shine a Little Love," "Confusion," "Don't Bring Me Down" and "Last Train to London") on my favourite radio station of the time (WIGY 105.9 FM, in the Bath/Brunswick area in Maine), and so when the opportunity came to purchase this record, I jumped on it.  Needless to say, I knew nothing at the time of Jeff Lynne's Beatles influence, although I was a huge Beatles fan--still am to this day; they will always be the Gods of Rock 'n' Roll in my heart--and it probably would have raised his stock considerably for me.  In the months to come, I would buy copies of ELO's Greatest Hits and Out of the Blue (mine being a cutout copy on United Artists that cost me just $4.99; this was a bargain for a double LP in early 1980).  In the meantime, I played Discovery as often as I could, and I loved it all.Fast forward to 2001.  Sony made their first attempts at catalogue remasters of ELO's albums; along with the classic Eldorado, their three albums from 1979-83 (Discovery, Time, and Secret Messages) were also remastered and reissued.  Wishing to rediscover a favourite of my 'tweenie years, I bought the remastered Discovery on CD.  22 years on, I realised that Thomas Wolfe was right--you can't go home again...and even if you could, nothing would be the same.  Your tastes change, and mine certainly had.  Here's my adult synopsis of Discovery:Only 3 of this album's 9 tracks are truly essential--"Shine a Little Love," "Last Train to London" (which is *not* instrumental, by the way--there are vocals and lyrics) and "Don't Bring Me Down" all keep things moving along nicely, even if "Shine a Little Love's" bridge rings a bit twee these days.  Three more tracks--"Confusion," "The Diary of Horace Wimp" and "On the Run"--are entertaining and move alone nicely, but I wouldn't rate them among this album's best tracks, just a little less painful than the other 3--"Need Her Love," "Midnight Blue" and "Wishing."  Of the final 3, "Need Her Love" is embarrassing in its twinkly saccharine-ness, which include unbearable naive-sounding lyrics and sweet synth arrangements (sweet enough to raise your blood sugar to dangerous levels!), thus making it the worst offender of the lot.  The other two are saccharine throwaways, just bad enough to be memorable.  What was forgivable at 11 isn't so at 37, when your perceptions have sharpened and your inner self hardened a bit against the depredations of the world.On the whole, this was truly the beginning of the end for ELO.  They had pared themselves down to just a quartet--Jeff Lynne, Bev Bevan, Richard Tandy and Kelly Groucutt--having dropped the string players after Out of the Blue (on which you can, of course, see trouble just over the horizon).  It makes some sense that Bev would sub on the drums for Black Sabbath on a couple of tours a few years later; perhaps even he needed some meat after this bit of cotton candy.

What can be said about this album other than "WOW!" From the first test notes of harmonica on "Five Days In May" to the piano outro of "Tell Me Your Dream" and everything in between this album is terrific! There are a lot of musical surprises, for starters: Greg Keelor's guitar solo at the end of "Five Days...", James Gray and Kim Deschamps trading solos on "Cynthia", special guest appearances by Sarah McLachlan (sp?) on several songs and the a capella section of "Know Where You Go/Tell Me Your Dream". Jim Cuddy also masterfully croons Rodney Crowell's "Til I Can Gain Control Again". I'd say if any Blue Rodeo album were a must-have, it's this one.
summary: Blue Rodeo is really on their game!

reviewText: Meteora is my second favourite right after the Hybrid Theory. As their debut this cd offers all great songs from the beginning to the end. Foreword is just an introduction, it's not a real song, it's just a mixture of sounds. My least favourite song on this album would be Session, which is like Cure For The Itch from the first cd, it's an instrumental song with sampling from Mr. Hahn. Don't Stay is a great song, with quite some rap in the chours, and Chester and Mike make it sound really good. Somewhere I Belong has an easier beginning with great chours and a bit less of rap throughout the whole song. Hit The Floor is a song with much more rap. Nobody's Listening is almost rap throughout the song, with interesting beginning and some flute samples in it. Figure.09 is a song with just a little rap, with great chours. There is much more rap in Lying From You. So, now to my favourites from this album. Beginning with Breaking The Habit. It is an easy song, with really catchy chours, but not much rap in it. From the Inside is also an eays, slower song right till the end, and then some hard rock makes it sound so good. Faint has one of the best beginnings, while the rest of the song is typical Linkin park song. Easier To Run is my second favourite song. It's a slower song, with a bit more heavier chours. There's also quite some rap in it. And then there's Numb. My favourite Linkin Park song probably (it's hard to decide). This one is also a bit easier in some parts and really hard-rocking in other parts. Every time I hear the piano/keyboard beginning I go crazy.So, this is Meteora, the follow up to Hybrid Theory. Although I like Hybrid Theory a bit more, that doesn'z mean that this one is any worse. They're both great.

A bit o' Kinks, Clash, and Costello. Not much new here at all, but it is still a fun album to listen to. This is a definite tribute to Joe Strummer and the Clash's influence all these years later. In fact, there are times when the two sounds are indistinguishable. I am not one to knock a band for deriving their sound from other bands, most would find it necessary. Unfortunately, the Libertines aren't bringing anything new to compliment their borrowed sounds, so the album is but an echoing of past brilliance. If you are looking for a new sound, this isn't it, but nevertheless it is still good for a listen...

Man Ras kass is really an underrated mc. He had a little hype from 1994 up till 98 with his Soul on ice sampler, some classic freestyles with other mcs, & of course this album & his second album Rassassination. Unfortunatley his hype pretty much faded out in the 2000s due to his lable priority screwing him over & other mishaps. Soul On Ice is truely a gem of lyrical finesse. this was ras at his best here great punchlines & metaphors alot revolving around religion & conspiracies. Ras kass is also a pretty controversial mc so if you're sensitive about certain topics I might not suggest this album for you in that regard LOL."On Earth as it is", ras kass uses metaphors of bibical themes to describe the state of hip hop & how hes gonna take the game over very creative. On "Anything Goes" he talks about how not only people living in the urban communities would do anything for money but also corrupt goverment officials as well. "Marinatin" is a smooth laid back track where ras kicks raps about hanging out with his homies at a house party & getting with chicks. Now my favorite track here is "Reelishymn" the beat for this song has a mellow vibe to it. Here ras raps about the pitfalls or making it in hip hop & life in general. he raps some of my fav lines here "I paid my dues till I paid due nots I never will let what you say affect the outcome see mommy always told be opinions are like buttholes cause everybody got 1 but you couldn't tell ish if I stepped in it once I enter psychosis paranormal focus I perplex brothas & sistas I play this rap ish closer than giletts against the neck & juglar vein" On "Nature Of The Threat" ras gets pretty controversial on here talking about what he believes to be true of christianity, jesus, gays, slavery, europeons, & mythology. This is probaly one of the most if not most controverial song in hip hop. ras got a buzz just off the hype of this song. I don't agree with much of what hes saying here but I can appreciate his take on things. "Etc' is a nice braggadocious battle rap track sampling buckshot's voice from black moon for the hook. On "Sonset" ras kass defends the west coast against naysayers (east coast) while maintaining hes got respect for all regions of hip hop. On "Drama" coolio joins ras in a song about how men play females to get laid & how women play men to get money. My second favorite track here is "The Evil That Men Do" this is a nice storytelling track about ras growing up having it rough, getting locked up, his grandfather beating on his grandmother, his uncle dying, having a dead beat father, etc. The we have "If/Then" where ras raps more braggadocius topics but for some strange reason the hook consists of females bashing men LOL. good nontheless Then we have the "Miami Life" where ras raps metaphorically about him wanting his life being a paradise like Miami. I would also like to point out that this track was featured on the soundtrack to the 1996 movie the Substitute. On The title track "Soul On Ice" ras gets introspective once again & theres also a diamond d remix of this song not found on the album which is just as dope but the rhymes & beat are different. Finally the album Closes with yet another controversial song "Ordo Abchao Order Out of Chaos" ras raps about the forever controverisal conspiracy about the whole illuminati/masons topic. This is a classic album unforgettable. If you're not too sensitive pick this album up & witness soul on ice!

Okay, to start off, "Snakes and Arrows" is not the return to form that old fans still pining for the sequel to "2112" have been wanting for decades. That Rush is long gone. And that is not a bad thing. Rush has never been a band that does the same thing over and over, or a band that wants to revisit the past, so why should they start now?On to the new record...it is a grower. It has some of the best melodies they have written in a long time, Neil Peart's lyrics are still as potent as ever, and, to the delight of this listener, there is more acoustic guitar than on any other Rush album to date.From a playing standpoint, this is Alex Lifeson's record. No, he does not dazzle us with solos left and right, although there are a few nice ones, but his playing throughout the record is top-notch. Some have called him the weak link in the band before, usually because of how prolific his bandmates are, but he owns "Snakes and Arrows." Geddy Lee and Neil Peart do their usual great job, too, don't get me wrong, but Lifeson's star shines the brightest.As I mentioned earlier, this album is a grower. The more you listen to it, the more those melodies get in your head, and before you know it, you can't get the cd out of your disc player. Every song is at least good, and quite a few range from very good to great, especially "Armor and Sword," "Bravest Face," "The Way the Wind Blows," "The Main Monkey Business," and "Malignant Narcissism."Is is their best album ever? No. Is it their best album since "Moving Pictures," their classic from 1981? No. But it is a very good record, and for a bunch of guys in their 50's, who have been together for over 30 years, it is awfully impressive.

reviewText: A little over a year after the success of the classic "What's Going On" album and the successful follow up album, "Trouble Man", Marvin Gaye decided to take a different spin: instead of the message songs that are in "What's Going On" and to a lesser extent in "Trouble Man", Gaye decided to just make a sexually explicit (for 1973) album, and he acutally pulled it off in great style! The ablum shows off Gaye's doo-wop beginnings when he began as a doo-wop singer with the Moonglows, especially with the song, "Come Get to This".The Expanded Edition also shows the different cuts to the songs for the completed album, plus some bonus songs like "The World is Rated X" and "Where Are We Going". Worthwhile purchase.
summary: Changing directons was Marvin Gaye's strength in his music...

reviewText: I bought this album right around when it came out, and I can still listen to it.  In fact, it's still awesome, one of the better debuts in rock and roll history.  The energy and dynamism are in there in abundance.  The fact that these guys have always been sincere in their politics and music helps immensely.  Too often many bands are posers politically, but these guys, whether you agree or disagree with their politics, really believe in what they're singing.  Despite the overly political nature of some of the lyrics, they haven't dated.  And the music is intense and totally kicks.  This is a great album, filled with great riffs and song.  I really like Bombtrack, Killing in the Name, Bullet in the Head, and Freedom.Rage Against the Machine only made 3 studio albums, a cover album, and some live albums, but they were one of the most unique rock bands from the 90's.  They weren't grunge; they weren't alternative rock.  They were just Rage Against the Machine.  They broke up for a time, but are back together and I hope a new studio album will be on its way soon.
summary: Still rocks after all these years...

reviewText: Forget Donald Trump; Donald Fagen, with his wry voice and uncanny ability to combine farcical metaphor with jazz inflected pop melodies, is the towering " Donald". Everything Mr. Fagen touches turns to gold. The only thing preventing this CD from entering perfection range is a little camp, but that never hurt anyone, right?" Morph the Cat". What does that mean? Is it an imaginary blanket of protection hovering over New York, reassuring everyone after the jolt of 9/11? Does it mean that "protection" can morph into strange alter egos, created by zealots? The rest of the CD would bear this explanation out.After the title track, Fagen briefly turns his attention to one of his offbeat character studies in " H Gang". Great beat, sounds like Steely Dan. " What I Do" is a fantastic imagined conversation between Fagen and legendary Ray Charles, presumably held at the beginning of young Don's adulthood. " Brite Nightgown", probably the best song ever about cheating death , is amazing, save a marathon closing." Mona" is another wandering spirit fabled to be depressed, to say the least. " Mary Shut the Garden Door" is a stab at the administration. They snuck in.... lock yourself away.This is a living legend performer who never runs out of fresh material. Shame on this year's Grammy panel for so little recognition!
summary: The true " Donald" continues the cycle.

Alice Cooper struck a universal chord with the title track from their fifth album and the group-penned anthem became the only Top 10 hit of their career--"School's Out" peaked at No. 7 in the summer of 1972.  [Note:  It was also a No. 1 hit for three weeks in the U.K.]While "School's Out" is the focal point (and only hit) of this apparent concept album, there are other classic Alice Cooper songs here, including the rockin' "Luney  Tune" (co-written by bassist  Dennis Dunaway and Alice Cooper), the snarling "Public Animal #9, and the jazzy "Blue Turk" (the latter two co-written by guitarist Michael Bruce and Alice Cooper). Two other strong tracks are the ones inspired by the music from WEST SIDE STORY:  "Gutter Cat vs. the Jets" and "Grande Finale." [It should be noted that Leonard Bernstein is given co-writer status on both of these tracks.]In addition to the terrific music, the original LP was housed in an album jacket that could fold into an actual school desk--and the record was not in a paper sleeve but a pair of pink women's underwear!  VERY HIGHLY RECOMMENDED

reviewText: Después de 3 excelentes discos (First-Horizontal-Idea, sin considerar los 2 australianos), los Bee Gees alcanzan su madurez y su punto máximo de creatividad en 1969 con Odessa. En medio de problemas internos que terminarían luego en una breve separación, los hermanos Gibb, Barry con 22 años y Maurice y Robin con sólo 19, entregan en este disco grandes temas con una densidad y orquestación pocas veces escuchadas antes. Pese a ser un álbum doble alcanzó el puesto 20 en EE.UU. y el 10 en Inglaterra, transformándose en el último éxito de su etapa "clásica" (1969-1973). Entre las canciones la más destacada es Odessa, que con siete minutos y medio demostró que ellos también podían hacer largos y elaborados temas sin caer en la monotonía. Resaltan tambien Melody Fair, I Laugh In Your Face y Never Say Never Again, aunque en realidad casi todas las canciones aportan, tal vez los 3 temas instrumentales sean excesivos, pero al mismo tiempo le dan a Odessa ese toque monumental que el tiempo se ha encargado de reforzar. No sólo el mejor trabajo de los Bee Gees, sino uno de los mejores del Pop de los años 60's.
summary: La obra maestra de los Bee Gees, y es 1969.

Take the Doves dense electronic-influenced rock and blend it with Coldplay's heart-wringing balladry. That's what Elbow sounds like. Vocalist Guy Garvey sounds a lot like Coldplay's Chris Martin. They share a hushed and breathy voice that carries you away, recalling the likes of Morrisey and Peter Gabriel. Garvey affects a mantra-like tone on "Anyday Now" pulling you into a world that's dark and yet soothing at the same time. "Little Beast" is gloomy but even more sinister; these guys must certainly have a few Massive Attack cd's in their collection. Its not a totally sombre affair and like many English bands they can overdo it with the tender sentiment. "Red" is a bit too sappy, though it is spurred along by a sprightly piano and a nice shuffling beat. Garvey comes across as a lonely troubadour feeling sorry for himself. You then wonder if he might be the happiest man alive. This album is hushed and private on one hand and soars with optimism on the other. The Doves and Coldplay have broken through lately with this brand of teary sensitive rock. You can count on Elbow to follow with what I think is one of the albums of the year.
summary: Elbow delivers a knockout first album

reviewText: Say what you will about Tori Amos, her second album bent music in a new direction. Once "Little Earthquakes" opened a whole new audience of sensitive women who liked their music heavy on mystic and or religious imagery, devoid of bombast and just speaking to a crowd that was being ignored, Tori Amos found that crack and made it her very own Teutonic plate. There's good reason for that. "Little Earthquakes" sounded like little else out at the time (bear in mind, this was the year of Nirvana) and. other than Kate Bush, no other woman was bending traditional pop structures at will.It makes Tori an anomaly. "Silent All These Years" missed the top 40, bit she's hit the top 5 albums constantly. She rarely uses electric guitars, "Crucify" starts the album with piano and drums only. Tori;s voice was often the most electrifying here, breaking from whispers and panting into tortured wails, then back again, like "Precious Things." (Which contains one of the most brutal put-downs of all-time in "So you can make me cum? That doesn't make you Jesus.") The painful alliance between womanhood and Christendom is a reoccurring theme on "Little Earthquakes," and Tori's "faeries" clung to it because they all understood where a riposte like "what's so special about really deep thoughts? You better hope I bleed real soon, how's that thought for you?" could spring from.It's why "Little Earthquakes" meets one of my main standards of 5 star/classic albums. Tori successfully leapt from Glam/Goth Gal on "Y Kant Tori Read" to a knowing singer/songwriter the likes we hadn't seen since Carole King. She has artistically outgrown that label a long time back, but "Little Earthquakes" made young adult women realize that there was a place for them in music that didn't have to be Nine Inch Nails or Phil Collins.

It's been a very long wait for an mlps version of an album that brings back so many nice memories for me when I was a kid just getting into music which has become over the years an indispensible part of my life in various forms.  As far as smooth pop goes very few albums come close to this with every track being just an outstanding example of great songcrafting.  In retrospect, looking at the credits on this album I shouldn't be surprised when you see the Hall of Fame talent that was involved on the various tracks:1. Say You'll Be Mine: great way to start the album with Nicolette Larson on background vocals and the great Jay Graydon on solo guitar (Jay also plays a great solo on my favourite Steely Dan track, "Peg")2. I Really Don't Know Anymore: another excellent track with Michael McDonald on background vocals and the brilliant Larry Carlton on solo guitar (Larry also plays excellent solos on my other favourite Steely Dan track, "Kid Charlemagne")3. Spinning4. Never Be the Same: fantastic solo by Jay Graydon again.5. Poor Shirley6. Ride Like the Wind: great way to start Side B of the album for those old enough like me to remember the good ole vinyl days when music sounded great before the gradual decline into cassette and cd and now the ultimate low of super-compressed MP3s; Michael McDonald again does a fabulous stint on background vocals.7. The Light Is On: Larry Carlton on solo guitar with Eagles' alumn Don Henley and many Eagles' tracks co-writer J.D. Souther on background vocals!8. Sailing: the magnum opus which still sends thrills up my spine all these years later9. Minstrel Gigolo: for knowledgeable guitarists, Eric Johnson on solo guitar!10. Mary Ann: the bonus track which is uninspiring filler and you can see why it was left off the original release in the first place but may interest diehard fans.There are few albums that stand the test of time as well as this one does for me and although this mini-lp replica sleeve (mlps) version isn't the best designed and assembled that I've ever seen I have seen a lot worse and the inner sleeve though is very nicely done with a 12-page booklet containing all the lyrics in both English and Japanese.  The all important sound quality does not disappoint and is as good as one can expect from an SHM CD.  Thankfully I recall this album already sounding very good on the old cassette that I had when I first heard it standing as a testament to the great production job done by Michael Omartian in the first place.Highly recommended for fans of mellow pop of the highest quality!
summary: Finally!  After Such A Long Wait Christopher Cross' Great Album Is Now in MLPS Format!

reviewText: I have listened to and collected recordings for 40 years, and currently have over 3,000 cd's,lp's, and tapes.  I love all kinds of music,and grew up loving the music of George Jones, Ray Price, Buck Owens, Merle Haggard and others.  IMHO, Dwight is the finest country artist/singer/songwriter on the scene today.Of course, he's got the honky-tonk sound down to a science.  But,as other reviewers point out, he covers an amazing range of traditional styles: rockabilly, "old fashioned", Flatt & Scruggs-style (Down the Road), Ballads, and even R&B (If There was a Way).  His cover of Queen's (Freddie Mercury, Brian May), "Crazy Little Thing Called Love" is as rocking as the original.  I will offer another humble opinion that "The Heart that You Own" is the greatest country song written in the past thirty years, and possibly second only to "Mr. Fool", recorded by George Jones in the 50's.  Guitarist/Producer Pete Anderson is also one of the finest string-bending, chicken-picking, volume-swelling, steel-imitating Telecaster players around, along the lines of Danny Gatton and Roy Buchanan."This Time" is as fine a recording as any of his others--very fresh and energetic.  If you really love any kind of country/rockabilly/honky-tonk/shuffle-type of music, you can't get any better than Yoakam, Anderson & Co.

The Brown Album changed techno music forever. Besides the first and last tracks which involve weird samples of people talking, it is a masterpiece. "Planet of the Shapes" is a wonderful 10 minute journey. "Lush 3-1" is a danceable, catchy, but serenely beautiful tune that is the first track to catch in your mind. "IMPACT (The Earth is Burning)" is another 10 minute epic, but it is catchier and more danceable. The last 2 real tracks are my favorite. The piano/string on "Monday" is woven together seamlessly. It is more complicated than any pianist could attempt, and very beautiful. "Halcyon + On + On" is arguably the greatest song to come out of electronica. It is long, it is beautiful, it gives off emotion. The haunting voice stays throughout, and the beat enhances the effect. I didn't like it at first because the intro was too long, but now that I do like it, my feeling about its beauty will never age or wither. An album that is in a class with few others.

Petra's "Jekyll and Hyde" is a major return to form for the long-running Christian rock band. This is Petra in a flat-out, no-holds-barred, in-your-face hard rock outing."Jekyll and Hyde" was produced by Peter Furler of The Newsboys who also plays drums on the album (filling in for the recently departed Louie Weaver). The band line-up is reduced down to a duo consisting of long-time vocalist John Schlitt and the return of Petra founder/guitarist Bob Hartman. The album is a solid collection of heavy guitar-based tunes which are short, to-the-point and downright catchy. As a whole the "Jekyll and Hyde" CD is similar to bands such as Aerosmith and Kiss. All of the tracks are extremely upbeat with the only 'softer' piece being the worshipful "Till Everything I Do".The only downside to this album is its length. With so many CDs running close to an hour or more these days, Petra does an about-face with only 31-minutes of music. The upside to this is that it's quality over quantity. Every song on "Jekyll and Hyde" is great and this will be a CD which you'll be playing over and over again."Jekyll and Hyde" isn't just another Petra album. It's an event! Petra hasn't rocked this hard in many years. Bob Hartman displays some of his best killer guitar riffs while John Schlitt sounds better than when he first joined the band in 1986. Add Peter Furler's stellar production to this and you've got a classic album! Check it out and Rock your troubles away!
summary: Petra Returns With Their Hardest Rocking Album Yet!!!

reviewText: Weezer was formed in 1992. Two years later after Kurt Cobain died, Ric Ocasek produced their first record. Once people saw Rivers Cuomo every geek in the world wanted to play guitar. More tours with No Doubt. Cuomo went back to Harvard. Soon their new album was released with the anthem "Hash Pipe." Who couldn't relate to that? What else does one do at Harvard? More band members came and went. There are about one hundred members of Weezer. The fourth album was made and The Muppets joined the band for a while too. Tears for Fears seems to have aged more gracefully than most other 1980s music, in part because the band relied more on real instruments than synthesized noise, in part because they really sang. Fifteen years after its release, Songs from the Big Chair remains the essential album from this duo.Beyond having two huge hits, which sound great even now, the album has a consistency and continuity. 'Head over Heels', for example, just fits best when it is bookended by the live recording of 'Broken'. 'Working Hour' is a fantastic vocal and instrumental romp -- why it never made it to the 'Greatest Hits' set is beyond me. While it might be stretch, I have always thought of 'Big Chair' as one of few 1980s concept albums. Every track is distinctive, but you cannot help but listen to the whole thing through.
summary: The essential Tears For Fears album
