Although hard to believe that this was released way back in 1976, they were unquestionably (with the possible exception of "Funkadelic" & "Sly & the Family Stone") the most progressive and damn right Funkiest Funk band of the 70's. Pushing the envelope further than anyone else in the genre of psychedelic funk. "Mothership Connection (star Child)", beautifully gets into gear with Bootsy Collins exceptionally freewheeling Bass Guitar, with an arrangement of Horns, Pianos, Handclaps & great dollops of spoken Word making this as far removed from traditional funk as humanly possible. But the real prize in an otherwise flawless album (bearing in mind it's only 7 tracks), is the magnificence of "Give Up the Funk (Tear the Roof off the Sucker)", which is was so influential that `Grandmaster Flash' would take what was started here, & include it for his 2002 seminal release "The Official Adventures of Grandmaster Flash".  I've only very recently started picking up Parliament (& Funkadelic), but I was wisely informed to start with this album first, and continue collecting the other albums from here, and that turned out to be the best piece of advice I've been recently given.
summary: Interested in Parliament.???.....(start your enquries here)

reviewText: 3.5 starsOver the years the songwriting themes of Death Cab for Cutie's main man Ben Gibbard have majored on issues of longing, forlornness and melancholy. As such his work has been plundered by those teenage rites of passage shows and films, which tend to dwell on the terrible torment of adolescent angst such as the OC or Garden State. A shame really since Gibbard has written some superb songs not least the monumental "Transatlanticism", the hugely atmospheric "Passenger seat" and the genius pop of "Such great heights" (with the Postal Service and brilliantly covered by Sam Beam).Death Cabs last album "Narrow Stairs" was a massive hit in the US although with the exception of a couple of songs like "Grapevine Fires" not a personal favourite. nor for that matter did it stand the test of time against their earlier releases. "Codes and Keys" is their 7th album and very different proposition to its predecessor's guitar heavy approach. Like recent albums by Radiohead and the Wild Beasts the instrument of choice here is the keyboard and the emphasis is back on songwriting as opposed to showy instrumentation. As a result Codes and Keys is a good album, which will be greatly enjoyed by old fans and new music lovers alike not least the five standout songs here.* "Home is a fire" - is an excellent bass heavy opener that loops and builds to a fine pop song with a trademark vocal by Gibbard* "Door unlocked and open" - demonstrates that the band has been listening quite a bit to the Cure with the song sounding like a more melodic update of "A Forest" on the most guitar flavoured track on the album* "Unobstructed views" - is a gorgeous and flowing synth ballad and a paean to lost love.* "Under the sycamore" - has one of those yearning melodies that are a Gibbard speciality and is such a strong song it could have happily fitted on "Plans" or "Transatlanticism".* "St Peters Cathedral" - is by a long stretch the best song on the album and sounds like a potential classic. It is a hugely entrancing song that builds from a slow echoing piano note to a wall of soundThe album however is let down by some real weaknesses. For example the single "You are a tourist" does overplay the lyric to the point of tedium with its constant refrain of "having dreams about you" which lasts until the last minute when it changes into an entirely different song. Similarly whatever the band were seeking in the track "Potable television" is hard to define since it starts off like Richard Clayderman and has possibly the silliest lyrics heard in an album this year. Equally the jury's out on "Some boys" which seems to try a bit to hard to different and ends up as indifferent. But let us end on a positive note since clearly marriage to the actress and singer Ms Zooey Deschanel has put a spring in Gibbard's step and no one would have ever taken a bet on him starting a song with the words "Life is sweet" in the very upbeat "Stay young and go dancing" an unlikely Death Cab title. It concludes "Codes and Keys" an album which is by no means a classic but contains enough high points to seek it out and invest listening time in an a work which will probably grow over time.
summary: Death Cab for Cutie - Seek to unlock a new direction.

reviewText: Stevie Wonder was and continues to be a once every few generations kind of genius!!!There's not enough words in the English language to appropriately articulate how GREAT he is as a musician and how OUT OF THIS WORLD "Songs in the Key of Life" remains.--Best R&B; album ever made in history--Best soul album ever made in history--Best double-disc album set ever made in history***Strong candidate for one of the greatest albums ever made by any artist, anywhere, anytime and any place in historyIf you're black, white, Puerto Rican or Asian, young, old, straight, gay, religious, secular, a music lover, music hater or just plain music deprived, this album's for you!!!!Can't say enough.Deserving of 10 stars!!!I'd put this album up there against any of the best of Michael Jackson, James Brown, Whitney Houston, the Beatles, the Temptations, Prince, Little Richard, Louis Armstrong, MaDonna, Boyz II Men, Elvis, U2, the Rolling Stones, Jimmy Hendrix, Aretha Franklin, Bob Marley or ANY of the other all-time greats I might've missed.Even better than "Innervisions" for those Stevie Wonder diehards.

reviewText: I kid you not, this is pure country.  But Emmylou has always had a huge non-country audience.  There is something in her voice, in her delivery, that one has to like, regardless of genre.I was a D.J. (among other duties) at a small radio station in Cottonwood, Arizona, when Emmy Lou came out with this, her first album.  That was over 30 years ago, and this still stands as a classic.Anybody listening to this album will have his or her favorites.  These are mine:"Too Far Gone", a soulful ballad in which emmylou's plaintive voice expresses a beauty, an integrity, which is still her trade mark."If I Could Only Win Your Love", which I believe was her first hit.  Whatever, it sounds just as fresh to me as it did thirty-something years ago."Boulder To Birmingham" is another enduring favorite, expressing Emmy Lou's versatility and ability to evoke emotion.It takes a truly great singer to take songs associated with other singers and present us with a worthwhile interpretation comparable in quality to the original.  Merle Haggard's "Bottle Let Me Down" could've been written for her, her version being uniquely styled.Dolly Parton's "Coat of Many Colors" again illustrate her superb way of handling another's song.  The current term of course is "cover", but in the case of these two songs, the term just doesn't seem to fit, IMHO.I will quickly mention one cut which I consider a lesser one, but well worth noting, Lennon/McCartney's "For No One".  Even at the very beginning, she showed off the diversity, the range of her talents.This debut album is brought to a close with the rousing, yet poignant "Queen of the Silver Dollar", written by the great Shel Silverstein.  Listen carefully, very carefully, and you will catch Linda Ronstadt's voice in the background.All in all, as I said from the beginning, this is a classic album which is pure country, yet with an appeal to all musical tastes.
summary: A classic for both country & non-country fans

reviewText: "American VI: Ain't no grave" is the final in the Rick Rubin produced "American" series of CDs by Johnny Cash. Like its predecessors, it comprises pared-back covers, as well as (in this case), an original (and purpotedly final) composition by Cash."I Corinthians 15:55" is the lone original with lyrics looking at his mortality and the hope of seeing his Redeemer. Mortality, love, redemption, and spirituality colour the 10 songs on this beautiful CD, and I must say, for what supposedly comprises his last recordings, he sounds a lot stronger than he did on songs like "If you could read my mind" (from "American V"), or "Bridge over troubled water" ("American IV), where he was slightly reedy."Redemption day" (a Sheryl Crow composition) is a beautiful acoustic ballad that wouldn't sound out of place in a Western movie, with Cash singing about the "train that's heading straight to heaven's gate", while "For the good times" (a Kris Kristofferson composition) is a heartbreaking farewell to his lover as they part and he reminisces the good times they shared."Can't help but wonder where I'm bound" touches on his journey on earth and his curiousity over his final destination. The solemn "Last night I had the strangest dream" finds him dreaming of a world with no more war, against a richer musical backdrop than the other songs.Highlight, in my opinion" is "Ain't no grave", his fearless and defiant proclamation that no grave can hold his body down when he hears the trumpet sound, and his looking forward to meeting Jesus, his mother and father. Chiming bell sounds, Soft guitars and banjo set to shuffling shackled-footstep sounds which provide the gentle beat to this stirring song.As with the previous discs in the series, Cash inhabits and makes each song his own. It is obvious he knew his sojourn here was done and the songs reflect his strong belief of a life well lived and being reunited with loved ones on the other side of eternity. A masterpiece!

Continued Silence EP was Imagine Dragon's first album, which only had 6 songs on it, since it was probably designed as a trailer for this album. Night Visions is ID's first real album, and I like it. We mainly got it for Radioactive, but every other song is good, too. Many of them have kind of a tribal feel to them, especially some of the older songs from Continued Silence EP. Let's go through every song.Radioactive: Begins the album off with a song from CSE. After a slow intro with Dan Reynolds singing softly, the music builds up into a timeless song about the Apocalypse. It's timeless because the Apocalypse could happen any time in history. Need I say more? Classic song! [5/5]Tiptoe: This is the first new one, which is a funky pop song. Makes you want to get up and dance. [5/5]It's Time: This song would have earned 4 stars [It was alright], but because of the scratchy and poor sound quality, I think it deserves a [3/5].Demons: You probably remember this song as "Kingdom Come." Other than that, it's another great song from CSE, including some powerful lyrics. [5/5]On Top Of The World: What can I say? Another classic that you probably have heard over the radio! [4/5]Amsterdam: After a slow intro, it turns into another great song. The lyrics remind me of Train, which is good because Train is another band that I enjoy. I like how the lyrics were nice and fast-paced. Amsterdam is also the name of a Guster song. [4/5]Hear Me: This song HAS to be played over the radio next. I love the lyrics and the beat is very energetic. Oh yeah, I forgot to mention the beat! The first thing Imagine Dragons fans might notice about it is that the band uses a drum, and not a gong. Not saying that that's a bad thing, but it's a little different. The song is fun and grows on you very quickly. It also includes a strange and quiet guitar piece at the very end before the songs change. [6/5]Every Night: "I'm comin' home to you/ Every night, every night, every night, every night!" This song is repetitive and catchy, but other than that, mediocre. A bit slower than the other songs, too. [3/5]Bleeding Out: Don't get me wrong, I like just about every song on this album, except this one. Long story short, it's boring and, actually, a bit annoying. Maybe it'll grow on me after a couple listens, but now, I just don't like it. [2/5]Underdog: Better than Bleeding Out. The simple intro reminded me of "Best Day Of My Life" by American Authors, but soon turned into another funky Imagine Dragons song. There are also some interesting 8-bit sound effects. I didn't like them at first, but they didn't bother me on the second listen. Just like Every Night, the chorus is repetitive and catchy. The "Hey!" makes you want to sing or dance along. [4/5]Nothing Left to Say / Rocks: Before I listened to this one I had two questions -- 1.) Why is the title the way it is? 2.) Why is it so long? Then I found out the answer to both of my questions -- This is two songs in one. I don't know why the band would want to do that, but it's certainly interesting. Nothing Left to Say is an epic song, once again, about love. I actually think they used an organ in the intro -- Creepy! The rest of the song actually reminded me of rushing to somewhere important on a rainy day. Eventually, Dan Reynolds starts softly vocalizing until the song ends at 6:32 [He does this for a long time, so it's a little repetitive]. Then the songs is completely silent, until song #2, Rocks, begins at 6:47. Rocks is a very fast-paced tribal sounding song about "Throwing rocks upon somebody's window." It doesn't seem like it would be the best finisher song, but it does a good job of ending the album, surprisingly. Very interesting song, overall... or should I say songs? [5/5 [for both songs]]Well, there you have it, people, "Night Visions" by Imagine Dragons. I heard a lot of people complaining that the sound quality was bad, but I only noticed that on Radioactive and It's Time. Best of all, it's perfectly clean! I would recommend this album for anybody, especially fans of FUN and American Authors. I wouldn't recommend Continued Silence EP, though, because the sound quality on that album is worse, and the thing is only around 19 minutes -- This album is 43 minutes. Now stop reading this and buy the album!
summary: Different From All The Other Bands That I Like, But Still Really Good!

reviewText: Thom Yorke's solo album THE ERASER sounds mostly like home demos of rejected songs written for a certain famous band that he's in. The musical material is based on electronic loops and a few piano parts. There's a certain lack of polish, and only the first three tracks are really memorable: "The Eraser", "Analyze" and "The Clock". That leaves the bulk of the album pretty vacuous, and I find that the song "The Eraser" works much better in its remix by Sasha onInvol2ver.I'd recommend THE ERASER only to Radiohead completists. As decent as the first three tracks are, there's much merit to the claim that no one would ever look at this album were Yorke not the frontman for such a famous band.
Although this version is high energy and fairly well done ~it's not quite the right mix for my taste.It's almost like they tried too hard to out-do the original.

"Release the Stars" is simply brilliant, an outstanding release by a musician with an immeasurable supply of talent.  It's as if Rufus Wainwright has channeled the combined essence of Billy Joel, Elton John and Neil Diamond, at the height of their music-making abilities, and created from it something so completely unique, fresh and daring.  The themes are definitely not hidden: life, love, boredom and disappointment from a witty, overeducated and pissed-off musician.  Wainwright has transcended the superficiality of society, American society specifically, and opted for a confrontational exposition of his artistry. His confidence is evident; Wainwright is unrepentant with his music, to be sure, but also with himself, his place in the world. And subsequently, he is not afraid to shine.Musically, this album is definitely ornate as described.  The orchestration, while slightly all-encompassing, fits in nicely with his ability for the flamboyant though it certainly is not excessive.  The album repeatedly switches back and forth between a highly embellished yet beautiful cacophony to the more intimate, sparsely-arranged songs born from loneliness.  For me, it's the former that's most impressive of the album.  Songs like "Do I Disappoint You", "Between My Legs", "Rules and Regulations" and "Release the Stars" are magnificent.  "Sanssouci", "Tiergarten", and "Slideshow" are equally catchy gems as well, which display Wainwright's maturity, resigned and melancholy though it may appear. Yet it is an artfully crafted melancholy that adds to the transcendence of this album.  Transcendent is a great word to describe this album; it's incredibly good.

I was deeply anticipating this album, and I was petrified I would be disappointed. Man, was I wrong!! This double-CD is some of the most beautiful music I have heard in my 34 years on this planet. Kate's voice is as pure as it was 30 years ago; in fact, it's probably better now. And her songwriting, while having gotten less conventional, has improved greatly in scope and depth."Nocturn" rocks my world; it's sexier than any Tori Amos or Madonna song you can find. And several songs have brought me to tears (on the first listen!), the most amazing of which is "A Coral Room." While Kate's single "King of the Mountain" debuted in the UK at #4 on the charts, it's nowhere near the best song on this CD. What is the best song? Who the heck knows? It's all so astonishing. And spooky. And it all oozes with remarkable truth and beauty.Thank you, Kate Bush, for restoring my faith in modern music! You are a great gift to music and to this planet!If you love great music: Buy this, buy this, buy this!
summary: Absolute perfection!!! Welcome back, Kate Bush!!!

Just got this cd and it's taken up residence in my disc player since purchase.  Bottom Line: IMO, the best Manics album in years, which is not really a slight against them, as they don't have any bum albums, but this one is a stunner - a return to their mid-90's form.  Very tuneful and energetic, lots of loud guitars, most songs like 3 or 4 min long and come out swinging, and there are great riffs and catchy hooks, moreso than the recent stuff of theirs.  There is some political stuff here, true to their history.  My Favorite Cut: "Your Love Alone is Not Enough" featuring Nina Persson of the Cardigans.  If you're not familiar with the Manics, i cannot highly recommend Holy Bible, Everything Must Go, and My Truth..... enough, for starters.  Always interesting band, WAYYYYYY underappreciated here in the States, and one of the few British bands of the 90's still growing and making still-vital music (i'd add Charlatans UK to that list). In Short: a worthy addition to their catalogue, and definitely worth a listen if you're inclined to hear some 'real' music.
summary: THEIR BEST ALBUM IN YEARS - very satisfying

reviewText: ...but System managed to beat the sophomore slump.  Toxicity is the second full-length album from the Armenian metal quartet, and it is head and shoulders above it's current peers in the music world.  Serj and crew draw on many things for the content in these songs; the mushrooming Prison-Industrial complex in the US, Corruption, State-sponsored violence, sex, drugs etc, and every song has not only thoughtful lyrics for us to ponder, but also stunning musical range to enjoy."Chop Suey" is probably the best-executed song on the album.  The rhythm changes are catchy, and Serj's stop-start singing style is infectious.  The unifying ingredient proves to be the beautifully sung chorus and final breakdown section where Serj dazzles us with the soulful side of his voice.  The song is a bona fide hit, and any metal band that gets a video into semi-regular play on MTV must be doing something right in that department.  "Needles" is at times humorous, but mostly sinister, and contains one of the most hauntinglt beautiful vocal sections where Serj sings: "Sitting in my room/with a needle in my hand/waiting for the tomb/of some old dying man."  His vocals are still as raw as ever, and they compliment Daron Malkian's crushing guitar licks perfectly.  However, there is much more middle-eastern style vocalization on this record, and the results are stellar.  Almost every track is a potential hit."Toxicity" and "Deer Dance" both talk about LA, and you get the sense that much of the inspiration for SOAD's work comes from their living environment.  The cover photo of the Hollywood sign re-worked is an amusing twist as well; is LA toxic because it's LA, or is System part of the problem?Other standout tracks are "Science," "Forest," "Jet Pilot," and "Psycho."  "Shimmy" is another one of my favorites, combining hammer-pounding riffs with anti-brainwashing lyrics and incorporating a quirky little jazz bit.  Many of the songs on the album are potential singles, and only "X" seems to fall flat from its repetition and lack of deep subject matter.  In a sense, System can't really go simple and repetitive, because we've already seen how good they are when they're complex and innovative.This band has come a long way since I first saw them in a tiny club in Santa Barbara in 1996, and they deserve any and all success that comes their way.  If they continue to put out albums with the same success rate as their first two, I think we can expect them to become heavy hitters in the metal world.  I can think of many bands that don't deserve it, but few that would deserve it more
summary: Don't ask me how they did it...

reviewText: If anyone's worried Interview is the first step in the wrong direction for Gentle Giant, fear not, because besides a couple questionable moments that are overlong and repeat a bit much, this is definitely a quality album on the same level as the previous GG albums.The odd time signatures, the vocal melodies that repeat a lot, but are quite catchy... all the things you love about the band have remained in check with Interview.  I sense the band was starting to feel worn out by this time in their career, which is indicated by the lyrics in a few of the songs, such as "Another Show".  My favorite song is "I Lost My Head".  Extremely good vocal melodies here.There's one song on here that has a tropical vibe with lyrics about money (how appropriate with todays economy!)  I'm amazed the lead singers voice is still in incredibly good shape- he hasn't lost a step since the previous album.  This is just great rock and roll that's played in a complex, yet very satisfying way.

Update 1/8/2012: I was blasting this CD in my car all day today. I said I was going to take a break from hip hop in 2012 because the music out now is so ridiculously bad. Yes, that includes that "Bad vs. Evil" CD. Huge disappointment! I have no idea why Obie Trice didn't become more famous for a CD like this. I think he's heavily underrated and six years later, I'm still blasting this CD like it's brand new.Original review: Pros: It's very seldom these days that I can just let an album run straight through, but with Obie's new album, I sure did.  He backhanded a sophomore jinx in the mouth and said "Whatever!"  It's VERY seldom that someone's second album is better than their first but his DELIVERY on this one is SICK. I'm so impressed.  I don't even change songs; I just let it ride through, even on the songs that I'm not too crazy about the topic matter.  Obie takes negativity and turns it into positivity; understands that Dr. Seuss' lyrics just won't do it and delving into multisyllabics is so beautiful.  He rides the beats well and his swagger is so contagious. You start feeling cooler just LISTENING to him.  I gotta give a round of applause to this man.  He started talking about current events and sociopolitical topics that folks aren't necessarily ready to hear: "My momma can't save me--her gender is wrong" on "Ghetto."  I was glad that he concentrated on his own style in his album though.  It doesn't hurt to have the excellent croon of Nate Dogg on here or to have Eminem, and you can't go wrong with Trey Songz, but Obie's strong enough to stand alone.Cons:  Some of the subject matter was a little too common for me, but honestly, it's the truth. On songs like "Mama," "Ballad of Obie Trice" and "There They Go," I'm tired of hearing about drop-outs becoming rappers and successful.  I'm glad they managed to bring their lives up to par, but at the same time, it's sending a bad message to those who are thinking of dropping out, because they can point out so many rappers and go "But look how he turned out!  I don't need school!"  I'd rather hear a lyricist regret dropping out of school when the government and politics are stacked against him, but that wasn't happening on this album.

You could say this was the last of Joni's "naive hippie waif" records.  The next year's BLUE would be a quantum leap forward...into Bohemia.  That's not to say that LADIES OF THE CANYON is without its very real charms, but by the next record, those sunshiney ladies with their hand-woven clothes, fat babie and fresh baked brownies would be replaced by Bohemian drifters and rogues and other denizens of those "dark cafes."The Woodstock dream so clearly articulated in Joni's 1970 anthem of that name would be replaced by a more worldy skepticism when 1971 found her "sitting in a park in Paris, France.." and realizing that "they won't give peace a chance/that was just a dream some of us had."  But it was a NICE dream while it lasted, and Joni (who famously did NOT go to Woodstock) expressed the vision of a Woodstock Nation about as well as anyone could.LADIES OF THE CANYON was then something of a transitional album.  It was also something of a grab-bag.  She finally put down a version of "Circle Game," a song recorded several years before by folk luminaries such Tom Rush and Buffy Sainte-Marie.  She wound up throwing in a track written for a film ("The Arrangement") which didn't make the cut for the acutal film, but she opted to include it here (maybe not the wisest decision after all, but that's just me).The record also boasts another two songs that were destined to become touchstones in Joni's career--"For Free" and "Big Yellow Taxi."  They are both instantly likeable, perhaps for different reasons.  "For Free" is one of the earlier expressions of liberal, hipster artistic guilt over actually playing for MONEY.  It's a theme, Joni would revisit on MINGUS and elsewhere.  But "For Free's" naivete is particularly affecting.  It has the hallmarks of a recent realization--no real jadedness about it."Big Yellow Taxi" maybe doesn't hold up quite as well, maybe just because it's been done to death by other people.  And I NEVER cared for the forced laugh at the end.  But it was another step forward for Joni thematically.  It's as though she were beginning to get that it wasn't just a matter of seeing things from both sides now.  On this record, she was starting to view things from SEVERAL sides.

reviewText: The intriguing life story of the man who was born Steven, lived his life known as Cat and after an encounter with the truth transformed into Yusuf Islam is worth writing a book for or making a movie about. In the seventies, people around the world were falling in love or were already in love with the music and the charisma of this poetic young intelligent well-spoken well-behaved englishman. One album after another, Cat Stevens made an eternal mark in pop/rock history books. From the witty "Matthew And Son" through the charm of "Wild World" and the maturity of "Father And Son" Cat's music was diverse and grew more and more intellectual and serious.One will sit through this outrageous compilation of songs written and performed by this man during the years he was an energetic Pop music machine and just smile. How could you not when you hear the catchy 'The First Cut is The Deepest", the sentimental "Lady D'Arbanville", the touching "Morning Has Broken" and "The Wind", and the smart "Moonshadow"? His lovely masculine voice empowered by the delicate string arrangements and his own guitar compositions became the tone and the rhythm of the era. "I've Got A Thing About Seeing My Grandson Grow Old" is the only previously unreleased track on the album, sounding as crisp as it would have been it was released when the song was originaly recorded sometime in the 70's, it's a grand track with Cat speaking about settling down and living his life for his children and grandchildren.Cat Stevens is no longer that same pop hit single machine anymore. He's not even Cat Stevens anymore. He's discovered Islam (which means Submission To the One God of all prophets and all humanity in arabic), and he has now become a devoted Muslim, father and husband. His recent recordings under the name he's had for over 25 years now, Yusuf Islam, are wonderful and inspiring Islamic teachings from the life of Prophet Muhammed peace be upon him, to the teachings from the Holy Quran. I recommend you pick up one or more of those albums when you have the chance.But musically, this album is a must have. Even though I do think that many good Cat songs were left out such as "I Think I See The Light", and "If You Want To Sing Out, Sing Out" I still love this album and recommend it to all.

This CD would have gotten 5 stars if it had not been for the inclusion of the syrupy "Black And White" at the end of the CD. Minus that, this is an absolute must-have for the progressive country-roots-rock lover.  The massive hit "Seven Year Ache" is included of course, but the  centerpieces of this compilation, in my opinion, are the roots-rockers  "Hold On" and "Never Be You". "Hold On" is  driven by a propulsive bass guitar that is in perfect harmony with the  confident lyrics. "Never Be You", (written by Tom Petty and  Benmont Tench), lets Rosanne rock out in great style. "Blue Moon With  Heartache" is gorgeous, and, like most of Rosanne's work, is  wonderfully written. However, one of her bigger hits is curiously and  disappointingly left absent - "Runaway Train". One of the most  important alt-country singer/songwriters of the 1980s, this collection  remains the best calling card to anyone new to Rosanne's music. The  compilations that followed were disappointing, leaving out many of her hits  and album tracks. Fans will have to be content with this one and wait for  the day a larger compilation including her introspective 90's work is  released.
summary: A superb collection of an important singer-songwriter

...and up your production on your next album. Here is Encore, Eminem's latest but far from greatest, due to the de ja vu lyrics and monotonous production with either sweet but agonized strings or fun but standard club beats. When "Just Lose It" hit MTV and radio airwaves, I thought "Em has got it down." It was a great club song that was witty, and blew "Without Me" out of the water. It also beat 50's "In Da Club" too, because of the great production and very clever lyrics. And that video really came out of left field too!Then came "Mosh", one of my favorite tracks on the album because it was great to know that somebody else had the same political views as me. In this Bush-bashing track released just before the election, Eminem addressed and stressed everything from bringing our troops home to voting issues. And it turned out to be one of his most excellent tracks ever, with laid-back, suspenseful production from Dr. Dre.Of course, I was ever so ecstatic to listen to this album on MTV's "The Leak", but after listening to it through and through again, I was a bit let down. Not really like, "This is a bad album", because it is an excellent album, but more like "We waited two and a half years for this?" Let me put it this way: Encore is a terrific rap album, but coming from Eminem, possibly the world's greatest MC, he has come up very short. Many of the tracks are clever, and I really like tracks like "Crazy In Love" and "Like Toy Soldiers" for some reason. But in other moments of the album, especially in the middle, Eminem has turned up with some rhymes and production work that is really lazy. One track is hardly distinguishable from the next in those poor moments. I hate to say it Em, but you need to add Kanye West to your production lineup, and Em YOU ARE BURNED OUT ON YOUR PRODUCTION WORK!!! The piano melodies and slow strings are cuttin' it anymore, big boy. Oh, and dump your D12 "posse". they can't hold a torch to Jay-Z or yourself. Simply put, their pathetic wannabes. That's why D12 albums are horrible.Eminem has come up with a great album on Encore, but I was pretty let down. In fact, I hate saying this, but I have been a little let down on all of his albums. The truth be told, I have never been let down on an album from, say, Jay-Z. Em, maybe you need to change your style, and get better rappers backing you up on tracks, or just put yourself on the WHOLE album next time. Jay-Z wisely used you on The Blueprint. You should have used him on Encore or The Eminem Show. I have always felt Em is missing something, but it's hard to know what. He has the rhymes, the attitude, the sharp-as-a-blade humor, but what is he missing? maybe it's sub-standard production and lowlife rappers backing him up nowadays. Eminem fans, the time has come for you to get his new album, definitely. The time has also come for Em to sit down and think about what he can do to improve.
summary: Em, You Gotta Change Yo Style...

Ok, let me get a couple of things straight from the outset. Im a huge Pearl Jam fan, and I didnt buy this album expecting, or wanting, to hear 'Ten' part two. In that respect, I wasnt disappointed. This certainly isnt a rehash of anything theyve ever done before: Pearl Jam cosistently branch out into new musical directions without sacrificing their artistc integrity or failing to showcase the remerkable talents of each and every band member that got us all interested in the first place. Sadly though, this certainly isnt Pearl Jam's best album. Its not their best since 'Ten', or their best since 'Vs', or better than 'Vitalogy' or 'No code'. Dont get me wrong, its not their worst either: it has wonderful moments. But let me tackle this in detail.I was struck at first by the way the albums two opening tracks act as a kind of simulacrum of the No Code formula. A slow opener, building into a racuous, full throttle rocker for the second track. Its a formula that worked perfectly in 1996: sadly, 'Cant Keep' and 'Save you' just arent anywhere near as good as 'Sometimes' and 'Hail hail', precipitating unwelcome comparisons. Despite this, 'Save You' is a great track, and the albums only real straightahead rocker. After all this negativity, now would be a good time to bestow some praise on one man: Matt Cameron. He contributes more to this album than Binaural, and im massively impressed. Many people forget he penned some of the best Soundgarden tunes, and hes well up to standard here. 'You are' is my favourite track here: a truly stunning song which takes Pearl Jam into uncharted waters, a really strange song that Ive fallen in love with irrevocably. Thanks to this Id honestly say its worth buying the album just for that track. Unfortunately one great track doesnt make a wonderful album. What we have here is a good album. 'Cropduster' and 'get right', camerons other compositions, are superb, 'I am mine' really is great, as is the folky 'thumbing my way', which once again shows us just what a diverese, talented songsmith Vedder is. Elsewhere, half full, and all or none provide other highlights. Its a good album, but i cant help feeling if it had all been up to the standards of you are or I am mine, it could have been their best. Still worth buying, even for the casual fan. Pearl jam continue to evolve and immpress, but theres an essential fire that has gone.
summary: Im glad I gave it a chance.

I loved "Little Earthquakes," but this one shows far more dimentions and growth on it.  Every song is a classic, particularly "God", my favorite song of  all time. It captures a feeling inside of us that every person on earth has  felt at one time or another. If you think about it, Tori is far more of a  spiritual person than most people because she says what she feels and lays  it all out on the table. Most Christians are only Sunday Christians. They  go to church on Sunday to strive to become more holy, but during the rest  of the week they live a life suitable of Sodom and Gomorrah. I love this !Do go and buy a copy of this album .Now for my review. I have bought alll of Elton John's many albums on CD and most of his singles too , so it's fair to say I am very familiar with his style and his capabilities. Obviously after 40 years , and as many albums, it would be really hard for he and Bernie to create piano-based songs that were entirely new or original-sounding so inevitably each new EJ-BT record has bits on it you can recognise from earlier albums. This one even has a recycled/updated concept in common with 1975's autobiographical Captain Fantastic and The Brown Dirt Cowboy album . It too is about Elton and Bernie's years as a creative writing team and draws from life experiences they have shared . Old '67 references the year they began writing together ( an incredible 39 years ago!)  and is a sentimental tune that is rather unusual in its direct nostalgia references. The title song The Captain And The Kid is an update of Elton and Bernie's story set to the intro music from the earlier album's title cut. It is nice , if a bit lightweight .Postcards From Richard Nixon is a series of vignettes from their triumphant US breakthrough of 1970-71 when suddenly Elton and Bernie were "where it's at" . It is a good song . Just Like Noah's Ark is a piano-driven rocker that chugs along enjoyably, while I Must Have Lost It On The Wind is a mid-paced pleasant country pop song that is also pretty good. Moving on to Tinderbox, we have a really good song about the flashpoint in the EJ-BT team in the mid-70's where they got on each other's nerves and split up for quite a long time (only reuniting creatively in the mid 80's again). The catchy melody of And The House Fell Down has been spinning around in my head all day today. This is a piano pop-rocker which covers Elton's bad trips when he was on drugs during the most frenzied part of his meteoric rise to stardom in the mid 70's .The best songs on this album, as I always tend to find with Elton John's music, are the slow , melodic ones. Blues Never Fade Away is about losing people. I think the lyric here is very lovely and quite sad , and tells of the undying hurt that you feel when someone you really love does die too soon. I think Bernie and Elton made a beautiful song with I Wouldn't Have You Any Other Way. This is as good as an Elton song can be , and I am sure I will get to really love this wonderful ode to NYC the more I listen to it. I know Bernie Taupin has been quoted as having mixed feelings about New York, but here Elton's delightful, warm melody wraps the city up with love! The Bridge was chosen to be the first single , I'd heard, so I was expecting a well-produced piano power ballad or maybe a synth-rocker. I was therefore surprised and delighted to hear this lovely, simple song with just Elton's piano and voice plus a little bit of vocal overdubbing. This was perhaps my favourite of the 10 songs on this album, and a lovely example of how a great song does not need elaborate overdubs, loud guitars or crashing percussion to make it good.Elton John sings beautifully on The Captain & The Kid. I am delighted by how very well he is singing; and though he is no longer young, he is still capable of beautiful melodies and fine songcraft. He has definitely not deteriorated after his early-decade artistic triumph of Songs From The West Coast. Obviously my rating of 5 stars may be a little inflated by my love of his music and me being a long-term fan , but I really do believe he has made a terrific album here , and it is definitely better than I was expecting it to be.I must also direct any Elton fans who may not have heard the original 1975 album Captain Fantastic to do so right away. It is a true classic and is just about faultless. In fact , don't stop there - listen to as much of his 1970-76 "classic period" music as you can , because it is truly wonderful.

First off...I was skeptical about buying this album, but it has proved a worthy purchase for five reasons. These reasons being, "Horses", "Little Amsterdam", "Father Lucifer", "Doughnut Song", and "Mr. Zebra". I was so surprised to see how these songs played out on a full albums worth of material, instead of on a collection of songs, or in a live atmosphere (which they work well also). "Boys For Pele" as many Toriphiles know, is one of Tori's favorite albums to play live. But it was also largely different from "Little Earthquakes" and "Under The Pink". Harpsichords are introduced here, in songs like 'Blood Roses' and 'Talula'. She also utilizes full orchestras and choirs, such as on "Way Down" and "Putting The Damage On". Now, this is not my favorite Tori album by any means, but it is a welcome addition in any collection. (My favorite being either the Choirgirl Hotel or Scarlet's Walk) There are some missteps here, some larger than others. Talula, a song I still cant listen to all the way through, and some of the latter songs in the album slow the pace of the album down. Twinkle is simply beautiful, but I think it loses its luster at the end of the album, after Putting the Damage on. Taken individually, I'm sure these songs work much better, but as a whole album, it has its high (Horses, Father Lucifer)and low (Talula) points.
summary: One Of The Most Misunderstood Albums of Her Career

Happiness is easily defined in terms of Tahiti 80's aptly titled Wallpaper for the Soul. This is such a brilliant, beautiful album, reaching far beyond the confines of its "electric-pop" pigeonholing. It's strange that I think of models walking down the runway as 1,000 Times cruises through the speakers, but jaunty showcasing of supernatural pulchritude is fittingly analogous to this record, since Wallpaper for the Soul is gushing with gorgeously refined grandeur that leaves the scent and feel of warm summer love as it wisps by. I couldn't call myself a fan of pure, fun, upbeat music if I didn't own this album. 1,000 Times, Soul Deep and The Train will envelop you with unprecedented zest and compassion. I Recommend this to all.

Before I listened to this album I had heard very little of 2Pac.  I had been avoiding rap as much as a could for a long time, but one day I caved in and started listening to rap willingly.  I decided I liked it (imagine that) and wanted to find some good rappers to listen to.  Obviously, 2Pac came to mind so I thought would take a chance on this 2 CD collection, and I am very glad I did!This collection is an excellent introduction to 2Pac if you're new to him and rap in general.  Tracks like "Keep Ya Head Up," "Brenda's Got a Baby," "Changes," and "Dear Mama" break the negative stereotypes often associated with rap (unnecessary violence, objectifying women, etc.) and help newcomers accept and enjoy the genre.  This collection also contains the notoriously heartless diss to his former friend Biggie Smalls entitled "Hit Em Up."  There are even some great tracks to simply nod your head to while driving, such as "I Get Around," "California Love," and "All About You."After listening to some of 2Pac's other cds, I do feel there are some essential songs missing from this Greatest Hits collection, but overall there are a lot of great tracks on here and is a great introduction to anyone new to 2Pac or rap as a whole.  However, anyone that has many of 2Pac's earlier cds could probably pass this one up.

I initially ordered this on Amazon but I received a disc that did not work properly. It was so scratched up you'd think that the seller would have tested it first. Three tracks did not work. Anyway, I ended up going to the used record store and purchased a used copy. I wasn't in the mood to wait for another week or so only to find that it did not work. I wanted to listen to Adam Ant's greatest hits.First of all, this album's quality is lacking. To be sure, it is not remastered. This is one of those albums that badly needs it. The sound quality is like a well worn cassette tape. Some tracks came out okay such as my favorites, Prince Charming, Desperate But Not Serious, Friend or Foe and Strip. The first half of this album sound pretty bad, actually.Sound-wise, the songs lack bass. I know that in the eighties bass was lacking in a lot of recordings and treble took the forefront. It was just the style back then. If you listen to a lot of eighties records as I do, you will notice that there is a strong treble in the recording and bass is pushed to the back. Not all recording was that way. The Cars had bass in their recordings. But I notice that many other artists back then had their bass toned down.What's great about this album is that there are 21 tracks. When I initially sought out an Adam Ant album I had heard it on Spotify and wanted to have it in my library. I was familiar with Goody Two Shoes from back in the day when I was in school. In the eighties Adam Ant was a big hit. With his strange getup and style. He had a style all his own. And his song, Goody Two Shoes harkened back to the old days. You could say that he was playing "old school". Now he IS old school.Now, I am going to have to seek out a proper Adam Ant collection that does him justice. One that sound decent, audio-wise. I think that the Essential Adam Ant is one that I am going to look for next. If you are looking for a good Adam Ant collection, this ain't it, folks. But if you don't care as you'll just be playing it on a boombox, this will do just for the sheer number of hits.

Robert Johnson lived from 1911-1938, and died at the age of 27. But during his years active as a performing artist, 1934-1938, he recorded some of the best blues ever.The recordings had been lost for many years, but in 1961, Columbia released them on the vinyl release 'King Of The Delta Blues Singers.' The record inspired guitarists like Keith Richards, Eric Clapton and Robert Cray. It remains, even to this day, one of the most influential records of all-time.Overall, if you like the blues, classic rock or great guitar playing, than you need this album. Highly recommended for anybody who appreciates music.One of the best records ever released. Highly recommended! ENJOY!!!

Now, I certainly hope you can take the word of a guy who has never been into country music.  I dip into so many genres, and country I had always avoided intentionally.  Listening to this cd I realized why that is.  For someone who doesn't like country, the only place you will hear any country is on the radio or on tv if you happen to be within earshot(or riding shotgun in a car with some schmuck who's blaring and singing along with it).  And what kind of country is played on the radio and tv, children?  Like any other popular music station, 100% Grade-A crapola.  Hank is certainly an eye opener.  Hank reminds me of the stuff my grandparents were listening to when I was very young; Stuff that sounded like it came from the heart and soul, not pop music with fake southern accents.  Hank is country the way I always felt it should sound.  Hank sings about heartbreak, drinking, and his idols.  He's not afraid to glorify drug use and make a slam on pop country every chance he can.  Kinda like the Manowar of country if you will.  The fact that Hank's singing from the heart comes right through your speakers.  You can practically feel it, and his enthusiasm and love for country becomes downright infectious.  You find yourself going, "Yeah, Hank! You tell em how it is!"  This is a guy right at home and having the time of his life playing songs in a bar with rowdy, dedicated fans, not prancing around in an enormous arena with 80 band members and wearing one of those secret service earpieces(that ever really seem "country" to you?).  Hank is "keepin' it real" as those wacky kids like to say nowdays.  Not one throwaway tune on Straight To Hell, so you need not bother with that skip button, just put it on and let it run.  Disc two shows us that Hank's also into experimenting with sound.  Lots of acoustic tunes with noises and sound effects in between.  If John Zorn were to do a country album, it'd probably sound something like this.  One of the sounds is a few minutes of a locomotive.  If you have a good sound system at home and turn this up, you'd swear you had a train going right through your living room.  Needless to say Brooks and Dunn won't be doing a disc like this soon.  But as I said before, you want the real deal, this is it.  I'm definitely no authority on country music, but I know what I like, and judging by the previous reviews for this cd, I seem to be on the right track.  Get yourself on track!
summary: Hell Is Right! For Me It's Freezing Over!

Sure,most of Mr. Clapton's stuff is reasonably good, but really that's only when it's compared to the immediate competition. Truly, when one is a rather naive 17 year old, some of these tunes may not sound half bad! But with some musical and worldly experience, this album, like just about all "Rock", fades away into the realm of adolescent sentimentality,bordering on noisy nonsense. Indeed, listening to say "Bell Bottom Blues" for a wizened old timer (now over 50) is simply an embarrassment, and the idea of these performers playing them now is even worse. Same with just about everything here. And the copy cat version of "Little Wing", originally written/recorded by Eric's old rival, J. Hendrix, does not come close to the original! Really, the best Clapton can still be heard on the older (1967-68)"Cream" albums, much of which still sounds fresh and unique, not just thumping re-treads of 3 chord blues with banal lyrics.
summary: Decent for its time..But gets old fast!

reviewText: It's always risky to close out an album with a novelty number as Annie Lennox does on this, her first solo release.  Actually, the very inclusion of a novelty tune at all is kind of chancy.  But thrown in as a closer, a jaunty bit of a lark can risk undercutting the mood of an entire album (at least for those who play CDs straight through these days).  And by rights, the capper on this album, a 1930s style chauvinistic chestnut called "Keep Young And Beautiful" could be said to undermine what is, after all, an otherwise moody and atmospheric set.But, go figure, but it works perfectly.  You gotta hand it to the Scots siren, after a good deal of introspective sombreness, this bit of Jazz Age fluff is just about the cat's meow.In fact, if the gorgeous gloom of the rest of the album (particularly as manifested on the tracks "Cold," "The Gift" and the big hit "Why") was kind of starting to get oppressive, the closer not only makes for a lighthearted exit, but actually makes a statement of sorts about "womanhood" in the '90s (when the record was first released) and the pre-feminist early 20th century.And that is simply this: as hard as it may be to be an autonomous, independent, and (yes) liberated woman, it's hands down better than having to "keep young and beautiful, if you want to be loved..."  Times have changed, and life and love have gotten maddeningly complex.  But would you really be better off with an empty head and "a Marcel wave in your hair"?  I didn't think so.As for the rest of the album, well, it suffers a bit from saving much of the best stuff for last, including two of the three titles I cited above.  "Why," of course, is the opener and it's just about a perfect pop record.  You fall into it and fall in love with it, even before you quite realize what it's about.  (I remember thinking it might have more social import or philosophical heft than it actually does:  songs with titles like "Why" sometimes do.)  But while I subsequently came to like the two or three songs that follow it well enough, they never seemed fully developed, never quite rich enough.  "Walking On Broken Glass" continues the broken heart theme of "Why,"  but its profession of heartache is (of course deliberately) set to a jarringly sprightly bounce of a melody and a kitschy ice arena arrangement.  Maybe it too should be viewed as somthing of a novelty tune.DIVA has been hailed for its musical and lyrical spareness, as even the prosaic titles ("Precious," "Cold," "Primitive," et al.) suggest.  Even when the title is a bit longer and more evocative, as for example "Legend In My Living Room," the narrative can be a bit skimpy.  Starts off promisingly as a reminiscence of the singer's wild and wooly years and then devolves into so many "Have mercies."  Tuneful enough, but there goes any hope of a grand statement, even if she does own up to being "the queen of doom"But those gospel-styled shout outs do remind us of one Lennox's trademark stylistic devices (and, arguably, one her chief strengths).  She can sing big, and she can sing black, but it's always a least a little ironic and definitely cold cold cold.  I read once that she's been called the "white Grace Jones."  But she's actually got a more powerful delivery than the devilish Ms. Jones ever did.  I'd call her more of a cross between Grace SLICK (now that would be a dream duet--Gracie and Annie) and Aretha (who actually did duet with Ann on "Sisters Are Doin' It For Themselves").  Heavy on the soulful inflection, even heavier on the irony.  If you hail from Aberdeen, and not Alabama, is there any other way to go?Well, you can go one up on Sting, say.  "Why" wraps up with a letter-perfect Sting-style litany ("This is the book I never read/These are the words I never said").  It builds so dramatically, so authoritatively that you don't want to argue with its conclusion. Yeah, that jerk never had a CLUE about how she felt.  Of course, we never doubt her assertion that for her part, SHE could always read what her lover was thinking. She knew how HE felt.  Post-modern sexual stereotyping? Or just a simple truth about a specific relationship. And is the song autobiographical enough that that relationship was real, or is it a fiction? Dunno. Things were so much easier back in the day of "Keep Young And Beautiful."

Aerosmith, January 1973, the debut album in all its unpolished glory. Sophistication was soon to come but what this band did not lack at this stage was balls and the songwriting chops of one young Steven Tallarico. Stage name of Tyler, you know, future rock god, reformed addict and king of sleaze. The songs are great on this terribly underated album, easily their most unsung. "Dream On" is of course an undisputed rock classic played a billion times so yes I am a little tired of it, but "Movin' Out"? "One Way Street"? "Make It" and the immortal "Mama Kin"? No way!! This record is a joy from start to finish (and what a finish - "Walking the Dog", could be the definitive version of this song!)The boys in the band give credible performances but I have to agree that the guitar partnership of Perry/Whitford does not impress as they would one album later. The production of the album leaves much to be desired and if the strories are true, blame it on the record company for cheaping out on this future supergroup. Who could blame them? Well all their money was going into Bruce Springsteen. Not a bad choice I guess. But Aerosmith would overcome many other similar slights and self destructive behaviors to emerge as the great American Rock n'Roll band that they are, sappy ballads asside. There is nothing sappy about 'Aerosmith', but more greatness was to follow.
summary: Working like a dog in a rock n' roll band.....

reviewText: Today, Jackson Browne may be much more conspicuous as an anti-nuclear activist rather than a rock musician. He was one of the rock musicians who joined Musicians United For Safe Energy after Fukushima nuclear disasters in 2011. His 1983 album is overall upbeat 80s pop rock particularly the title track LAWYERS IN LOVE. But his upbeat music belies his cynical message just like his first major hit DOCTOR MY EYES in 1972. This album proved that upbeat rock and deep-down messages can go hand in hand and his longtime friend BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN made a megahit album BORN IN THE U.S.A. the next year to uphold this trend. It is true that this may not be his best album to date but I really enjoy this album. DOWNTOWN is his way of tribute to PETULA CLARK's SIGNATURE HIT of the same title. He took the same theme with much more reality to it. FOR A ROCKER the third single from this album mentions session musicians for his music such as CRAIG DOERGE, RUSS KUNKEL and DANNY KORTCHMAR. This album may be easier to get in for the starters who love his compilation works.Verdict: Jackson Browne with 80s radio-friendly beatRating: 88 out of 100Recommended for: 1983 album completists, and early 80s rock fans in general.

The Buddy Guy cd Sweet Tea starts with Buddy singing in a tired old voice typical of those found amongst North Mississippi Hill country artists "I'm an Old Man."  As soon as he kicks in with his guitar licks it becomes clear that he is anything but old and why Eric Clapton lauds him as the Best blues guitarist and why he is the current King of Chicago Blues.With Sweet Tea, recorded at the studio of the same name, Buddy Guy, the King of the Chicago Blues has an affair with the North Mississippi Hill Country Blues.  Buddy Guy, the preacher man of the blues whose lives shows are a veritable sermon of blues styles and artists, launches into a study of North Mississippi Hill country Blues using songs by hill artists, Junior Kembrough and T-Model Ford as a vehicle to tour the genre. This affair acknowledges Guy's humble country roots and shows how far he has gone from them since hitting Chicago and setting the town in a spin in 1957.The cd highlights heavy and primitive drumbeats which contrasts effectively with Guy's flaming guitar rifts and some of the best examples of Guy's  vocals.  Many of the songs contain extended Jam's that seem to go on forever, with Baby Please Don't Leave Melasting 7:23 and I Gotta Try You Girl running a whopping 12:09.  Oddly they don't feel too long.  The feel is more like a visit to a juke joint deep in the Hill Country and jamming it up all night long.Guy's version of Lowell Fulsom's Tramp starts with a long guitar rift before launching into the vocals:"Tramp, you can call me thatIf that makes you feel goodCause I'm a loverThat's all I'm gonna doTramp, call me country right from the woods.I'll answer when you callIf that make you feel good."This is a unique and interesting cd among the Buddy Guy collection.  I believe that it is one that shouldn't be passed by.  Prepare to jam all night!  Old man, indeed!

In 1994, Guru and DJ Primer were already 3 albums deep under the name Gangstarr. There is no doubt that Gangstarr is or should be one of your top 10 rap groups of all time. Around this time there were many side projects that were either finished or underway. Guru had the Jazmatazz series and Primo were producing beats for artists like Jeru and Group Home as well as Nas and a lot of others around that time. So somehow they were able to record their 4th LP Hard To Earn, and I seriously thought they were running out of fuel in the hip hop game with the other events going on thinking of the worst, such as a bunch of reject Primo beats from other artists ending up on this. Boy was I wrong.Hard To Earn really showed Gangstarr getting stronger lyrically and production wise. Guru comes at many listeners telling sup-par emcees to step their game up on "ALONGWAYTOGO" while Primo chops up some Tribe samples. Guru also realize the negative effect guns would have in their society as he would rhyme on "Tonz O' Gunz" as he would say "...check your nearest overpopulated ghetto/they greet you with a pistol not trying to say hello..."Production wise, Primo is genius. Well known for his NY style production, scratching samples and using his drums on most tracks, songs like "The Planet" and "Mass Appeal" comes off in a strong way. The latter song as well as the earlier mentioned "ALONGWAY..." is a great example of Primo never going wrong when he scratches records and sampling voices. Even if the beats just so much were a bunch of rejects from side projects, they still maintain their excellence.Guest vocals come off okay as most of them are within the ('94) Gang Starr Foundation. Jeru who makes the best impact, does a good job in the song "Speak Your Clout". Greg Nice and Smooth B. do a decent job rhyming in the song "DWYCK". Other vocals are Group Home and Big Shug.Although Hard To Earn was a good LP, but it also suffers a couple of faults too, believe it or not.Problem #1: Why Is Guru's voice carry a monotone throughout the album? It's not as annoying as some people want you to believe it is, but it seems like his mood changes, his voice constantly holds the same level. (The track "Mostly Would Be The Voice" would be sort of a contradiction in the album)Solution: True, but that doesn't take away on how dope he is behind the mic. What could have solved this problem is more guest appearances to fill that void. It makes me mad that some of the emcees that Primo produced such as Nas, Masta Ace, and A.G. and many others make a 5 second appearance leaving messages on Primo's voice mail in the interlude "Aiight Chill". I wouldn't mind Nas giving us an Illmatic touch on this album.Problem #2 (and many detailed reviewers pointed this one out also): Why is Primo's most sickest beat on this album; A. given to a weak emcee Melachi the Nutcracker from Group Home; B. clocking in just over a minute (taking out the 20 second intro to the song)? I can't tell you how perfect that fast piano flows throughout the song is almost waisted because of those factors.Solution: The beat is perfect. Hell, I wouldn't have minded if Melachi went on for another minute or so, because the beat carries the song and would make up for weak rhyming he has. I can only imagine how sick this song would be if people like Jeru and Guru tossed in a verse, wow...Other than that, this album is a real nice album that Gang Starr has came up with. I really can't call if it's their best because I only own two of their albums (this and The Owners), and haven't heard the rest of them, mainly Moment Of Truth. This album came out in '94, said to be hip hop's best year, and it's good to see that Gang Starr was apart of it. I recommend this to many hip hop fans of the early/mid 90's, and enjoy Primo's production.Lyrics: A-Production: A+Guest appearances: B-Musical Vibes: B+Overall: A-Favorite Tracks: ALONGWAYTOGO, Tonz 'O' Gunz, The Planet, Speak Ya Clout, DWYCK, Mass AppealHonorable Mention Track: Words From The Nutcracker
summary: Guru and Primo Earned Theirs With This One (4 Stars)

reviewText: The Dipset is pretty much a pointless clique these days. Never really making a real impression on the industry, they've really been lucky to even still be around. Cam'ron was the front man, and he couldn't even muster a formidable solo career when he finally got on the Roc. The creation of Dipset seemed like a desperate move to make everybody think Cam'ron really was a worthwhile rapper and leader. From the start, it seemed like Juelz Santana had just a little bit of an edge as far as charisma and skills. Juelz' first album was like most other Dipset releases and did very little in comparison to the rest of the Roc-a-fella roster. Fast forward to today and the release of his second solo album, an older and more experienced Juelz proclaims in his title that he is What The Game's Been Missing. And after one listen, you will wish that this album had stayed missing!There are a few cuts from this album that Juelz actually pulls off. "Shottas" is a pretty good mix of hip-hop and reggae with Cam'ron and Sizzla giving their flava to the song, but Juelz manages to shine better than both of them. Juelz does the same thing on "Whatever You Wanna Call It" with Hell Rell giving less than stellar lyrics on the song. "Good Times" is a passable song as well as "Gone" and "Daddy." But the rest of the album is plagued with horrible production, uninspiring verses, and little creativity."Oh Yes" gets the Cam'ron award, where Juelz has one of the most annoying choruses you will ever hear. Runner-ups for the Cam'ron award include "Kid Is Back" with kids singing the hook and "Violence" with Juelz yelling throughout the entire song like he's the lost member of M.O.P. or something! "Make It Work For You" featuring Lil Wayne and Young Jeezy is the top choice for the Noisemaker award, with production that sounds like a demo track from a Casio keyboard. Other vote-getters include "Freaky," "Changes" featuring Razah, and "Rumble Young Man Rumble." And of course the Another Bad Creation award goes to "Clockwork," a track makes no sense at all. "Kill Em" featuring Cam'ron, "There It Go (The Whistle Song)," and the ridiculous "I Am Crack" are even more examples of songs the should have never seen the light of day.Juelz Santana has been able to keep himself the most viable member of Dipset as of late. But What The Game's Been Missing falls short of even being borrowed from a clueless co-worker or a 5 for $10 sale from your local "street vendor" for that matter. Seems Juelz will have to separate himself from Dipset to even have a chance at a long career. If he chooses not to part ways, then he could end up being one of those "street vendors" selling albums from other rappers that are still in the game!
summary: (2.5 Stars) The Potential Is There...But That Only Gets You So Far

I had the great pleasure of paying a closer attention to legendary country singer-songwriter Willie Nelson's last three CD releases that I couldn't let this new CD 'To All The Girls' (18 tracks) pass me by without a spin. The last three albums I'm talking about are his impressive collaboration with icon trumpeter Wynton Marsalis and the graceful Nora Jones in the 2011 CD 'Here We Go Again: Celebrating The Genius Of Ray Charles' (a live recording), the 2012 country gem CD 'Heroes' and the incredible 2013 diverse CD 'Let's Face The Music And Dance'.Like wine, Willie Nelson (WN) at 80 shows no sign of slowing down and he's on a roll in this great duet album 'To All The Girls'. WN is great on guitar and his voice is great and enticing as ever. The 'girls' are great female singers that the record label team could invite and assemble for this project (diverse 18 singers mainly from country music genre but also those from other genres as in Mavis Staples, Norah Jones, Alison Krauss and Emmylow Harris). It's an incredible display of song arrangements and dueting by Willie Nelson, his producer and guest artists. Great classics are given a fresh dress-up in this CD release as in the tracks "Far Away Places" (orchestral based track featuring Sheryl Crow), "Always On My Mind" (slow-tempo track with an incredible melody & vocals featuring Carrie Underwood) & "Have You Ever Seen The Rain" (slow-tempo track with a beautiful melody and vocals featuring Paula Nelson). My real surprise was the cover track "Dry Lightning" from 1995 Bruce Springsteen's acoustic album 'The Ghost Of Tom Joad'. It's well done featuring Emmylow Harris and even The Boss should be impressed.Stands-outs/gems/my favourites are the tracks "From Here To The Moon And Back" (orchestral, great melody & vocals. It's a Dolly Parton composition for the 2012 movie Joyful Noise and features the lady herself: gracious vocals), "Please Don't Tell Me How The Story Ends" (wonderful violin, melody & vocals featuring Rosanne Cash), "Always On My Mind", "Somewhere Between" (slow-tempo track with beautiful accordion & melody featuring Loretta Lynn), "Back To Earth" (incredible music instruments arrangement. Melonie Cannon, her vocals are incredible), "Will You Remember Mine" (orchestral, slow-tempo track with wonderful melody and vocals featuring Lily Meola), "Making Believe" (featuring Brandi Carlile) & Creedance Clearwater Revival classic cover "Have You Ever Seen The Rain". There is no weak track or CD filler in this great CD 'To All The Girls'.On overall, legendary singer-songwriter Willie Nelson is incredible in this new CD release, great music by the master, wonderful guest artists ('the girls') and production. A highly recommended CD for your listening pleasure.
summary: Legendary Country Singer - Songwriter Willie Nelson Is On A Roll, Again!

As the troubled, but at times hopeful 1980’s came to an end, Elton John againprovided us with another blockbuster hit in 1989 that finds him in top drawer formand back on top of the music charts.  Showcasing its highly versatile combinationof first rate multi-layered keyboard artistry, high voltage rock and roll, R&B;, socialcommentary, solid background, drum and snare back-up and outstanding diversesongs, Sleeping With The Past showcased another powerful masterpiece packeda new set of time-honoured music and utmost musicianship.  Heralded by a hard-driving track set which begin with the pulsating reggae-powered Durham Deep (adenunciation of Apartheid), the classic tracks include Healing Hands, Club At TheEnd Of The Street, Stones Thrown From Hurtin’, the ballad Sacrifice—it would behis first ever Number One hit in Britain, I Never Knew His Name and Amazes Me,which Elton and Bernie Taupin handles with outstanding care and real perfection.Already free from cocaine addiction and alcoholism, Elton John had done it againwith this wonderful album that is filled with hope and struggle, as it strike the rightnote at the same time without missing a beat.  Truly hailed as one of his greatestand most important achievements, Sleeping With The Past is a bonafide five starmasterpiece that will live forever on as a timeless testament for Elton and Taupin,and as a time-honoured classic that will remain as aspiring for countless of ages.
summary: This One Is A Superb Work Of Stunning Genius!

Robert Mile's DREAMLAND is probably my favorite trance album to date. It's dreamy soundscape has a much softer tone to it than most other artists in this genre which makes for a nice release from all the happy dance music flooding mainstream radio today. Don't misconstrue what I'm saying, though. Dirty Vegas, Kylie Minogue and Paulina Rubio are among the best artists to emerge in 2002 but I've recently needed a break from all these sappy love songs and wannabe dance anthems, so I turned (with little surprise) to the old but never out-dated DREAMLAND by Robert Miles. 23 AM (which is a little more new-agey than this) is another amazing album by Robert Miles but I think that DREAMLAND still remains my favorite. I might buy ORGANIK someday but from what I've heard it's not too great, which is hard for me to fathom because everything I've ever heard from Robert Miles is simply amazing... DREAMLAND is a fine mixture of smooth electronica, new age and trance.My favorite songs include "In My Dreams", "Children (Dream Version)", "Fable (Messsage Version)", and "One And One", which both feature the gorgeous vocals of Maria Nayler who deeply contributes to the album's magical and very surreal atmosphere which is sheer heaven to the senses. So do the world a favor by purchasing this masterpiece of an album which is probably already considered a classic to trance fans that know a gem when they hear it.This is highly recommended.

Elton has a record of spotty albums since his 70's pinnacle. For every "Too Low For Zero," there has been a "Leather Jackets," and "Peachtree Road" is the backslide from "Songs From The West Coast." A lot has been made of this album's returning to a Southern Gothic feeling that informed "Tumbleweed Connection," but it only holds true for a couple of the numbers here. The majority of "Peachtree Road" sounds stale and uninspired. At this time, Rufus Wainwright and the Scissor Sisters are doing Elton John better than Elton is.The CD starts off promisingly enough, as "Weight Of The World" finds a laid back Elton singing "I'm happy to say I'm amazed that I'm still around." The southern influence continues on "Porch Swing In Tupelo," a bluesy paean to Elvis. But then the gospelish "Answer In The Sky" plops in, and it's a belly flop of a song. Sounding way too restrained and hokey to be uplifting, it comes off completely unconvincing. Unfortunately, the album never really gains momentum after that. "They Call Her The Cat" is embarrassingly dumb (and this from the man who once sang "Solar Prestige A Gamon") and "Freaks In Love" is pointless, especially when "Songs From The West Coast" covered the emotional landscape with so much more poignancy.I would have a hard time recommending this to anyone but Elton's longest fans. There is nothing here that sticks in your mind after repeated listenings, and it's just too slick to generate any empathy for the performances. "Peachtree Road" is a lazy coasting through the middle of an Adult Contemporary Highway.
It's Duffy, afterall.  She is great and her sound is unusual yet specific.  I would definately reccomend her album to my friends and family too!!!

"Roll the Bones", to my ears, represents the first time in a long time that all the elements of the band are coming together-- after experimenting with softer sounds and cleaner tones on the last couple records, and synth-driven rock before that, Rush seems to have found a good balance with "Roll the Bones".  With Lee's confident vocal delivery supported by unparallel musicianship, great songs, great lyrics, and (finally!) great arrangements, Rush has turned out an album as good as the work they'd done ten years beforehand.A trend with Rush albums is that they seem to be putting the songs I enjoy the most right up at the front of the album, "Dreamline", opening this one, is no exception-- what a great song, churning verses breaking into a driving chorus, blazing guitar solo, its a song born to be listened to rolling down the highway (likely a bit too fast at that...).  The band shifts gears into the rolling grooves of "Bravado", a great minor key ballad, clearly showing how much better they'd gotten at this form than on "Presto".  Following this up is one of the more interesting cuts on any Rush album, the title track, "Roll the Bones".  Funky rhythms, synth hits, interspersed acoustic guitars and a bizarre rap make this one totally unique in the Rush catalog.  Its a lot of fun-- this is an element of the band that started to emerge at this point, the fact they COULD have fun, but beyond that, its a great piece, stellar vocals, and a compulsively funky bassline accentuated by great playing from Lifeson and Peart.So this was a pretty golden start, the album does kind of drift after this-- similar to the Rush albums of old, none of the material is really bad, it just doesn't grab you-- "Face Up", "Where's My Thing?" (the latter being an instrumental-- first on a Rush album since "YYZ" on moving pictures), a pair of funky songs, like I said, both really listenable, and good album tracks, but not noteworthy.  Ditto for "The Big Wheel", "Heresy" and "Neurotica".But there's one more gem on in here as well, the stunning "Ghost of a Chance"-- a straightforward love ballad, really a rarity on Rush albums (the only other ones I can think of prior to this is 1980's "Entre Nous"), this one is really a pretty, sweet song, and for a band that doesn't really explore these themes, they succeed quite well at it.Bottom line, "Roll the Bones" is a great record, probably the best the band did in eight years or so at this point.  Recommended.

Jeff Buckley has been enormously over-praised since he died in 1997, for a man who only released one album in his short musical career, that being this album, "Grace". "Sketches for My Sweetheart" has some terrific songs on it, but the songs that Jeff was mucking about with on 4 track really suck.It's common for artists to be glorified after death; Jeff and his father Tim, are no exception to this common rule."Grace" is a great album; what bothered me about Jeff was his tendency to go into Led Zeppelin territory with his guitar playing and singing. I love "Mojo Pin", "Lilac Wine" "Lover You Should Have Come Over", "Dream Brother", "Grace", "Hallelujah" and "Corpus Christi Carol" which always bring chills up my spine.The only out of place song is "Eternal Life" which is a plain rock out and doesn't belong on the album! The rest of the album is classic, but this song brings it down.Jeff was a very talented young man, blessed with a great voice. He showed a lot of promise with this album and some of the songs on "Sweetheart"; it's really a shame he can't be here to show us.By the way, Jim DeRogatis, the music critic, is a total retard. In REVOLVER, he just totally slammed both Buckley's, especially Jeff, just to spite them. That's not what I'm saying at all. Jeff was very talented, but just needed to make a couple more albums to really show his full talent. DeRogatis is a fat critic who doesn't know anything at all.

To be honest, I like 2 songs on this CD, Downtown Train- greatly saved by  G.E. Smith's guitarwork- and Hang Down Your Head.  Tom Waits's music is a  bit too strange to work on any sort of pop level and for that he became a  cult hero.  His lyrics are certainly an avant-garde poetic interpretation  of urban streets and are worth a second and third look.  How he puts it to  music is certainly tough to handle at times and even how he sings can be  really rough.  Still, Waits is a treasure, a special songwriter.  He can  weave through his rough vocals a certain storytelling quality that is  undeniably strong and charismatic.  Downtown Train is electrified through  Waits vocals and Smith's guitars.  It is hands down better than Rod  Stewart's version.  This album may lack a certain rock-pop quality, but  what it does contain is a genuine character telling some great stories.  Tom Waits is amazing, I can tell that just by this album.

On this 'record' Elton finally returns to the sound that made him a superstar in the first place. Primarily Voice, Piano and Band. Hints of Tumbleweed Connection, great songs, and most of important of all the production. Oh what a relief to hear an Elton John album that isn't completely ruined by being over-produced, like so many were in the 80's and 90's.The only weak track for me is 'The Wasteland' which just sounds like a bit of a filler. However, one track sums this album up for me, and its "This Train Don't Stop There Anymore". This is the best single track Elton has recorded since the 70's in my opinion, and certainly in my top 10. This track would be worthy of a place on Goodbye Yellow Brick Road, or Honky Chateau.From what I have read recently 'The Captain and The Kid' may also be a return to 70's form for Elton. If it matches this one I'll be buying it.

This is such a great, great record.The music, like the artist, is muscular, feminine, smart, and sexy sexy sexy as hell.A big chunk of the credit has to go to producer Pierre Marchand, who put together an aural landscape that grabs the listener and gives them a firm shake.But, for all the fine performances here--the rock hard drumming on "Building A Mystery," the great guitar play all the way through--the star of the show is McLachlan's angelic voice.  She sells the rockers, but to hear her whisper "I Love You," or the CD-single accapella versions of "Sweet Surrender" through headphones is just too much heaven.And, as she proved to the nation on "Saturday Night Live" and a thousand live audiences during her North American Tour, this woman is all that and more.  If a boy-band had put together a live act or an album with 1/10th the depth and magnitude of this stuff, Arista would have multiplied the hype budget by 500.This is NOT a "girl group" LP.  It's full-blown Pop at its best, a masterful album from a top flight artist. I can't get enough of it.
