"Streetlife Serenade" was the third album released by Billy Joel.  His prior album, "Piano Man" enjoyed some commercial success.  "Piano Man" contained such signature songs as the title-track and "Captain Jack".  From a commercial standpoint, "Streetlife Serenade" was considered somewhat of a disappointment.  It failed to build on the momentum of Joel's 2nd album.  However, this album is at not loss from a quality standpoint.  In fact, there is some very good material from both a musical and lyrical standpoint.  Overall, this album (along with "Cold Spring Harbor") probably is Billy Joel's most overlooked album and therefore provides a refreshing change of pace - especially when you are someone who has heard Billy Joel's chart topping  hits..I look at Billy Joel's career as having three phases. The first phase is what I call "Old Billy Joel". This basically includes all of his material from "Cold Spring Harbor" through "Turnstiles". These are perhaps the strongest days as the piano sound, but they also contain most of Joel's least heard material. The next phase is what I call "Middle Billy Joel". This was his most successful period and covers from "The Stranger" to "Billy Joel Greatest Hits Volume 1 and 2". Joel would go through a transition during this phase - expanding his musical horizons and exploring different avenues. The final phase is the "Later Billy Joel" phase - this covers "The Bridge" to "River of Dreams". In this phase, Billy would start to incorporate some of his older styles of music while not abandoning his desire to continue to explore new avenues.  "Streetlife Serenade" falls into the heart of the "Old Billy Joel" era as it solidifies Billy's reputation as the 'Piano Man' with lots of piano based tunes.Following his 1971 debut album of "Cold Spring Harbor", Billy Joel would leave the familiar surroundings of New York and go to California.  The song "Piano Man" reflects Billy's experience as a lounge singer in Los Angeles.  "Streetlife Serenade" continues the theme of Billy reflecting about his personal experiences in California.  It would be his follow-up album to "Streetlife Serenade" - "Turnstiles" where Billy would "Say Goodbye to Hollywood" and return to New York.One thing to note, the remastering of this album is going to make a great difference.  This album was released in 1974, but  the sounds that are going to come out of this album are amazing - you would think it was recorded in the 1990s.  It is amazing what technology can do.Here is a Track by Track breakdown:"Streetlife Serenader":  The opening piano notes are going to set the stage for the album - and Billy singing over the Piano and then folding in the rest of the band shows a staple of what would become his career.  Lyrically this is a good song as Billy as he perhaps describes himself being a product of "the simple life" when it comes to music."Los Angelinos": A staple of Billy's career has always to sing about places.  In this song, Billy pays tribute to the people of Los Angeles.  This is more of a guitar and rock song, but it works well.  Billy delivers great passion."The Great Suburban Showdown":  A soft song that won't excite you musically, but this is a strong one musically.  In this song Billy sings about "flying east" to "Sit around with the folks".  Definitely reflects Billy's visits back to New York from California."Root Beer Rag":  This is one of two instrumentals on this collection.  In my opinion, Billy should do more instrumentals.  This is an Old "Rag-Time" Style piano number.  This is the Piano Man at his best.  It's a shame this song often gets forgotten about."Roberta":  In this song Billy describes an experience (whether its based on fact or fiction, we don't know) with a prostitute.  Billy's piano is outstanding in this song.  Once again Billy delivers some passionate vocals."The Entertainer":  This is the most well-known song on the collection.  This features a combination of synthesizers and guitars.  I think the best part of this song is the lyrics.  Billy delivers a strong commentary against what was the current state of the music industry.  In a lot of ways, this is something that can still be applied to today's music - such as: "Today I am your champion, I may have won your hearts; But I know the game, you'll forget my name; And I won't be here in another year; If I don't stay on the charts" and "If you're gonna have a hit you gotta make it fit; So they cut it down to 3:05""Last of the Big Time Spenders" : Another tune where Billy sings over the Piano and then folds in the rest of the band.  This song definitely reflects on Billy's time as a struggling musician while in California as he sings lines such as "When it gets down to desperation; You make the best of the situation"."Weekend Song":  The Piano and the Band strike a good balance here.  This song reminds me a lot of some of Billy's material from the "Later Billy Joel" period and sound ahead of his time.  Lyrically Billy sings about looking leaving a day's work and looking forward to kicking back."Souvenir": This is a short song on the album (about 2 minutes).  It doesn't excite me very well, but it is well written.  Billy sings about the memories being a stronger "souvenir" than the actual physical souvenirs."The Mexican Song":  This is the album's finale and is the second instrumental on the album and is another gem.  It starts out with Billy on the piano and the band comes in.  The "Mexican" theme reflects on the close distance from Southern California to Mexico.  This song has a very catchy feel to it.The remastered collection includes all of the lyrics.  Overall, there is some good stuff that gets forgotten about when looking at Billy Joel's career.  This is highly recommended.
summary: Contains many forgotten Billy Songs - especially of his LA Days

reviewText: "Winner Takes All" was somewhat of a creative setback for The Isley Brothers. The band was making a transition from its rock-and-soul sound to one more suited for the dancefloor/disco scene of the late '70s. Unfortunately, some of the songs are filler and for the first time the classic sound shows some wear and tear.It seems like Ernie and Marvin Isley wanted more of the slapping guitar-and-bass sound popularized by The Brothers Johnson. It works on the lead single "I Wanna Be with You" and the title track, arguably the best uptempo songs. However, it was getting a little repetitive by the time you heard "It's a Disco Night (Rock Don't Stop)" and "Liquid Love" sounds like the group was struggling to merge its classic rock style with the newer style.Fortunately, The Isley Brothers didn't abandon their penchant for ballads. In fact, because "Winner" is a double album it gave them the leeway to put more ballads than usual on an album. The ballad "Let's Fall in Love" seems to pick up where "Groove with You" left off and two-fer "You're the Key to My Heart" and "You're beside Me" are two great songs married together by Ernie Isley's guitar playing. Add the yearning of "Love Comes and Goes" and the slow drags, while not as brilliant as some of their earlier ballads, are the true gems.In the pantheon of the 3+3 era, I would rank this as The Isley Brothers' ninth best album. It's an above-average set and even good in certain spots, but it pales compared to their first six albums and IMO ranks behind "Go All the Way" and "Between the Sheets."
summary: The bloom was coming off the rose, starting here

reviewText: Like many people, I heard of "Jason Falkner" after many years of listening to "Jellyfish". Though this album isn't the caliber of those from his former band, it is similar, and still very good. It's smart alt-pop, well constructed and easy to like. I tend to enjoy the first half of this disc more than the other, but it's all good at the very least. There's also a 12th track on the album called "Untitled", which is actually one of my favorites, and a great ending to a great record. As with most albums, this too gets better with each playing.

After their second album 'Talk On Corners' deservedly broke through in the UK fans were eager for a good follow-up.  As one of the few folk acts to do well in the UK it was a shame that the group seemed to sell out a bit and go for a polished pop album rather than retaining their Celtic roots.  Working with Robert 'Mutt' Lange (Shania Twain's husband and also the guy behind a lot of the best Bryan Adams material) on tracks 'Breathless', 'All The Love In The World' and 'Irresistible', the studio effort is plain to see.  In this it loses a lot of what made the Corrs popular in the first place.That certainly isn't to say that this is a throwaway album as there are some outstanding tracks here, just that they don't seem personal enough.  In particular, the excellent 'No More Cry' and 'Rain' written about the death of their mother shouldn't have been polished to the extent that they were.  But there's still the British number one 'Breathless' here, which is one of the group's best ever songs as well as 'Radio', which some may recognise from the Unplugged album.  Other recognisable tracks include 'All The Love In The World', used in the hit movie 'American Sweethearts'.  Undoubtedly the faster songs are better here, apart from the surprisingly sweet 'Somebody For Someone'.  Yet the only reminder of their roots comes in the instrumental at the end, 'Rebel Heart', which is prime Corrs.As an album unto itself this is very good, but as a follow-up to 'Talk On Corners' it doesn't cut it.  Anyone who's heard 'Queen Of Hollywood' will know what I mean.  Thankfully though this isn't due to the songwriting or the vocals - both remain intact - just the production.

Finally! One of the very best "lost albums" of the early 80's arrives on CD!!!!!Many of you will recognize the tracks "Girls Like Me" and "Shelly's Boyfriend" from the movie Valley Girl. But there's MUCH more to this CD than those two tracks, and not a single dud to be found!This is an amazing album that should have had HUGE SUCCESS when it was originally released in 1982. Unfortunately, because it was released on the upstart "Slash" label, it didn't have the same backing as other similar efforts by artists on major/mainstream labels. Fans of the Go-Go's, Josie Cotton and 80's "New Wave" will LOVE this CD! "Good Clean Fun" perfectly captures the magic and fun of the early 80's new wave era. In fact, I would choose it as one of the top 5 albums of 1982 and one of the VERY BEST ALBUMS of the 80's, period!Bonnie Hayes is a sister of Chris Hayes (lead guitarist - Huey Lewis and The News).The follow-up release to "Good Clean Fun" was "Brave New Girl" (a six song EP in 1984). While it contained a couple of decent tracks, it lacked the magic of her debut. Bonnie went solo in 1987 with a very ordinary and over-produced effort. She has continued to record and has always managed to deliver a few great tracks on each album. Good Clean Fun still remains her best effort and is an amazing tribute to a wonderful time and place, known as the "early 80's" :)My only complaint about this release; they could have perhaps included the six tracks from 1984's "Brave New Girl" as an extra.Get this CD... you'll absolutely LOVE IT! Guaranteed!JM
summary: One of the all-time best albums from the 80's!!!

reviewText: This was a great point in Roy Oribon's career b/c he was resurrected out of obscurity by his inclusion with the "Traveling Wilburys" supergroup.Back in the later 80's, all of the Traveling Wilburys had albums that came out at around the same time with each other of the friends helping each other out.If youy like the Traveling Wilburys (and who could not!) then you would have to enjoy this work. I think that Tom Petty, George Harrison and Roy all had their cds produced by former ELO frontman Jeff Lynne. This cd is an extention to Petty's "Full Moon Fever", Harrison's "Cloud Nine" and Lynne's "Armchair Theater".Of course, the trademark sound of Orbison's yearning vocals, twangy guitar, hook filled choruses and rockabilly themes are still there.Some highlights of the cd is the often heard "You got it", plus the gems of "Shes a mysrtery to me", "California Blue" and "Dream you". The rest of the songs are great and there is definitely no filler on this final tributory album.There are a lot of collaborations/assistance from other noted artists but, unlike the Santana nonsense ( I hate it and see it as a corporate raid into otherwise sacred rock music), the help is very subtle thereby preserving this as a true Orbison work.This cd has the essense of a true classic and should always remain timeless.

The best thing about Smash Mouth is that, as much as they love music, they never take themselves too seriously.  Their sound ranges from sixties party to contemporary pop, with a heavy influence of early rock.  Their lyrics are often satiric or downright humorous, with undercurrents of more serious concerns."Diggin' Your Scene" evokes the late sixties with a beat that one can imagine woman in vinyl mini-skirt dancing to while their stoned guys stand mesmerized by the colored lights.  The lyrics poke fun at the sixties lingo while describing a guy's obsession with a dangerous woman.  The following "I Just Wanna See" has the same kind of fun sound with hippy philosophy:  "Doctors and lawyers race for the ball/And I don't even wanna understand it all/I just wanna see."  "Then The Morning Comes" nods to the Beach Boys and to the surfer movies of the sixties; you can almost see the montage of skinny hippies and girls in polka dot bikini running toward the ocean. Not all the tracks are retro (except for the fact that the album was released in 1999).  The pop chart favorite "All Star" is a catchy tune about embracing the life that fame brings.  Ironically, "Stoned" sounds less retro than one would expect.  The group's foray in reggae ("Road Man") is less successful than the other tracks."Astro Lounge" is rock/pop for those who miss the sixties and seventies -- or wish they had lived through them.  -- Debbie Lee Wesselmann
summary: A CD Influenced by Early Rock

reviewText: Content: 4 stars; Sound Quality: 2 stars = Overall: 3 stars.This album represents the best work that Sly has done from his "happy", optimistic period before he had a severe attack of pessimism (realism?) shortly after so evident on "There's a Riot Goin' On".  Lots of good singles here that would make it on any best of compilation of the band like "Stand!", "I Want To Take You Higher", "Sing A Simple Song", "Everyday People" and "You Can Make it if You Try".  That's 5 out of the total of 8 tracks from the album!  Other than "Don't Call Me Nigger, Whitey", the other tracks resemble little more than filler and that's especially the case for all 14 minutes of "Sex Machine".  Still, this album is a classic for the impact that it has had for the future of funk music and its influence on music since then cannot be underestimated.  This mini-lp replica sleeve version very faithfully recreates the original lp design down to the inner sleeve and includes a 12-page colour booklet which has an essay by Barney Hoskyns and all the lyrics.  There are 5 bonus tracks as well which are single versions of "Stand!", "I Want To Take You Higher" and "You Can Make it if You Try" and two previously unreleased tracks: "Soul Clappin' II" and "My Brain".  The only disappointment for me of this version of the album is the poor sound quality.  For an album that's supposed to be remastered, you can only presume that the quality of the master tapes have deteriorated so badly that this is the best that they could do which doesn't amount to much sadly.  A shame really; Sly's classic really does deserve better.
summary: Sly's Best from His "Happy" Period; Too Bad about the Sound!

reviewText: "Forgiven, Not Forgotten" is a stunning, infectious debut for this wonderful Irish family to begin with. Of the 3 studio albums the band has done, I think "Forgiven, Not Forgotten" showcases the band's roots the best especially with the instrumentals like "Erin Shore" and "The Minstrel Boy". "Heaven Sent" and "Leave Me Alone" are my two all time favorite songs off this excellent pop cd. Those two songs are two excellent examples of combining pop with Irish music. The band may have been a little green when this album came out but I think this album really shows the listener their talents as musicians. Other than their unplugged cd, I consider "Forgiven, Not Forgotten" my favorite Corrs album.

The Game's Documentary is a somewhat solid opus from G-Unit. I am personally not a fan of G-Unit. But I've been dedicated to Hip-Hop before many of these other reviewers even knew that Hip-Hop existed. I'll try to keep my review really short here. I will try to collectively dissect the album all together without getting into detail about every song.The Documentary offers a great deal of potential. The Game is a good but not superior lyricist, proving that he can paint pictures and create verbal imagery extremely well. He also seems to have a great understanding of balance in terms of his delivery, vocabulary, wit, and wordplay. In my book, these are the characteristics that make MC's great. The Game proves this relentlessly. However, The Documentary is not really a complete album or a classic. First of all the album lacks the continuity that many classic albums have from a production standpoint. This project was created for one sole purpose....to generate hype...and then to generate sales! This is evident , due to the number of high profile producers jumbled up into producing this album. The Game and so many other of Hip Hop's current rappers suffer from this. Many of the listeners will find themselves overtime skipping songs throughout the album to find their personal favorite, rather than playing it without skipping one song. Secondly, even though The Game has shown potential...he must avert from the continuous name dropping that is so prevalent on the album. It's one thing to give respect to the legends, but to continuously ride them and to compare yourself to them is in my opinion weak. He's a self proclaimed legend...promoting a self proclaimed classic. The streets and the overall audience determines who the legends and classics are, not you the artist. I also find myself struggling to believe The Game's credibility. It seems as if he's so busy trying to prove himself. Whether it be through gang affiliations or just sitting there posing giving his hardest mean mug look. Come on...The Game reminds me of a quote I once heard from E-40 "I gotta mirror in my pocket, so I can practice looking hard".Why is he so infatuated with NWA??? Is it because he's just as phony as they were? 50 Cent, The Game, and G-Unit all together are obvious gimmicks. re-creations of Chris Rock's satirical look at gangsta rappers in CB4. A real gangsta doesn't have to continuously prove anything to anyone. If this kid didn't have the G-Unit stigma attached to him, this album would have been a lot better. This also would have been much better if he would have regressed from the constant legend comparisons and name references which become even more redundant as time progresses. If he's claiming to be the resurrection of The West Coast, then why does he have this psuedo New York thugged out accent? My west coast counterparts as well as myself don't know of anyone from LA who talks like this. Hell, I had no idea he was from Cali until he said so. But that's not really the important issue.Ultimately I love this kid's potential...He really wants to show his dedication and love, but he's caught in a paradox, trying to please too many people, and not genuinely being himself. I honestly believe that he can stand on his own without being connected to Aftermath or G-Unit. If he can ultimately prove his maturity one day as an MC. Who knows what he'll be capable of. The Documentary is a listenable, but not timeless album.
summary: Album has potential, but is plagued in a few areas 3.5 Stars

I am genuinely sad to give this CD a three star evaluation; it's the first time I have awarded anything by Mark Knopfler less than five stars. I have loved both Dire Straits and Mark's solo career uniformly up to this point, but I have listened to "Kill to Get Crimson" several times over the last couple of weeks, and it has largely failed to grow on me with a few exceptions.There is no question that the musicianship here is first rate; there are few things that I enjoy more than listening to Mark with an acoustic guitar in an ensemble setting (although I love the Stratocaster, too, of course!) but my problem with this release is the startling uniformity of the songs. One of the things I always appreciated about Mark was his ability to master different musical genres and styles within a given album; here the songs are simultaneously excellent, yet predictable. With the exception of "Punish the Monkey" the songs on this CD are largely interchangeable stylistically, to the overall detriment of the work. It pains me to say it, but some of the album is just...well, boring. While any given song can stand by itself, as a collection I was underwhelmed.I liked the first half of the CD less than the last half, with "The Fizzy and the Still" being my least favorite in the collection. The second half of the CD is more interesting. I like the corporate intrigue that is so well illustrated in "Punish the Monkey," which I consider to be the best overall song on the CD. The other standout is "The Fish and the Bird," a song about two star-crossed lovers who could never be together even though it creates lifelong pain; it's a beautiful song about responsible romantic realities. "Let It All Go" is another winner that highlights Mark as an ensemble musician.While I am reluctant to give any Mark Knopfler CD three stars, I still recommend the album to fans, particularly to Mark completists, folk, and country audiences. I am glad that I bought the CD, and though it will never be my favorite of his works, I will surely revisit it on occasion, and will certainly see him on the tour that supports the CD release.
summary: Punish The Monkey; The Fish And The Bird Have Been Through Enough

Mike Oldfield cautiously dips one foot into the early 80's synth-pop waters whilst still clinging to his prog-rock life raft in this interesting, if somewhat uneven offering. The inevitable 20 + minute opus is surrounded by some poppier, more conventionally structured songs. In fact, I'm sure there are millions of Hall & Oates fans blissfully unaware that the blue-eyed soul duo's top ten hit "Family Man" was penned by Mr. "Tubular Bells" himself! The title song bears more than a passing resemblance to M's seminal synthpop dance hit "Pop Muzik" (and may in turn have "inspired" 1984's "One Night In Bangkok".... Not a masterpiece, but a well-executed and mostly satisfying listen.
summary: "Only THREE stars?! This just won't do for our little club. UNHELPFUL!"

RIGHT TO BE WRONG - Joss sings about how it's okay to make mistakes ("My mistakes will make me strong") and how she has the right to do her own thing. 8/10JET LAG - She compares her love for her significant other to being jet-lagged, how it makes her feel light-headed and dizzy. It's a love song, but I never though jet-lag was something people enjoyed. Regardless, it's a really nice track. 9/10YOU HAD ME - The first single. This one is about not putting up with a guy's drug/alcohol/etc. problems anymore and how it's time to move on ("I don't want you here, messing with my mind... I'm taking back my life"). 9/10SPOILED - This song is about a girl whose boyfriend's love for her is/was so undeniable, how he spoiled her with his love, and how no other man could ever live up to him. It's very sweet. 8/10DON'T CHA WANNA RIDE - This is just a fun, breezy song to listen to while you're driving down the highway. Don't really know what it's about, but it's a nice mid-tempo song. 6/10LESS IS MORE - For those in a suffocating relationship, you can relate. Joss sings about needing some space and how she doesn't need a guy calling her 24/7 or bringing her a dozen roses, and how, sometimes, less truly is more. 9/10SECURITY - Love this song! It's beautiful. One of my favorite tracks. It's about being there for a friend when times get rough and they feel they can't go on ("If your heart is locked and you can't find the key /Lay your head upon my shoulder/ I'll set you free /I'll be your security"). 10/10YOUNG AT HEART - You know when you're dating someone and everyone you know says he's no good for you? Well that's what this song is about in which Joss sings "You're wasting your time trying to tear us two apart /you can't stop our plans /we were destined from the start /He loves me; I love him". 7/10SNAKES AND LADDERS - Joss compares her relationship with a guy to the game `Snakes and Ladders ("Are we gonna to take that last step together /Going round and round and up and down/Feels just like snakes and ladders"). It's cute. 7.5/10UNDERSTAND - Joss sure hopes you understand that she can't always be there every time you call. It doesn't matter who she's with or what she's doing. All that matters is that she's in love with you, so please understand. OK, that's basically what they song's about. It's alright. 6/10DON'T KNOW HOW - This reminds me of junior high school, in a way, how a girl has a major crush on a guy and wants the guy to be with her, but doesn't now how to make it happen. 8.5/10TORN & TATTERED - Never much cared for this song, but it's about being sick of "living my life singing the same old song", pretty much. 5/10KILLING TIME - To be quite honest, I'm not really sure I understand what this song is about, but I love it. However, I think it's about how you shouldn't waste your life. In it she sings "You better stop what you're doing before you do it all wrong again" and "We struggle with the tide/Falling with our hearts but then in my mind no point in killing time". This took a while to grow on me, but once it did...WOW! I'm lovin' it. 10/10SLEEP LIKE A CHILD - This song has a very haunting feel to it that I love. It's beautiful. It's very calming and relaxing. I think this song is about death or how you shouldn't be afraid. I'm leaning towards the latter. 10/10
Maybe it's because I'm a male but I wasn't too impressed with this disc. Jazmine does have talent and I can't wait to hear her live when I go see Maxwell live, but the CD just didn't anything for me.

reviewText: Wu tang clan is the greatest rap group in hip hop history. Period point blank no doubt about it. This group of 9 m.c's has absolutely  revolutioned the rap world with a supreme level of talent never seen before in no genre of music. I have supreme respect for the legendary groups( Run Dmc,  Epmd, A tribe called quest, NWA and outkast who comes closet). But  Wu tang Clan's legacy and influence is world wide spread and it has no bounderies. I,am a former army vet and I have met people from all over the world with very unique foreign backgrounds that loves the Wu tang clan's music. So many classic albums and successful careers has been launched from this one group that it is dam near insane to believe. People wanted RZA to make the same dark type rugged tracks he produced on 36 chambers but a artist and genius producer like RZA would never take such a lazy approach by doing the same thing twice. I love the slick grandiose back drops found on Wu tang forever. You can tell that RZA  had been studying music arrangements and orchestra compositions by the polished instrumentation of many tracks off the album such as " impossible" and "Reunited".  Who could get away with putting violens in a hip hop song but RZA? Remember now, this was back in 1997 when hip hop purists myself included demanded that hip hop stay hardcore and true to the art. In today's rap scene its customary to have soft sounds, vocals and watered down beats to sell out to a wider audience. Wu tang clan forever is raw unfilthered hip hop from the bows of the streets, the sound is just more refined and epic on their second album. Some people will find something to complain about no matter what a artist does but I commend RZA and the entire clan for putting another classic out that has its own vibe, sound and legacy. 97 truly was the God year as RZA stated in his memoir "The Tao of the Wu" . Wu tang clan made a gavalnizing but lyrically sinister album stocked up with a plethora of jewels. I love the one joint "Bells of War" where at the end the RZA says to a kid, "you don't even have to go to summer school shortie just cop the wu tang forever album and you will get all the education you need".  Its ironic that statement was made because I cut school and listened to this album all day when it was first released (lol). I got so much information, knowledge of self awareness that it left a lifetime impression on me from a young 18 year old hopper until even now. Wu tang clan forever is a masterpiece of epic proportions. And the few who complain only wanted a 36 chambers part II instead of another chapter of the wu tang saga. We all have opinions and the right to be objective but it is weird to me  how new artists will put the same old song and dance out and people buy into it everytime?  Very boring uncreative and uninspiring to say the least. Wu tang clan forever comes from the nineties when being versatile, creative and different were some of the ingredients to making a classic rap album. Lyrically superior and musically ahead of its time, wu tang clan is a definitive album that has maintained its monumental standing as a master stroke of genius by the greatest rap group in hip hop history.
summary: The Tao of Wu tang forever.

reviewText: FUEL! This band recalls the lost days when fearless rock gods roamed the earth and assaulted people's ear drums with crunching ferocity. In a pathetic age of packaged garbage passed off as music, FUEL rumbles into town with "Something Like Human", their 2nd major label release. These guys don't hold back and look to kick anyone's a** that gets in the way. Don't bother comparing the new album to their previous "Sunburn" CD because...well,why?  I find "Hemorrage"(In My Hands) to be a anthem for the 21st Century. "Innocent" has so much emotional kick, you'll need Kleenex after listening to it. The rest of the tunes are superior as well...no filler. Just embrace them as your own, play them loud and proud, and never be a sellout. Ahhhhh, I remember the days when bands that rocked like FUEL were revered and honored as....Something Like Human, but more like gods.

After hearing the beautiful cover album 'Girl Versions' by Emm Gryner, a music executive approached Tori with the same idea.  I think it was a great decision Tori made by making one.  Some of these songs are really excellent like the spell binding 'Enjoy The Silence' and the beautiful 'Time' but I don't see what the hype is about ''97 Bonnie & Clyde' for yes, it is sad and truthful but it's not good.  It's the worst song on the album, it's all talking, maybe if Tori sang it, it would be better and maybe even more tragic but I always skip this one for it can get annoying at times.The title track 'Strange Little Girl' is a great cover, a little different than Tori's main focus (the piano) but it steps it up and shows fans that Tori can have a really great song without having it completely piano driven.  And I don't understand why some people dislike 'I'm Not In Love', it's a little different sort of atmosphere but it's hauntingly beautiful.  I also really enjoyed 'Raining Blood', 'Rattlesnakes' and 'New Age'.  This is definitely a must for any Tori fan, I think that some Tori fans were disappointed because it's not completely original but open your ears and mind with this album and you'll find a lot more than you bargained for.

Steely Dan, a definitive soft rock/ jazz rock group, have had a lot of greatest hits/ best of compilations released over the years with a lot of recycling of the same tracks. "A Decade of Steely Dan" was originally released in 1985, & it manages to somewhat stand apart from other Dan compilations such as "Gold" and the 1978 "Greatest Hits". With Steely Dan's 1972-1980 output being, in general, so astonishingly consistent and filled with brilliant songs, plus the fact that their biggest hits do tend to rank among their best work, it's pretty hard to screw things up when assembling a Steely Dan greatest hits/ best of. The tracks on "Decade" are not presented in chronological order, however there is at least one track from each of their '72-'80 albums, & with the track selection being as as strong as it is, this is a great listen and an effective overview of their career. The only inclusion that's particularly questionable is the Duke Ellington/ Bubber Miley-penned instrumental "East St. Louis Toodle-Oo"--yes, I like it, & it's certainly clever, but it's a questionable choice when such total Dan classics as "Any Major Dude Will Tell You", "Any World (That I'm Welcome To)", and "Haitian Divorce", among many others, are missing in action. Still, like I said, this is an effective overview of a band who had boundless creativity when it came to sophisticated, arresting compositions. The thing that really sets this compilation apart is something the previous reviewer has also pointed out--it contains a version of the soundtrack tune "FM" that has a haunting, extended song-ending guitar solo passage from Walter Becker; this is the only Steely Dan CD I know of that contains this superior version of this classic song--the "Citizen" box set, the 2 CD "Show Biz Kids" set, and the aforementioned "Gold" CD all contain the inferior version that ends with an extended sax solo instead. Also, the musician/ performance credits for each individual track are a solid bonus. With a band like Steely Dan, obviously there's a lot more you need than just what's on this disc, but still, it's filled with great songs and is an effective compilation.(P.S. Somewhere along the line the "A Decade of Steely Dan" CD was indeed re-released ("original recording remastered" as they say), but the packaging remained extremely similar. The sound quality on the older version certainly isn't BAD, so it's a solid bargain if you see it around for a couple bucks somewhere. I wouldn't recommend spending a LOT more for the newer version.)
summary: 1 of many SD comps, but one oddity helps this disc stand out

Double albums can be tricky endeavors. Most of them could have easily been whittled down to a single great album (The Clash's "Sandinista" for example) while other double albums wouldn't be the same if a single track was removed.Stadium Arcadium falls in the latter category.I've been a Peppers fan ever since I first got to hear the Uplift Mofo Party Plan CD and I've been hooked ever since. The only release that I don't care for at all out of their entire catalog was 1995's One Hot Minute, which suffered greatly from one time guitarist Dave Navarro ruining their overall sound (not to mention the songs were awful for the most part).Some people have seriously complained about the more mellow direction that the Peppers have gone in starting with 1999's Californication (which was the return to the fold of guitarist John Frusciante).  People forget that now, these guys are in their mid 40's for the most part.  If you want to hear the in your face youthful aggression of their earlier stuff, then just go back and listen to their earlier stuff. Quit complaining that their new stuff isn't Blood Sugar Sex Magik 2.I'm 31 years old now and in a much, much different place than I was 15 years ago. I'm sure the same is for the Peppers as whole as well. I have found that the Pepper's change in direction to a certain extent over the last couple of albums mirrors my life as I've gotten older.But Stadium Arcadium is kind of a kick in the pants with some tracks harkening back to their older style of music. There's other stuff that is more in the laid back mode of 2002's By The Way, but it still has a bit more vibrancy than the stuff on that otherwise great release did.Cd #1 is a little over 62 minutes in length while CD #2 is just a few seconds shy of topping out at exactly an hour in length.That's a lot of music to digest. But the smorgasbord of styles they gallop through on this release makes this one of the best CD's in quite some time to just sit back, chill out and let the sounds envelop you.Some might argue that this release could have been paired down to a single CD of material, but I wholeheartedly disagree. Every song is a gem.Is this as great of a release as Blood Sugar Sex Magik is? Only time will tell, but I can say that it's their best release since that monumental 1991 classic.
summary: Truly amazing and every song is great.

reviewText: "Transmissions..." is the record that showed the Flaming Lips were basically a great guitar pop band, albeit a very strange one. Sure, this is the one that has the big hit ("She Don't Use Jelly") but this is one of those albums that, cliched as it may sound, needs to be listened to in its entireity to really be appreciated. I'm not sure why, but I enjoy this album best during the late summer/early fall time of the year; something about driving around listening to "Turn it On" loudly brings back a certain carefree point in time. The skronk and squall of the Lips' earlier recordings is very much present, but the hooks are clearer and the songwriting seems less like the product of two-day LSD binges. Some of the best tracks here include the wistful "Superhumans," which hints at the pop majesty of the Lips' later work, "Pilot Can at the Queer of God" and the industrial-sized grooves of "Slow Nerve Action."
summary: The Lips' Poppiest Record (at that point)

reviewText: The CD was recorded at different venues, from clubs to arenas, and wanted to emphasize that there was life before "The Stranger".The band sounds tight and polished doing these songs, and some of the versions here blow away the studio versions, esp. in the case of "Everybody Loves You Now", "Miami 2017", "Ballad of Billy The Kid", "Captain Jack", and "Say Goodbye To Hollywood".Because this came out in 1981, I feel that a lot of good songs he had done live were cut out, and now that it's 20-plus years later, it would be great to have a full-length concert from this period, not to mention live cuts that I've heard via bootlegs that really show Billy and his band off as being a "must see" band.He's put out live material since (Millenium Concert, and The Russian Concert), but those are more about documenting an event. He's done a lot of covers in his shows over the years as well.Just going by pre- "Stranger" material alone, an extended version could include the following songs which he did in concert: Travellin Prayer, Somewhere Along The Line, Root Beer Rag, Souvenir, Prelude/Angry Young Man, Still Crazy After All These Years, The Entertainer, Worst Comes To Worst, Ain't No Crime, Weekend Song, James, New York State Of Mind, going back into the Hassles bag with "You've Got Me Hummin", and an early 1972 radio show recorded for Philly's WMMR.There was footage shot for "Songs In The Attic" for video, some of which is available on DVD: "Los Angelenos", "She's Got A Way", "Everybody Loves You Now".There are also some known TV appearances and promos that he did in the 70s: Saturday Night Live, Germany's Musikladen (some of which has been shown on VH1 Classic), England's Old Grey Whistle Test, Don Kirshner's Rock Concert, and Midnight Special as well as a special called "Tonight" he did in 1976.. a lot of which have songs that he either stopped playing altogether or rarely plays. A lot of it is interesting stuff...
summary: Supersize "Songs In The Attic" into a Legacy Edition!!!

reviewText: Norah Jones' latest effort was dissapointing to say the least. I felt there was potential to her when I listened to her first album, but after listening to this album certainly I am not "feeling the same way." The first few songs stand out, but in general the album is (yes, you've heard it before) booooring and repetitive. It's hard to put your finger on almost any song after the fifth track because they all sound very similar and, in a way, dull. "The Prettiest Thing" and the closing Ellington song "Don't Miss You At All" are the only other songs that stand out in the second half of the album: the rest I can totally live without. Granted I loved the use of electric piano on some of the tracks, giving them a bit of an edge, overall I don't see this as more than a two-star album. I recommend Jacqui Naylor's 'Shelter' -far better!

Don't be alarmed if you are somewhat baffled after listening to this album for the first time.  Jack White's description of the album is as intriguing as the album itself, and it doesn't help that it's so ambiguous that it doesn't really explain anything (he describes the album as dealing with "characters and the ideal of truth".  But hey... if he didn't think in such obscurities, he probably wouldn't be as talented as he is :-).  This album is unconventional to say the least, but it is bursting at the seams with interesting ideas.  Jack White is definitely the best of the new class of modern rock guitarist (who else could pull of what he does on the intense, VERY Hendrix inspired "Instinct Blues"?, {although he should have ended the song 30 seconds before he actually does}), and he has one of the greatest minds working in music today.  He manages to orchestrate the mixing of everything from an egg-shaker to the marimba, and the results are consistently musical, even if they are a little obscure and off-kilter.  Jack is also a really good songwriter who's cleverness and sense of humor also make him stand out amongst the crowd of most modern songwriters.  Such a good songwriter is rare in today's murky landscape of talent-less, whiny, self-absorbed rock stars.  Just check out the clever and absolutely hilarious bluegrass ditty "Little Ghost", where the subject falls in love with an apparition that only he can see.  The seemingly sarcastic "Passive Manipulation" is pretty hilarious too (in spite of or perhaps partially because of Meg's poor vocals).  The raw production on this album spares it from being marred by the factory produced, assembly-line-corporate-product feel that plagues a lot of modern music, covering up the "artists'" lack of talent.  There is no such talent deficiency here (well, at least not with Jack, Meg's perfunctory percussions are functional at best).  Jack totally rocks out on the piano on "Doorbell" which is reminiscent of both "I Want You Back" and "ABC" by the Jackson Five.  The almost Dylan-esque "As I Ugly As I Seem" (which basically uses the melody from an old gospel song but I'm not sure what the name of it is) is also pretty impressive, and he sounds like he snuck Aretha Franklin in the studio to play the piano on "I'm Lonely (But I ain't that lonely yet) (which I also find oddly humorous).  Jack White makes it obvious that his artistic ambitions are his top priority given the huge risks that he takes on the CD, especially after their breakthrough success with "Elephant".  He takes a serious gamble here when he could have easily just ridden out the success of the previous album.  This is a daring album that their fans who are uncomfortable with the unfamiliar, unexpected, or unconventional will likely have trouble with.  I encourage everyone to have patience, because you'll be in for a real thrill once this album sinks in.  It is now mid-October, and this is the best new release that I've heard so far this year!

Steve Earle has a voice that is the antedote to computer-enhanced and radio-friendly voices, and that makes his music all the better. This album is a fresh sound from what you hear in mainstream country. There's rawness  of rock and roll combined with the simplicity of country and folk. Steve  starts out rocking with the great first two songs, "Transcendental  Blues" and "Everyone's In Love With You." The guitars are  fierce. They are not indicative of the album, though - Steve decided to  show off his talent with a variety of different styles, and I didn't feel  like pushing the skip button once. The songs are so interesting that you  won't feel awkward through the journey. His love songs use original  phrasing that is very yearning. Regardless of your views on the death  penalty, the last song, "Over Yonder," will make you see things  from the criminal's side. Just one example of the power of his songs.

reviewText: This is an album that, like D'Angelo's "Voodoo," takes some time to get used to and ultimately appreciate.  After a couple of listens, the disc began to grow on me, and now I'm at the point of keeping it on repeat  throughout the day and night.  Her voice is stronger than on previous  recordings, and the songs and production are beautiful.  More than  anything, though, it's her sense of pacing and building a song (similar to  that of Diana Krall) that really stands out.  I love Mariah Carey most of  all female pop/r&b singers, but she could learn a thing or two from  Toni's vocal stylings insofar as not overdoing a song.

DJ Shadow goes hyphy! _The Outsider_ represents a departure in sound for him, even if the the spoken word intro promises something ominous and "This Time" is a piece of sunny upbeat funk. But "3 Freaks" brings in the granddaddy of hyphy, Keak Da Sneak, for some grindy hip-hop more interested in partying than head-nodding. And things continue in that vein for pretty much the entirety of the album. "Seein Things" takes on an angrier tone, addressing the government's mangled response to Hurricane Katrina, leading into the electric guitar blues of "Broken Levee Blues." After some more nonsense, "Triplicate/Something Happened That Day" gets us back to what made DJ Shadow (almost) a household name. After that, the album takes on an indie rock vibe, with "The Tiger" and "Erase You." Christina Carter's delicate voice buoys "What Have I Done." And if "You Made It" sounds suspiciously like a Coldplay sound... well, I blame Chris James for that. But, jarringly, "Enuff" throws the hip-hop back in the fold, even if it's not as grating as the hyphy of the earlier half. I won't even comment on "Dats My Part." It's a maddeningly uneven album, but perhaps it's naive to assume that DJ Shadow would continue doing _Endtroducing_ over and over again. I'm eager to see how he develops next.

Wonder,sort of,had a hit in January 1985,WE ARE THE WORLD,by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie,which was recorded by an all-star ensemble called USA For Africa. reviewText: 'Floodland' is an alternative rock classic, undoubtedly. Andrew Eldritch came back after a difficult three-year hiatus which included the "corrosion" of his band and the Sisterhood project (which was his way of preventing the bandmates from using a name that too closely resembled his Sisters Of Mercy; they later became The Mission UK). Left with a drum machine and new bass player, Patricia Morrison, Eldritch made what is probably their most popular and well-received album. 'Floodland' is a very well-produced work that mixes the pomp and bombast of 70s rock, and the Sisters' more familiar goth-alternative sound. To achieve this mix, Eldritch used Jim Steinman, of Meat Loaf fame, to produce the album. 'This Corrosion' roars on for nearly eleven minutes with a huge forty-piece choir, chugging synths and guitars, and a very upbeat dance rhythm. While the result does sound dated today, it is still an absolute production marvel. 'Lucretia My Reflection' is driven by a forceful, repetitive bassline that sounds doomy as their previous work, but still manages to stick in your head. There is even a sad piano ballad, in the form of '1959' to balance the album out.This reissue of 'Floodland' only proves how well-produced the original album was. The remaster doesn't add a world of change to the old cd issue other than a slight volume boost and maybe a bit more low-end. The packaging is first-rate, however, with an attractive digipak and a booklet filled with pictures and an essay about the album, along with complete lyrics. The four bonus tracks (two of which were added to the original cd pressing of the album) are very welcome, especially the epic twelve-minute full-length of 'Neverland'. Overall, if one is considering repurchasing this because of the remaster, the price is a bit steep for a remaster that only slightly improves the over fifteen-year-old cd. The packaging and bonus tracks might be an incentive to repurchase this, however. This reissue is for fans only; those unacquainted with the group would be better of picking up the cheaper domestic pressing.
summary: Album itself deserves 5 stars, but reissue is spotty

reviewText: When Stevie Wonder applied his tremendous songwriting talents to the unsettled social morass that was the early '70s, he produced one of his greatest, most important works, a rich panoply of songs addressing drugs, spirituality, political ethics, the unnecessary perils of urban life, and what looked to be the failure of the '60s dream -- all set within a collection of charts as funky and catchy as any he'd written before. Two of the highlights, "Living for the City" and "Too High," make an especially deep impression thanks to Stevie's narrative talents; on the first, an eight-minute mini-epic, he brings a hard-scrabble Mississippi black youth to the city and illustrates, via a brilliant dramatic interlude, what lies in wait for innocents. "Too High" is just as stunning, a cautionary tale about drugs driven by a dizzying chorus of scat vocals and a springing bassline. "Higher Ground," a funky follow-up to the previous album's big hit ("Superstition"), and "Jesus Children of America" both introduced Wonder's interest in Eastern religion. It's a tribute to his genius that he could broach topics like reincarnation and transcendental meditation in a pop context with minimal interference to the rest of the album. Wonder also made no secret of the fact that "He's Misstra Know-It-All" was directed at Tricky Dick, aka Richard Milhouse Nixon, then making headlines with the biggest political scandal of the century. Putting all these differing themes and topics into perspective was the front cover, a striking piece by Efram Wolff portraying Stevie Wonder as the blind visionary, an artist seeing far better than those around him what was going on in the early '70s, and using his astonishing musical gifts to make this commentary one of the most effective and entertaining ever heard.

This album is one of the most wicked metal albums ever made. The Scorpions  were out to tear it up and they do it in spades on "Blackout" .  "Dynomite" rocks so hard that it feels like Godzilla is stomping  down your house until there's nothing left. "China White" comes  on like a modern day "Kashmir" in its groove yet it is completely  original in terms of lyric and melody. The band sings a dedication to their  fans on the raucaus and fun "Can't Live Without You."  "Blackout" is a tidal wave of bonecrunching mindmelting metal  that ends with Klaus Meine producing a teutonic scream that would have made  Richard Wagner proud. " When The Smoke Is Going Down" is a  beautiful ballad that is melancholly in its melody yet powerful in its  spirit. This album also contains the fantastic "No One Like You"  which was The Scorpions first top ten hit. This is a great song with a  irresistable melody and a guitar solo that is devastating in its precision  and passion. What can i say except that this is The Scorpions tour de  force. reviewText: It seemed like Ice Cube lost a bit of credibility after starring in Are We There Yet. Before I saw it, I said that dissing Cube because of that really wasn't fair, because he had to redeem himself (although now that I HAVE seen it, it seems like it would've worked better had it been a Disney movie). When my brother asked how doing that movie could be redemption, I simply said one thing: "Did you HEAR Terrorist Threats?"But Cube came back with Laugh Now, Cry Later, an album that seems to get a little better with each listen. As other reviewers have mentioned, things start off on the right foot with the interesting "Why We Thugs". And note to the editorial reviewer: "Child Support" isn't really about that; it's a metaphor about the clichéd lyrics of young rappers. At any rate, that's also a highlight, as is the title track. "Spittin' Pollaseeds" (whatever that means) is also pretty solid, but I don't know if it's really fair to call WC a guest on that track because he's talking, not rapping.There are also a few songs I could do without, especially "Smoke Some Weed". And the filler tracks come in the form of been-there-done-that tales, like cars ("Chrome & Paint") and hardcore sex ("Steal the Show"). Furthermore, the chorus to "Growin' Up" features an out-of-place sample of Minnie Riperton's "Memory Lane". I also agree with my brother when he said that EVERYone's not waiting for another Next Friday (see the "Dimes & Nicks" skit starring Mike Epps).While not the best album Ice Cube has ever done, Laugh Now, Cry Later is still a whole lot better than a lot of the rap that's out right now. Pick it up.Anthony Rupert

I want to give this an honest review because when I first heard it, I was highly disappointed but you know how music can grow on you after you keep listening to it.So now, I'm ready to give my thoughts about "The Original 7ven" (formerly known as "The Time") Condensate.Besides Parliament/Funkadelic & Cameo. "The Time" is my 3rd favorite All-time R&B;/Funk group. Now called "The Original 7ven" (The name change is because "Prince" owns the legal rights to "The Time" name and refuse to let them record this project under it) all the original members (Morris Day, Jimmy Jam, Terry Lewis, Jellybean Johnson, Monte Moir, Jesse Johnson & Jerome Benton) are back after a 21 yr hiatus (That's the same age as my daughter) so I had high expectations that this project is going to be kickin' like their debut album "The Time" or "What Time Is It" & "Pandemonium" but what I heard is more of a Crossover type of R&B;/Rock/Poppish kind of funk instead of that raw gutter funk.They are still using those vintage sounds & Morris Day is still doing his thing vocally but then it dawned on me. This is the first project that "Prince" wasn't involved with the production which can explain why most of that raw gutter funk is missing but nevertheless "The Original 7ven" is STILL funky but not the kind of funky that got me interested in them back in 1981 but I understand it's a new time and era and upon hearing "Condensate" the fellas have incorporated so many different styles that it makes this project really unique from there previous four.One thing I like about this project is that it is pure, unadulterated "Morris Day & The TIME" they didn't try to come back with a New school type of sound instead They kept it slick, funky, rock, hilarious and very creative especially the skits with Morris & Jerome.I was a bit disappointed that my mentors as producers "Jimmy Jam & Terry Lewis" signature melodies were virtually non- existent with the exception of "Faithful" & "GoHomeToYoMan" but on the other hand Guitarist "Jesse Johnson" wrote some killer rock tracks like "Sick" & "Aydkmn" that man plays a mean guitar.Now the hit single "Trendin" is a vintage "Time" groove but I don't see it being a chart busting smash actually none of the songs on the "Condensate" are really Chart topping hits but thanks to today's record executives that pushes bubble gum artists like Lady Gaga, Justin Bieber, Nicki Minaj, Drake & Lil' Wayne. REAL R&B;/Funk Music is NOT going to be played but because "The Original 7ven" are not only great Musicians but also great Performers. They should have pretty good success with promoting "Condensate" I don't see it going "Platinum" but definitely a "Gold" certified album."If I was yo Man" is my favorite cut off the new project but I also like "Trendin", "Cadillac", "Sick", "Lifestyle", "Faithful", "Aydkmn" & "GoHomeToYoMan"I didn't care for "Strawberry Lake" because it reminds me of "Ice Cream Castles" and I didn't like "Ice Cream Castles" when it was released in 1984 and honestly "Ice Cream Castles" is my least favorite album by "The Time" but if you liked "Jungle Love" & "The Bird" you will indeed like "2 Step" & "A Toast To The Party Girl" which is too Poppish for me. "Condensate" & "Role Play" I'm just NOT feeling and "Hey Yo" sounds like a song they should have given to T.I. to Rap on.Even though I'm really not crazy about "Condensate" but I bought it just because of who they are and what they mean to the music industry now celebrating 30 yrs. Check out the DVD documentary that comes with the Cd at Best Buy but overall "Condensate" is just okay but I'd rather see them Live in concert.NOTE: Rumors have surfaced saying "Jesse Johnson has once again left the group" and according to his Facebook page "It's True!" but I certainly hope not because if so then how are they going to be called "The Original 7ven" don't tell me I'm gonna have to wait another 21 years...OMG!

reviewText: On his self-titled debut on J Records, Luther Vandross delivered another classic album. The leadoff single "Take You Out" nearly broke into the top forty, and the followup "Can Heaven Wait" had big success in, of all places, the clubs. (Why anyone would make a club remix of a Luther Vandross song is beyond me.) After that nobody was really talking about his album any more except for people who actually own it...which SHOULD be everybody.Smooth crooners should stay true to their formula, and Luther does just that. The aforementioned "Take You Out" is the kind of simple yet catchy track that more albums should start off with; and "Let's Make Tonight The Night" has that similar style. Then you'll hear him tackling subjects that everyone goes through but only HE can make sound good...case in point: the best track, "I'd Rather": "I'd rather have bad times with you/Than good times with someone else." Then there's "How Do I Tell Her", discussing how a person can be in a relationship with someone and suddenly have the feelings go away. There are also doing-me-wrong songs like "Are You There (With Another Guy)" and "Like I'm Invisible" that compliment Luther's talent magnificently.This album has the same production and arrangement team that has accompanied Luther practically throughout his whole career. They stay true to their formula as well, but in some places it sounds as if the producers are trying to fit in with the kinds of songs through the 14 to 20-year-old R&B circuit; particularly they shouldn't try any faster beats than the beats in "How Do I Tell Her" and "Grown Thangs". But the songs aren't bad by any means. After all, there's no such thing as a bad Luther Vandross album. SO WHY ISN'T THIS ALBUM A FEW TIMES PLATINUM??? HMMM???

Before you purchase your copy of Robert Johnson's Complete Studio recordings, there is another copy out there that has a much different sound remaster:The Centennial Collection.  Unlike this version, it removes much of the old ambiance of the old record (the scratches, the pops, as another put it, the sound of Pre-WW2), and the guitars are much clearer.  However, I actually, have to admit something, that I actually prefer this version of the recordings.  I don't know, while the guitars are much clearer and they sound excellent, the atmosphere of the old recordings, the crackles, pops, and the like, just adds to that grittiness of what makes these recordings even more the newer remastered version just didn't have.  This is just preference, listen to the two and see which sound you prefer more.Robert Johnson, what else can be said about him?  He's an amazing blues artist, and perhaps one of the most influential guitarists and songwriters of the 20th century.  With an influence from almost everybody out there, especially the forever humble Eric Clapton, it's easy to see why he's in almost every guitar poll and creative influence writings.  His life was even more interesting, from being poisoned to death, the famous story about him selling his soul to the devil, and the fact that he lived the life he sang, from every Juke Joint, street corner, and dance event in the Deep South.  Most importantly though, he transcends his already interesting, almost legend like aura to him, and can create some timeless, rich, and always engaging, and absolutely amazing, unbelievably atmospheric, and genuine acoustic blues.I'll be honest, Robert Johnson isn't for everybody.  The very old production values, coupled with only an acoustic guitar, make Robert Johnson an acquired taste.  Even fans of electric blues (Freddie King, Otis Rush, Buddy Guy) and the like (heck, even Howlin' Wolf, for that matter) may not particularly enjoy the extremely stripped down and lo-fi Delta Blues that Robert Johnson is known for.  However, Robert Johnson's earnest music, intricate, varied, and evocative guitar playing, and the realistic breeding ground for which the music itself was spawned just bleeds through the atmosphere of the song, can quickly grown on you, and once it creeps up into you, it never goes away.  The fact that he was nobody, living the actual life of what he sang, just makes these recordings even more authentic than they already sound.  Indeed, this is pure, unfiltered, and totally REAL (all caps for a reason, after all), as pure and artistic as other totally authentic masterpieces such as Nick Drake's Pink Moon or Joy Division's Closer, the akin of stepping into someone else's own soul.I can't think of a single filler track on this record.  Even the alternate takes are interesting and compelling to listen to, with enough change and interesting alternations to make you want to sit through it yet again.  And hey, maybe it's just an excuse to hear the same glorious songs TWO times!  The lyrics themselves are great as well, taking on themes of loneliness, the devil, long lost love, poverty, and every other subject you would expect from a record like this.  While the whole album is good, I would have to single out Crossroad Blues, ____ hounds on my Trail, Me and the Devil Blues, Sweet Home Chicago (check out Buddy Guy's version while you're at it), Traveling Riverside  Blues, Phonograph Blues, and the completely different but absolutely infectious They're Red Hot.  Really though, it has to be heard understand, and then you most certainly will.Whatever copy you prefer, though, Robert Johnson is essential to check out.  There's not much else to say here.  No, Robert Johnson isn't the ONLY "acoustic blues" artist worth listening to (for starters, two other influential artists who played old school blues, Leadbelly and Son House, are just as good, and that's just the beginning of the list), but few did it as well as him.  If you are sick of facile hacks like John Mayer and the like plaguing the blues legacy, pick up Robert Johnson's studio recordings and experience the real thing.  Absolutely essential.

reviewText: Harry Nilsson is one of those classic singers and composers of the rock era that I have the utmost musical admiration for. This man grew up rather hard in Brooklyn,worked from an early age,never was given any sense of entitlement. Yet at the same time,he always maintained his sense of musical elegance and melodicism. Harry's music was as complex as his personality. Intensely catchy to the point of being singalong,cumulative lyricism and one of the sweetest,most broad singing ranges as the genre of rock 'n roll began to transition into the pop/rock era. He had a lot of Paul McCartney and Stevie Wonder in him in that regard,where his own ideosyncracies came together into a music that spoke directly from his soul to the listener themselves. The Beatles and their publicist Derek Taylor were both so captivated by Nilsson's early albums such asPandemonium Shadow Showthat they referred to him as "a fifth Beatle over seas". After covering Randy Newman albums and having his first smash pop hit with "Everybody's Talkin'" from the soundtrack toMidnight Cowboy,Nilsson teamed up with producer Richard Perry and the best pop and rock session players of the day for an album that entirely changed the trajectory of his career."Gotta Get Up" develops from a piano solo into slow bouncing drums as well as from conversational lyrics to more confessional ones regarding the changing experiences of the younger members of the "silent",pre-baby boom generation. Though Nilsson never claimed much for it,"Driving Along" is a strongly musically crafted pop/rock number dealing with personal growth. "Early In The Morning" is one of my favorites here-a stripped down,highly soulful blues with Harry's reflections on a long as well as a both literal and figurative hangover against a ringing electric piano that is just as reverbed as his soaring voice. "The Moonbeam Song" is another of his classic cumulative songs: the lyrics and the melody grows like a flower through his voice and the piano. "Down" has Harry straight in blues mode-with a steamy,slow funky rhythm and Harry's voice dealing with the emotional complexity of the song. "Without You",yet another song Harry interprets by another writer,is probably his ballad masterpiece with its epic expression of emotion. "Coconut" is a witty,comic bluesy folk number with a mild New Orleans soul bent around it. "Let The Good Times Roll" has Harry's simple piano on a melodically catchy country-rock number while "Jump Into The Fire" is a hot,steamy Stonesy rocker with a lot of soul-which Harry just works out on vocally as well. "I'll Never Leave You" concludes the original album with another cumulative and heavier orchestrated ballad.As for the bonus songs "Si No Estas Tu" reworks "Without You" into Spanish. Harry has a terrific facility for foreign language interpretation and exhibits the flair of a seasoned Latin vocalist here actually-returning to English on the second chorus interestingly enough. "How Can I Be Sure Of You" is a folky rock ballad with a fascinating lyric about a someone who seems rather bound by literary conspiracy theories and...well the title says it all for what Nilsson has to say to the character. "Lamaze" is an unusual number. Rapped partially in faux melodramatic French,the song soon goes into a less musically ornate mode as Harry gives very dry "Lamaze" instructions before ending the song in laughter. "Old Forgotten Soldier" is another ballad with a very straightforward narrative that probably speaks to the internally hardened,streetwise man Harry Nilsson was. Of The two demo's? "The Moonbeam Song" is closer to the original where "Gotta Get Up" sounds more like something out of Harry's more psychedelic late 60's albums. Overall this album did something that only happens with the right combination of talents and inspiration: it bought the talent of Harry Nilsson to everyone. He was no longer a mere musicians musician/one hit wonder after this album. Not only did it prove he could totally carry an album that was both tuneful and popular. But also that he was more than album to zero in on the most vital aspects of his musical talent and continue to fly with it. Everything just clicked with him on this album. And for those already familiar with any of Nilsson's music would be well advised to seek out this classic album. You will likely soon discover why its considered as such!
summary: Harry Nilsson Finally Earns His Musical Tunesmithing Wings!

reviewText: Metric's 2009 FANTASIES marked a new direction for the band.  Much of the band that recorded the critically acclaimedOld World Underground, Where Are You Now?, can still be heard on this album, but the band streamlined its sound with an electronic, glossy, pop approach.Emily Haines and Jimmy Shaw don't sound much like they did with Broken Social Scene.  Instead, their music is a slick, well-produced mixture of electronic synthesizers and rock guitars.  It's reminiscent of the New Wave movement of the 1980's, but it's also very creatively forward-thinking.  The result is a sound that is both retro and modern.  The album begins with "Help I'm Alive," a great single that highlights some of the creative hallmarks of Metric.  From here, the songwriting never fails -- the album is consistently good.  FANTASIES closes with the crunchy and distorted "Stadium Love" that showcases how much fun the band appears to be having with their songwriting.Fans of The Dandy Warhols (circaWelcome To The Monkey House), Blur (circaParklife), M83, or The XX will find a lot here to love.  Preexisting fans of SYNTHETICA or OLD WORLD UNDERGROUND should really enjoy this album.  Highlight tracks to sample: "Help I'm Alive," "Gimme Sympathy," and "Gold Guns Girls."

There are some uncharacteristically fine reviews of this album amongst the usual dross found on Amazon:  For once I encourage those interested to take the time to absorb the opinions noted by consumers.  And this is really only fitting considering that Cyndi is/was/always will be an artist of "the people".Which brings me to the few additional points I can add to those already found here...The strongest statement one will find within this album is perhaps the fact that the glitzy high-stepping and "shirtless wonders" are all an aside:  a corny decoration not always at place amongst the earthy, often bitter finery of life's true colors.  Which is not to say it's bad to aspire ("High and Mighty" is a beautiful contemplation of aspiration and its ho-hum place in real life) or that the celebratory nature of nightlife is anything less than noble at its best ("Set Your Heart").  It's just that we seem to sacrifice our humanity and sincerity when we bow to the gods of glamour.  Cyndi's biggest accomplishment here, lyrically, is in re-balancing these elelments of humanity.To that end it must be pointed out that she's utilized considerable compositional and musical skill to summon at least two icons who managed to finesse that equilibrium in thier work:"Raging Storm" pays brilliant homage to Curtis Mayfield: Cyndi somehow cystallizes Curtis's vocal phrasing within the very alloy of her own industrial-strength pipes.  I have never heard an artist successfully mimic this side of Mayfield, let alone take his spirit even further by remaining themselves in the process.  "Raging Storm" is a masterpiece of subtle yet effective tribute.  To continue the spirit of Mayfield's music and observations into times and troubles his eyes had not seen is the very essence of artistic class.In "Lyfe" it is Marvin Gaye and "Inner City Blues (Make Me Wanna Holler)" that is being summoned (and exquisitely so).  A fragment of a riff here, the meter of a lyric there, and of course the essence of the statement itself are milled through the mind of a true fine artist to create her own original work and yet honor a lineage that inspired her profoundly and likely made her dance through her own troubles.Note that thought:  "Dancing through" as opposed to "Dancing away".I sense a vein of "You Can't Fool Me" running through this entire project.  Cyndi's not pointing any fingers, she doesn't need to.  She just raised the bar that others had been slyly attempting to lower while we weren't looking.  Like the scolding nudge of mother, her action was indeed felt by the miscreants. Whether they react like children or fall back in line is entirely up to them.The Bonus Track (not available on this package) of "Got Candy" is so essential to this album's musical acheivements that I encourage all to find it anyway they can!CYNDI:  What were you thinking?  That song is GENIUS!  PLEASE find a way to use it as a single.  There's an entire generation of 18 year olds trying to make that record as we speak, and you just showed em how girl!What is it about Cyndi that when she sings of love, struggle, hope and friendship we believe her like no other pop singer in history?Perhaps the biggest compliment I can pay this work is to say that when I heard and absorbed it I wanted to find Cyndi and throw my arms around her and give her the biggest and longest hug I could possibly sustain. Thank God there is still an artist who can sing and dance and think at the same time.Post Script: Aretha Franklin sounds like Curtis on "Sparkle" because Curtis was writing for Aretha and presumably feminised (at a minimum he romanticised) his delivery to meet her halfway or to simply meet the demands of the project. From the what I've been able to compare, Aretha did an awesome job of "getting" Curtis while remaining Aretha.  It is this romantic sound that Whitney Houston also summoned quite skillfully for the "Shoop Shoop" song. So to give credit were credit is indeed due, I'll scold myself for the oversight and I'll clarify and say that at his most masculine and political I'd not heard a dead ringer: male or female, until now.

"Kizz My Black Azz" is the first solo EP from former N.W.A. member MC Ren. Quiet as it's kept, Compton, California native Lorenzo "MC Ren" Patterson allegedly signed on to Eazy-E's Ruthless Records as a teenager with the intent of being a solo artist. So the story goes, a fateful opportunity presented itself when N.W.A. founding member Ice Cube took a leave of absence from the group to attend an architectural-drafting vocational college in Arizona. Eazy allegedly asked Ren to contribute to ghostwriting raps for Eazy and making guest-appearances on recordings like "Ruthless Villain". By the time tech-school grad Ice Cube came back into the fold, Ren was a full-fledged member of the group.While N.W.A. as a group managed to change hip-hop and pop-culture forever with their groundbreaking and controversial music, unfortunately, Ren's solo debut was clouded in the aftermath of the group's disintegration in the early 1990s. By the time of this release, Ice Cube had quit the group and had released two solo albums, and Dr. Dre (along with associate D.O.C.) had recently defected from Ruthless to form what would eventually become Death Row Records. Within N.W.A., Ren had done solo-style cuts before ("If it ain't Ruff") but this is effort is clearly driven by Ren's direction."Kizz My Black Azz" finds Ren treading familiar territory, telling tales of wayward young women ("Behind the Scenez"), reckless gangbangers ("The Valley"), post-fame hangers-on ("Hound Dogz") and bitter rivals (on the title cut).The production on this release is exclusively handled by DJ Bobcat (see also- Ice Cube, LL Cool J, Tupac), who proves himself to be just as capable as his contemporary Dr. Dre in crafting head-nodding, sample-heavy breakbeats which alternate between uptempo and pre-Chronic G-funk.The best song on the six-cut effort is the battle-anthem "Final Frontier"--no Star Trek references, but Boogie Down Productions' "The Bridge is Over" is given a West Coast-revamp.In retrospect, there are some criticisms to bear here- Ren continues the unabashed sexism of N.W.A. here, and, viewed at face value, "Behind the Scenez" crosses into gratuitous territory (the narrative climaxes with incest and group sex). Also the title cut finds Ren bashing rap acts that involve live musicians in their performance lineup; it proved to be kind of nearsighted in light of the rise of acts like the Roots, Black Eyed Peas, Lauryn Hill and others. Ren gets props for being honest in his opinions, but some of them were clearly off-base.Ren's future solo albums would prove to be somewhat uneven production-wise, so this is arguably his most sonically consistent release. For fans of Golden-Age West Coast rap, this is a worthy buy, but for the uninitiated, N.W.A. and Ice Cube's first LPs should come first.*Note: The 2003 re-release features the music video to "Final Frontier".
summary: NWA alumnus Goes Hard on Solo Debut

reviewText: A Fine Frenzy's first studio album, ONE CELL IN THE SEA, marks a promising start for the band and in particular, singer/songwriting Alison Sudol. Unfortunately, the production on the album lends itself to generic top-40 pop music. Even so, there are many times where the songwriting overcomes the bland production to create memorable, (and remarkable) pop songs. For example, "Almost Lover" drops most of the music in favor of Sudol with a lone piano accompaniment, and the results are outstanding. On ONE CELL IN THE SEA, we find Sudol still working on finding her creative voice. The lyrics and music are all personal, but it is sometimes lost in the noise.In terms of A Fine Frenzy, I prefer the second album,Bomb In A Birdcage.  Either album is a good place to start listening to the band.  Fans of Ingrid Michaelson, Sara Bareilles, or Feist will love a lot of these songs. Recommended tracks to sample/download: "Almost Lover," "You Picked Me," and "Come On, Come Out."
