This experimental, avant-garde album gave no indication of the Eurythmics' subsequent melodic pop direction and mega stardom. It fits in more with the work of late 70s experimentalists like Brian Eno, Holger Czukay and is not commercial at all. Sometimes it even sounds like the later Cocteau Twins or the more ethereal type of world music. This direction is all the more odd in the light of Lennox and Stewart's previous band, the brilliant but underrated pop group The Tourists. In The Garden is a very atmospheric work and does contain at least two classics: the intricate Belinda with its cascading guitar textures, mournful drone and oriental backing vocals building up to a scorching climax is quite impressive, as is She's Invisible Now, a sorrowful song with a haunting countdown effect. English Summer is replete with crickets & stuff, whilst Your Time Will Come also has a catchy melody. So, not recommended for Eurythmics fans. People who like Delerium, Rose Chronicles, the above-mentioned German artists, Brian Eno's My Life In The Bush Of Ghosts, Deep Forest etc. will certainly enjoy it.

Coming off the success of 1980's British Steel, Judas Priest released Point of Entry, which marked yet another stylistic change for the band. The songs were shorter, the tempoes simpler, and with a more mainstream feel overall. Indeed, this albums has more of a '70s rock feel than any of their '70s albums. It sounds almost as if it's an evolutionary dead end, a brief foray into mainstream rock before the metallic assault of Screaming for Vengeance. However, even as a dead end, it makes a killer album. The songs are consistently good, with the expected screams from Rob and the dualing Glenn/K.K. solos, and for once in the Dave Holland era, some excellent rythem playing. Rob's lyrics, often silly to near the point of self-parody on later albums, are effective and well-written here. Songs like Desert Plains, already instrumentally great, are pushed over the limit with some great lyrics to accompany them. All in all, if you're a Priest fan who already has most of their releases and is looking to round pout the collection, this is a must-have.
summary: Different, but One of the Most Consistent Priest Efforts

reviewText: An epic, visionary, and spell-binding album that takes on great operatic/thematic/ and instrumentally inspired twists and turns along the way that separate this work not only from other Duran albums - but most of the stuff that is in the charts today by other bands. Normally it's possible to evaluate a work independent of its producer, but in this case the listener cannot help but tip their hat to the inimitable Mark Ronson. Not just tip your hat, but drop your jaw...It's as if magic was distilled in some musical alchemical process in the "lab" that managed to take what we love from DD stuff way in the past and merge it with a successful futurist bent. I never explored the Timbaland exercise of "Red Carpet" but I am even more unlikely as I cannot tear myself away from the current one long enough...Astronaut was all right, but this new one takes things to lofty new heights.DD are the great survivors. Remember that chill up and down the spine when "Ordinary World" catapulted the charts round 94? Here we are in 2011 with an album that's all the Wedding Album was and even more! You cannot count this band out. They keep moving forward with such talent and accomplishment. They don't just cash in on the oldies.The leopard song is a stroke of brilliance; and its preceding instrumental is a lush, hypnotic audible appetizer. It's really quite addictive and enduring. The little antique violin touches, and BBC-like simulations, are indicative of the attention to detail and mastery of touch that distinguish albums like this - where the listener feels as if assiduous work and love certainly were infused into the entire production.A band of this pedigree still putting out such effort is indeed impressive. That someone had the divine insight to tap Ronson is simply one among many nuances of genius that permeate the latest incarnations of DD.It's so nice to see Roger Taylor back; and the question of how these English blokes look better in their fifties than they did in their twenties is a philosophical conundrum I'll leave other pundits to ponder...Am so looking forward to this live show.(On a side note, I think we should remember one of the musicians critical to keeping DD on the map during sketchy times, though his views on 911 are comical: Warren Cuccurullo.)

Judas Priest's 9th studio album released in 1984. Defenders of the Faith is yet another great album.Many fans consider this album to be Priest last great album or the band's finest hour. It's not quite Priest's best (the title goes to Painkiller) but it's still excellent. In fact this is in my opinion the band's only great album from the 80's, everything else from this era (yep, including Steel and Vengeance) didn't cut. You may ask why. This is basically the album where Glenn and KK became real guitarists, unlike on the band's 3 previous efforts where the riffs were repeated over and the solos were mediocre, here it's not only the guitarist's best work but also some of the best dual-guitar attack I've ever heard, what also makes this the band's 2nd heaviest album (next to Painkiller).The album starts off with one of the best Priest album openers, 'Freewheel Burning', which is heavy, thrashy and has an excellent solo. 'Jawbreaker' is pretty good also. The 3rd song is my favorite song on the album, 'Rock Hard Ride Free', while is not that heavy and pretty slow everyone is phenomenal here. It's basically a song about a Harley rider, it has also the best riffing on the album. Then comes a fan favorite, if not somewhat overrated, 'The Sentinel' where Rob does a great job here. 'Love Bites' & 'Eat Me Alive' are groovy and catchy despite what Rob Halford is. Then comes the hit off the album 'Some Heads Are Gonna Roll' which has great chorus but maybe a bit repetitive. The last 3 tracks are 'Night Comes Down', 'Heavy Duty' and the title track, they are okay although I never really cared for them, still great way to close the album.It could have been better. Therefore I took a half star from the rating. First the production is not great, I don't know if the original version sounded better since I've only recently got this CD. Rob Halford while he did here a decent job on the vocals, this is his worst work and that doesn't say much when it's Halford, but sometimes he uses high-pitched vocals that sound raspy and this is somewhat annoying. The drums here are still mediocre. But despite these flaws it still worths the price.Favorite 3 songs:Rock Hard Ride FreeFreewheel BurningThe SentinelLong live Priest!!

This album will always hold a special place in my heart, because it helped me get through a very rough time in my life. "Little Earthquakes" is a self-portrait of a young woman coming to terms with the demons of her childhood and youth. By spilling her guts in such a raw and honest way, she makes her personal pain universal. "Crucify" explores the self-hatred every human being grapples with, and also ties it to the shame that many in the Christian church perpetuate. "Silent All These Years" deals with the parts of ourselves that we constantly censor, and yet are always dying to come out. "Precious Things" recalls childhood needs unmet, and "Leather" is about sexual partners who have no real emotional connection. And "Me and a Gun", an a capella song describing a rape, is one of the most disturbing (and maybe important) songs ever recorded. Since this album, Tori's music has become lyrically more vague and musically more adventurous (though still excellent). But this frank and stripped down debut will always be my favorite of hers.

As fine as their four previous studio albums had been, Earth Wind And Fire were clearly on fire as a live act, as evidenced on "Gratitude". Recorded during the first rush of megastardom that greeted "That's The  Way Of The World", the live portion of the album catches them playing  raw but tight, stretching out the solos and arrangements and adding in  several delightful new songs ("Sun Goddess", "New  World  Symphony") of a progressive nature.  Taken as a whole, these tracks  are the definitive  versions and show that the band was as strong  instrumentally as it was vocally (Philip Bailey is in awe-inspiring form  here).  However, as  perfect as it is, the live portion also sadly sums up  the best era of the group's long career--with the five new studio tracks  hinting at the increased slickness and commercialism of what was to follow.  Still, "Sunshine" and "Can't Hide Love" are good  songs.  On the strength of these and of course the live stuff, I would  recommend "Gratitude" as the best starting point for those  wanting to get into the group.

Despite the many accolades by current artists that I admire, until recently I didn't give Joni Mitchell much thought. Her biggest commercial success was during the 70s when I was a child and if she registered at all on my radar, it was as an earnest guitar strumming folk singer in the Judy Collins mode.One day, I was in the supermarket of all places when Help Me came on over the loudspeaker. I remembered the song from my childhood but some reason on that day, the song's vocal and instrumental arrangements had me totally entranced. I actually avoided getting in line until it was over. Soon after, I had to buy Court and Spark even though it had been probably 30 years since its initial release.Ever since, this CD has stayed on regular rotation. The songs have aged well. My favorites are Help Me and Free Man In Paris, a song to which I can relate even though I'm not a music mogul a la David Geffen. Other favorites include Court and Spark, People's Parties and Twisted.Mitchell's storytelling is strong and her musical intuition is sharp. In retrospect, one can hear her jazz leanings and understand that she was already headed toward a more experimental phase in her later recordings.If you can't understand why baby boomers complain that music is not what it used to be, pick up Court and Spark to see what they're talking about.

reviewText: If it wasn't for me reading a VIBE magazine and noticing that this is one of the must-haves of my album collection, I wouldn't have this D'Angelo album.This album is explicit. The booklet features its lyrics. The songs on "Brown Sugar" are mellow, featuring Jazz elements and luring falsetto vocals at times. My initial experience with the album was impatient because I didn't like the first 5 tracks, but they grew on me. The worst track is "[...], Damn, [...]." Other than that, you get a groovier cover of Smokie Robinson's hit "Cruisin'" and a couple of optimistic tracks ("Alright" & "When We Get By"). "Higher" is elements of Gospel in it. All the other songs are lovely and decent. Another problem is that there's unnecessary repition towards the ending of selected songs, making this album longer than it had to be.I'd say the best track on this album is "Smooth." That VIBE suggestion to have this album did not go in vain.

Sheryl Crow's debut album is a good one, though the jewels were yet to come (Her self-titled second cd and the masterpiece The Globe Sessions, that I already reviewed).Tuesday Night Music Club begins with Run, Baby, Run, a gorgeous mid-tempo song whose lyrics match the music perfectly. It's actually one of the best songs to lead off an album I've ever heard. After it comes Leaving Las Vegas, apparently a light-hearted song but this is only in the music - a close look at the lyrics reveals otherwise. Third track is Strong Enough, a ballad I like more each time I listen to it. Another song with a somewhat bitter lyric, but what's wrong with that? Musically it's another excellent number, with a great vocal performance from Crow. Fourth song is Can't Cry Anymore, an uptempo song whose highlight is the lyrics as well as the music. Nevertheless, the live version from Shepherd's Bush Empire is far superior to the studio cut.These four tracks are actually the best of the album, since the next two are not as great. Solidify and The Na-Na song ain't as enjoyable as the previous four. Fortunately things improve a lot with the gorgeous ballad No One Said It Would Be Easy, whose lyric is once again pretty good. The following song, What Can I Do For You, finds things going slightly flat once again, but All I Wanna Do comes in and the fun is back. While a pretty catchy song and not my fave from Sheryl, I admit I find it irresistible to like or sing along to. Next song is We Do What We Can, a jazz-flavoured ballad that shows how eclectic is this debut album. The lyrics are good and one more time fit the music perfectly. The album closer is I Shall Believe, another ballad that, despite its quality, drags on too long and would have benefited from a shorter running time. The chorus are repeated too much for their own good and with one or two minutes less the song would be perfect.In a nutshell: though not her best, a pretty good debut album, far superior to any other released in the early Nineties as far as I am concerned. Not that it was only Sheryl's work. It was a collaborative effort, as she admits in the sleeve notes.4/5.

Norah Jones sophomore effort is a continuation of its predecessor. A loose blend of jazz, folk and country, coupled with her clear, almost breathy vocals. Right from the beautiful surreal cover art, you know you're in for a treat.`Sunrise', the lead off single, opens the cd to good effect. It's a light, breezy song.`Carnival town' is an excellent cabaret style number, one of 6 songs penned or co penned by Jones.`In the morning' is another beauty, with some great bass playing.`Humble me' is a beautiful song of contrition and forgiveness, almost Gospel like.`Above ground', The long way home' (with delightful guitar strumming), The prettiest thing' (very pretty song), and `Don't miss you at all' (a tender piano ballad which samples Duke Ellington to good effect), are other standouts from this stark, understated gem.This cd will do your collection no harm.

While Eric Clapton kept on topping the rock and pop charts for the rest of the 1970’sand appeared at live venues on a regular basis, The Guitar God deeply impressed themusic world in 1977 with this ambitious landmark album that not only became anothergreat masterpiece, but what perhaps as his most sophisticated original album to date.Produced with world class excellence, finesse, ambience and richly diverse melodies,Slowhand highly showcases Clapton in his most original and sophisticated form as heoffers a high fidelity mixture of enlightened music, which is peppered by dashes of theblues, mainstream rock, pop and country and western as they deliver it’s full house ofbright intelligent notes from start to finish.  Starting with the compulsive, bluesy shuffleof J.J. Cale’s Cocaine, the kaleidoscopic track set proceed with eclectic pace on othertimeless hits like the romantic Wonderful Tonight, the Top Ten hit Lay Down Sally, histake on the blues classic Alberta, We’re All The Way, The Core, Peaches And Diesel,Mean Old Frisco and Greyhound Bus.  Hailed as Clapton’s best album, what you alsoget from the Super Deluxe Edition of Slowhand are a couple live performances whereDisc Two includes uplifting live versions of Hello Old Friend, Sign Language, Tell TheTruth, Steady Rollin’ Man and Can’t Find My Way Back Home, while Disc Three haveepic takes on Stormy Monday, Badge, I Shot The Sheriff and Layla, where the deluxeedition sustains itself throughout the course in a more towering format.
summary: This Timeless Masterpiece Just Got Bigger And Better!

reviewText: Shellac, fronted by famed producer Steve Albini (Nirvana - In Utero, Bush - Razorblade Suitcase, Chevelle - Point #1), are impossible to compare to any other act in modern music.  Their sound is completely unique, aided by guitars that Steve built himself, and the famous "room mic" technique that Steve has perfected to give drums a sound that makes drums on other records sound like sticks banging on plastic buckets.  This CD is a staple for those of you looking to get into underground music.  Just listen to the end of "In a Minute".  That is about the most difficult progression for a band to pull off seamlessly, which Shellac seems to do with ease.  That's only one of the many accolades for this album.  I could literally go on and on.  However, I'll just leave it at this: as far as indie music goes, this is as good as it gets.
I think I bought this one mainly to complete a Til Tuesday collection and to hear everything Aimee Mann has done. It's a good listen but nothing especially memorable.

This woman has a great voice, and her phenomenal backstory was a huge, myth-making moment in popular music.  Ms. Boyle has pretty good taste, judging from the song selections here, if indeed she has done the choosing.However, and this is just personal, I wish there had been more variety in the arrangements, and that she had picked some more uptempo numbers.  I think she could have rocked a bit here and there.  I can do completely without yet another version of "Amazing Grace," and like so many other vocalists, Boyle has missed the point of "Cry Me A River."  It's not a sappy ballad, but a gutsy, angry torch song (why do so many singers not get the lyrics of this piece)?  Ending the CD with a Christmas song was a dumb idea, too.On the positive side, it was pretty cool to hear her tackle Madonna and The Monkees, and on the gospel tune, "Up To The Mountain," Boyle really cuts loose near the end, showing us how powerful and moving she can be.  Likewise, "Wild Horses" is heartbreakingly gorgeous (the best song on this CD).  The title tune was inevitable, and no doubt, it will be her signature song for a long time to come.Based on the success of I DREAMED A DREAM, there will surely be at least a second CD, if not more to follow.  I hope Susan Boyle's next effort will be more creative and adventurous, that there will be some drums (or at the very least some rhythm), and that her producers will steer her further from the middle of the road.  I believe Boyle is capable of so much more than is offered here.
summary: Too Much Hype; Doesn't Quite Live Up To It

Once I got used to the "stripped down" garage style, which is more evident here than on Eyes, I started to really enjoy this disc.  Alice's wit, sneer, and sarcasm are all evident.  Most songs are catchy and made me drive 20 MPH faster than I should (that was the fault of "Run Down the Devil" and "Your Own Worst Enemy").  And hey, I even liked the rap song.I'll compare this one to Lace and Whiskey, with the diversity of songs and low production value.  That's a good thing.  Too much polish wouldn't help what he tried to achieve here, but two garage albums is just enough.
summary: I doubted the master, for that I bow in shame.

In 1972 Deep Purple released the third in a trio (the others being Led Zeppelin's Zoso and Black Sabbath's Paranoid) that is now considered the "How to..." guide to heavy metal. 25 years later the Purple strike again, releasing one of the best "remastering" remastering packages ever!I'm going to try to not put much emphasis on the album quality, as anyone who is considering this has already bought the vinyl/tape/CD, and is also a hardcore collector. I will however say that if you are a heavy metal fan, it is your obligation to own this in one form or another, as it contains some of the most influential riffage in rock and roll. Thundering, powerful riffs and solos (Thanks Blackmore) such as the opener to Smoke on the Water, Highway Star, Maybe I'm a Leo, and Space Truckin' have been plaguarized in one form or another by everybody from Aerosmith to Judas Priest to Metallica. At the same time the progressive keyboard-guitar jams throughout the album (particularly Lazy) proved just how far the heavy metal genre could be stretched, and layed down the groundwork for the progressive metal movement of the '80s and '90s. Then there's Ian Gillian, relaxed and more toned down in a genre dominated by over the top screamers. And who could not forget one of the finest rhythm sections of their generation; Roger Glover and Ian Praice. Add in some great ensemble playing and some unique lyrics and you have quintessential '70s rock and roll, and something that every person claiming to be a rock fan should own.Now to the package. This is the first time that a re-release really tried to offer something to the collectors, as opposed to ripping them with this one "new" song on a best of. First off, the originally Machine Head, while a classic, sometimes was a little tinny. With this the instruments are given more breathing space, spread out through the full range of your speakers (which, I should add, should be turned up until you can't hear your neighbors shouting at you) There is also more depth in the bottom end of the music, giving you clear, resounding bass and drum lines. The album also contains When A Blind Man Cries (a B side which makes its first CD appearance)which shows a haunting, melodic side that is rarely seen in this band. The quadrophonic mixes are also interesting displays, giving the instruments more power (particularly the bass), but less clarity, over the vocals. Then there are the remixes. This is the true gem for collectors. The album is given a more live in the studio feel, with chatter, unheard intros (brief drum solo at the start of Pictures of Home), and false starts. There are also many never before heard instrumental parts, such as the new guitar solo on Highway Star and an extended Smoke on the Water that keeps going past the original's fade point until they completely stop.If you have been a long time Deep Purple fan then this is a must have for your collection. Packed with rarities, killer sound, and some of the greatest music ever, no fanatic could possibly go wrong!
summary: "Smoke on the Water, and fire in the sky!"

This is the 1st MB release with Justin and John as members of the band. I think it's safe to say that without J & J, we would be saying stuff like..."the Moody who's?" This one album guaranteed that we would remember. Every once in a while an artist makes art that is timeless. The Moodies did just that in 1967 with the release of their critically acclaimed 'Days of Future Passed'. There is something for everyone here. The songwriting and storytelling aspect is unique and believable. The music segues from theme to theme seamlessly. Sometimes soaring, sometimes rocking, always appealing to our sense of the truth. Days is the defining Moodies release - if you like it you'll probably like most of their stuff. A day in the life of 'everyman' put to music, prose and song. The cross-fades and segues weave a tale worth hearing, a tale that is still applicable today - nearly 40 years later.

With the 'Stay On These Roads' album a-ha began a venture into a new direction. The 80's pop sound was a good but eventual ephemeral one. You can feel and hear a sound that is in transition from Pop to Rock on this album, yet the overall sound is somewhere in between the two making this album a rather curious oddity. You get the impression that they were being pulled in two directions. 'The Blood That Moves The Body' and 'Stay On These Roads' are examples of this. Even the title of the album can be interpreted as a question and suggests wonder for what may lay ahead. Yet they still meld lyric, melody and their unique sound into something that transcends the definition of music in whatever manner they perform. My favorite song on this album is  'The Living Daylights' originally written for the James Bond film. In 1987 Paul Waaktaar was commissioned to compose the theme for the James Bond film with the John Barry. Due to rumored disagreements between a-ha and Barry, two versions of 'The Living Daylights' were recorded, one for the movie soundtrack and the version heard on this album. I really like this one and I think it is the highlight of the album.

Some people were annoyed, if I remember right, when Ani DiFranco made this album -- much more brooding and with a lot more backup band than her others.To them, I said:  "She already made like a gazillion albums in her other style!  She recorded more songs already than most artists ever will.  How long was she supposed to keep going before trying something new?" I figure she has to either reinvent herself or get bored, and I think she made the right choiceI think this album is a TRIUMPH. It's mopey, honest, and absolutely heartfelt.  Her lyrics are just as smart as ever.SUPERHERO is a fantastic song about how when we fall in love, we all become ridiculous cliches ... no matter how 'above it' we thought we were before.ADAM AND EVE is a powerful, brooding feminist statement about men who "leave you in the morning".OUT OF ME, ONTO YOU is more or less ... a curse on someone you hate.I think DILATE is a gem, and every Ani fan should take it back out again and listen to it with fresh ears.

The first time I listened to "Gran Turismo", I could not believe that this was the same group that brought us "Lovefool". After that first listen, I knew that I was a fan of the band. The lyrics here are great, the music is buzzing with electronic influences, and each song is irresistably catchy, you may just find yourself becoming a fan as well. The best songs here are "My Favorit Game", "Erase and Rewind", "Starter" and "Marvel Hill". This is an impressive album from beginning to end, a good alternative to pop-rock fans who are sick and tired of Matchbox 20 and the Goo Goo Dolls releasing virtually the same song over and over again. "Gran Turismo" is more than worth the price to check out, because it has the potential to really surprise people and get in their heads.
summary: Made a fan out of me

reviewText: Neil Diamond --Classics: the Early Years, Columbia PC 38792  (May, 1983 vinyl Lp)RIAA gold Lp certification on 8/09/89; the title went platinum on 7/22/91.  I believe the CD version only dates from 1996+Track list:side one--Kentucky Woman/Cherry, Cherry/Solitary Man/You Got to Me/I Got the Feelin'/Thank The Lord for the Night Timeside two--I'm A Believer/Girl, You'll Be A Woman Soon/Shilo/Do It/Red Red Wine/The Boat That I RowThis Columbia $5.98 mid-price album is the Columbia stock version reissue/repackage of the Columbia House AAR-1 Frog King record club press.  The mixes on this album are the same as that Lp, missing the true stereo cut of "Kentucky Woman" still found only on the 1978 Frog King Lp--"Kentucky Woman" on the CLASSICS 38792 repackage is rechanneled, though the Columbia rechanneled "stereo" on this Lp are not as drastic as the usual Columbia "Electronically Re-Channeled for STEREO" 1960s era high-low out-of-phase fake stereo.The Frog King true stereo version of "Kentucky Woman" features most of the mix centered or slightly left of center, excepting the rhythm acoustic guitar rocking away (yum!) on the right channel; the rechanneled version on this Columbia 38792 Lp is the same as on the NEIL DIAMOND'S GREATEST HITS Bang BLPS 219 Lp from 1968 or so (same kind of rechanneling on both versions of that album)."Solitary Man":  the original hit version of "Solitary Man" can be found in an odd "ping pong" faux "stereo" version on the early copies of the Bang GREATEST HITS BLPS 219 album, which is the mono single's version with a "Ping-Pong" balance change (the recording engineer apparently had his hand on the left-right balance knob and twisted it back and forth on the phrases "holdin' Jim (right)," "lovin' him (left)," "me and Sue (right)," "that died, too (left)," "part time thing (right)," "paper rain (left)," "right or wrong (right)," "weak or strong (left)," and then a to-the-right balance change at the horn break fading over the left, and back over to mono center.).  Later versions of the album have "Solitary Man" with a true stereo DIFFERENT mix than the version of "Solitary Man" found on both this CLASSICS Col. 38792 Lp and the Frog King/Columbia House pressings--the tell is the different electric keyboard riff missing after "till the time that I found her" phrasing comparing the alternate true stereo versions of the song.  Of the two true stereo alternate mixes of "Solitary Man," I prefer the Bang Lp's stereo mix to the Frog King/Columbia 38792 CLASSICS version.The stereo mix on "Girl, You'll Be A Woman Soon" and "Do It" on this album and the Frog King Lp are the same--either a very, very narrow stereo mix or slightly rechanneled.  "Do It" on the 1968 Bang hits' Lp is a more annoying back and forth fading "ping pong", though only between maybe about 11 and 1 o'clock from the center (12 o'clock) mono.Although both this 1983 Columbia PC 38792 and the 1978 Frog King albums feature the same tracks --the Frog King press has a different title play sequencing than the Columbia reissue/repackage, and the absence of "Kentucky Woman" stereo mix--, I find the Frog King Lp a little clearer and brighter than the Columbia CLASSICS album (on vinyl).  The listed credits are the same on both albums, although the mixing credit is slightly different.  Both show "Mixed by Neil Brody"; however, the Frog King Lp has the added "...assisted by Herman Rojas."The PC 38792 album charted on Billboard's 200 position regular album chart in the lower ranges in June-July, 1983, and reappeared on CD starting March, 1996 as catalog.  The Lp/cassette were $5.98 mid-line list price; the CD was $9.98 list in 1996+.  On Cash Box, with like numbers, the title charted for just over two months, beginning 6/25/83, hitting a peak at #166, coming between the HEARTLIGHT and PRIMITIVE albums (October, 1982 and August, 1984, respectively).
summary: A nice and affordable intro into Neil Diamond's 1966-1968 Bang era

Steve Albini may be a genius but that doesn't make this album enjoyable.  Albini really is a great producer (sorry..."studio engineer") and the level of innovation he brings to his guitar playing puts Thurston Moore to shame.  When it comes to unique guitar tones and sounds, the only guy in Albini's league is the great Kevin Shields of My Bloody Valentine.  But Albini's virtuosity is actually Shellac's biggest downfall.  Albini has said several times in interviews that he doesn't care about songwriting, just sound.  This obsession with sound and total disregard for songs renders "At Action Park" nothing more than a nice art project no matter how physically powerful and inventive the playing is.  "My Black Ass,"  "Song For The Minerals" and "The Admiral" all sound great, but they are all essentially the same.  Albini starts out with a crazy-sounding but ultimately repetitive guitar figure and then the rhythm section comes in with awkward time signatures to try to mask the inherent hollowness of each song.  Also, most of Albini's vocals are incomprehensible here so we don't get the wicked sense of humor that elevated his (superior but still overrated) old band Big Black.  At Action Park is great to listen to if you're interested in studio recording techniques and is even enjoyable in small doses when you're in the mood for some brutal pounding and nothing more, but on repeated listens it just doesn't hold up.  Albini should stick to recording other artists who actually know how to write songs because his studio techniques really are incredible and he's done amazing work behind the boards for PJ harvey, Jesus Lizard, Dirty Three, Mclusky, and though he hates to admit it, The Pixies.  I'd reccomend buying any Albini-recorded albums by the above listed artists instead of blowing your money on Shellac's three (interchangable) albums.

reviewText: Notorious BIG only had two albums, both of which are arguably the greatest of all time.  Life After Death was his last statement before his untimely death.  He wasn't even alive to see how much this album was appreciated by the people.  One of the few double albums that have been released in the past years hits on all cylinders and then some.  From deep dark songs like "You're Nobody (till somebody kills you)", "Long Kiss Goodnight", "Somebody's Gotta Die", and "What's Beef" to more uptempo (happy) songs for lack of a better word like "Going back to Cali", "nasty Boy", "Mo, Money Mo Problems", "Hypnotize".  But whether he is deep and dark or uptempo and proud, Biggie delivers.  His amazing flow really shines on "Notorious Thugs" when he collaborates with the Bone Thugs.  His flow switches to quick and witty just like Bone Thugs always do.  "I Gotta Story to Tell" does exactly what the title says in which biggie tells a story about a woman.  An  amazing laid-back beat accompanies that track.  If you haven't heard this album yet by now, you're missing out on something spectacular.  I recommend this for everyone.

reviewText: This album was Diana Ross's first solo project after leaving the Supremes in 1970.  This album has some slow tracks on it such as "Dark side of the world", and a cute track called "Keep an Eye".  This album also has what would become Diana's signature song "Reach out and touch somebody's hand".  This album was not the monster smash that Motown would have hoped it would have been for Diana's first solo gig without the other two girls - actually, Mary Wilson, Cindy Birdsong, and Jean Terrell, Diana's Supreme's replacement, beat Diana to the top of the charts in 1970 with their hit record "Stone Love", and "Up the latter to the roof", much to Berry Gordy's chagrin.  Diana would actually have to release a few more albums before she got the really big hit record she needed to solidify her solo freedom, and she actually didn't do that until "Love Hangover" in 1975.
summary: Diana's first solo project after the Supremes!

Rush took several years off after "Counterparts".  Alex Liefson recorded his "Victor" project and the band was even rumored to be broken up at one point.  So it was with great anticipation that fans looked forward to the release of "Test" in 1996.  Unfortunately this album was a letdown and in my opinion is one of the band's weakest.  It starts out really good with the first two tracks "Test For Echo" and "Driven" getting things off on a rocking high note.  After that things begin to fall somewhat flat.  "Half The World", "Resist" and the instrumental "Limbo" are all decent.  The rest, although tolerable is nothing that is going to stick with you for a long time.  "Dog Years" and "Virtuality" have choruses that are particularly annoying.  Rush has never made a bad album, and if you are a fan this one is worth owning, but it is far from essential in my mind.

Whenever someone complains that electronic music is totally void of warmth or realism, I just point to this album. New Order play electronic music with the urgent and manic shifts of rock. Bernards vocals are earnest yet detatched, with guitar work that is jagged, random and sparse; Gillian and Stephen's percussion and synth sequences are both lively and rigid, an up-beat/down-march; Peter's basslines are fluid yet kinetic. This is a work of ironic friction. The warmth and humanity flow thru the restrained and urgent detatchment. The whole album sounds like a friend that wants to say something but can't, hiding it behind his/her eyes.I would consider Power, Corruption & Lies an artistic/pop masterpiece in the true sense. The electronic and post-punk meanderings are only the charms that envelope the wonderfully angular pop sense that Bernard brings to his lyrics. Everything is so vague and pretty; it's like the album cover...just a random slice of still-life, full of colour and restraint. Tracks like 'Your Silent Face' or '5-8-6' explode with edgy, manic shades of light, sorta like impressionism via expressionism.You won't be let down by this album. With the band themselves producing it, it's a natural workout of rock and electronics, perfectly blended together to make a classic.

First of all, this album contains "You Don't Know my Name", "If I was Your Woman", "Karma", and "If I Ain't Got You". I can't think of anything except Janet's 1993 album that has so many classic tracks one after the other. One of my favorites remains the album opener (I love how Alicia always has a quiet piano intro that breaks into a big song).However, moving past the obviously amazing singles, there is much here to drool over. 'Samsonite Man' in particular - there is something very unique about that track. When most people think of this CD, they almost always remember "If I was Your Woman" first, but I would say that I personally think of "Dragon Days" first - its a slow burner, but when it hooks you in, it really never lets go.Alicia Keys made a better album on "Unplugged" (she has never sounded better before or after that album), but as a studio album, this will always be my favorite Keys album. There is something special about it, you can just put it on ANY time of day, let it play and do its' thing, and it will never disappoint you. Her debut album is certainly not 'timeless', but this one definitely is.If you are at all into collecting classic R&B; records, then this has to be in your collection already. If you're new to the scene, there are very few albums on Amazon with so much repeat value. Get this today!
summary: One Of the Real Classics : Put It On, Let it Do Its Thing

reviewText: No autotune, no hype - thank God. With the entire pop music industry going down a slippery slope into a vortex of scum, Adele is the pinicle of a rare few who actually display class and talent. No tats to speak of, no shards in her lips, no dressing up like a circus act just one hell of a voice and song writing talent. I have heard that young people are taken with her and maybe, just maybe, they will begin to see that to be really unique, free, and different, you have to go against the flow and truly be your own person. In 2011 there is nothing more lemming-like than to paint your body, pierce yourself with cheap hardware, and spike your noggin-hair. Yet "artist" after "artist" come along and sport this contrived image and then sing through another contrivance (autotune) and then pen lyrics that amount to some goofy repetition of some meaningless sophmoric phrase. For God's sake somehow, someway music has to return to music, to art and get away from being a forum for gangsta, thug, rump-humping displays of lowbrow sideshow culture.Adele on the other hand needs no showbiz distraction to take your eye off the talent search. You listen to her, you have found the real deal. Yes, I agree with some others that her influences are very apparent and she has not surpassed the likes of Aretha, but she is bringing back the focus on real talent and for that she deserves a thousand Grammys.

In my mind, "Love Box" pales a wee bit in comparison to its 2001 predecessor, "Goodbye Country (Hello Nightclub)," but that doesn't mean Groove Armada's latest isn't noteworthy.  It is.  They bring on the funk on smooth cuts like the aptly named "Groove Is On," and they spin the disco ball on house-ed up jams like "Final Shakedown," "Easy," and the title track.  But for me, "Love Box" is a noteable record because it marks the return of the gone-but-mostly-forgotten Neneh Cherry, who lends her voice on the piano-laced slow jam "Think Twice."  But there's no need to "think twice" about getting this disc.  Groove Armada have been leaders in smart, beat-heavy electro pop, and they've released a party of an album worth crashing.  Open the "box," and jump in.
summary: Groove Armada is Back! (And They Brought Neneh With Them)

reviewText: Reading a couple of these reviews reminds me of a comment the Emperor of Austria once made about Mozart, "too many notes." Well we don't know if that's exactly what he said (although how ironic if he had).  History has demonstrated that the Emperor was wrong about Mozart. Sure the  guy had his musical flaws but inventiveness wasn't one of them. We do know,  however, that some folks consider this talented quartet to be too clever by  half with too many notes for their liking. Personally, I'd take the  criticism as a compliment.Perhaps they are too clever. How boring the  world would be without the daring shown here on their last album as a four  piece. Lazy Ways and I'm Mandy Fly Me feature melodies filled to the brim  with wit and as rich as anything the Beatles or Beach Boys dreamed up. I  Wanna Rule The World reminds you why these guys were held in such high  esteem by their peers (like the late Frank Zappa, John Lennon and still breathing Paul McCartney); it's a twisted turn down paranoia street that  manages to entertain as it informs.The second part of the CD (or what  used to be side 2 on vinyl) beings with the strong track Art for Art's  Sake. It was originally written around the time of their previous album The  Original Soundtrack but unrecorded. AFAS manages to satirize the art world  in the same fashion as the band's Worst Band in The World (from Sheet  Music) did the music biz. The songs that follow AFAS prevents this fine  album from taking on any water and sinking beneath the waves of mediocrity.  "Don't Hang Up" plays like a mini rock opera (much the same as One Night in  Paris) in the tradition of the Who's "A Quick One While He's Away". Kevin  Godley's angelic voice provides an ironic counterpoint to the possesiveness  that clearly drives the character singing the song.I've changed my mind  about the bonus track. After the involved closer, Get it While You Can  manages to close the album on a simple and elegant note. It actually sums  up most of the themes on the album well and provides perfect closure to a  fine album.How Dare You is flawed but those flaws don't undermind this  compelling, funny and melodic rock album. It's also clear listening to it  that from here the original quartet didn't have any place else to go so it  made sense for Godley & Creme to leave the band. Stewart and Gouldman  continued to develop the 10cc sound and add more accomplishments to their  achievements.Be aware that the remaster has some alternate takes included that differ slightly from the original vinyl and CD's released by Mercury. That said although this isn't a perfect edition, it sounds much, much better than the original U.S. CD release which was sourced from an inferior copy of the original master tapes.By the time they recorded this album it was clear that the  democracy wouldn't work as well as before. How Dare You! allowed the  original line up to perform a fine encore and take a bow before the final curtain dropped.
summary: No lazy ways evident on last album by original quartet

I've said it once, in my review of The Very Best of Fleetwood Mac, and I'll say it again:  Best of collections are NOT FOR LONG TIME FANS, who have every album and can make their own compilation, if they so please.  They are for those of us who may not be fan enough to buy every album, but would like a nice collection of the songs they love in one, easily accessable place.  If that's what you're looking for, then ignore all these guys complaining that their favorite album cuts were excluded, or some hit that only made the lower end of the top 40-- most of us don't remember it anyway!Now that I have that off my chest, let's get to the album.  This is the best comp from Styx I have ever beheld.  Some years ago, A&M released one as part of their "Classics" series (now out of print).  Including live cuts where there should have been studio and lame chopped-up edits we don't even hear on the radio, this was a failure.  Then, they released Greatest Hits 1 and 2-- expensive and sold separetly.  And still missing "Man In the Wilderness"!Finally, a double album, remastered and economically priced.  NOW I can spend my money!  Only snafu-- and some of you have rightfully complained-- the top ten hit, "Don't Let it End" is nowhere to be found.  But, ah, who cares?  Compared to Styx's other material, it's pretty teeny-bopperish anyway.  Nice to have for completion's sake, though I actually found myself relieved that it wasn't there.  While they were at it, they could've axed "The Best of Times", too.Oddly enough, some of you long-timers complained about the inclusion of the Wooden Nickel tracks.  Shame on you!  I'm not that big a fan (preferring mid-western sister-band Kansas, instead), but I've heard those first four albums and thought they were great.  I would have chosen different selections, say, "The Earl of Roseland" and "The Grove of Eglantine", but at least something was recognized from those obscure years.  Most bands prefer to pretend their pre-hit days never existed, and that they were always hit-makers from day one.  No such arrogance here.  Here we have the full history.So, want the common radio fare, and some cool additions as well, with crisp, clean re-mastering to boot? Then don't let the die hards scare you.  Just buy this.

"Straight To Hell" is a revelation. This two-disc album offers as much as anyone can hope for from high-tempo pickin' to raw analog recordings. From its sinister opening on the first disc all the way throughout the 42-minute "Hidden Track" on the second disc there is a lot here to take in.The first disc is a showcase of some of the finest example of classic country with very little in the way of over-produced production. It gets right back to the basics of what country music should be and doesn't let up. Sure there are the occasional sound effects but that doesn't detract from the overall roots feel to the material.The second disc kicks off with "Louisiana Stripes", a fitting piece that finds Hank III channeling the late Johnny Cash. afterwards is the aforementioned "Hidden Track" that throws about as much into the mix as possible laced with darkness (a track is deliberately slowed down to a sinister growl) and dark humor (the cover of Cheech & Chong's "Up In Smoke" with an intro by one of Hank's stoned friends via an answering machine message).This is stuff not meant for radio play. But then, considering the stuff on the radio, that's a blessing. It's certainly not a boring album over here for I find myself listening to it from time to time. Not a bad album at all!
summary: This is not your daddy's country music!

reviewText: This deluxe reissue of the band's classic first album features the original album remastered plus a second disc of b-sides, outtakes, demos and live tracks. The original album sounds terrific here--much warmer and with much more detail than the previous CD version and captures the feel of the original vinyl release much more accurately than the first CD version.The second disc consists of songs recorded as b-sides such as the classic "Cuban Slide","Porcelain" (both of which originally appeared as both a b-side and on The Pretenders "Extended Play" release that follow this album but preceded "Pretenders II")and "Swinging London". It's missing "In the Sticks" a Martin Chambers b-side which I suspect was probably just overlooked. The two former tunes sound much better than the previous CD release on the budget import "Don't Get Me Wrong" odds and ends/hits CD. "The Wait" showed up on the boxed set previously in demo form and again here. We also get "The Phone Call", a cover "I Can't Control Myself", "Kid", "Stop Your Sobbing", "Tequilla" (which is a different earlier version with the original line up as opposed to the one from the boxed set which featured the Hynde-MacIntosh-Chambers-Foster version of the band), "Nervous But Shy". We also get five tracks recorded for a BBC radio cast. " I Need Somebody" (which has been on various bootlegs over the years), "Mystery Achievement", "Precious" (again different from the boxed set version), "Tatooed Love Boys" and James Honeyman Scott ripping through a hit for Dave Edmunds' old band Love Sculpture "Sabre Dance" as the concluding track.The artwork includes all the original artwork for the album as well as a booklet with a insightful essay on the origins of the band and the recording of their first album. We also get the lyrics for all the songs (a first for this album). My only complaint about the design of the packaging (which mirrors an LP sleeve although it folds out unlike the original release)is that the two CDs don't come in plastic protective covers which would prevent them from being scratched in the cardboard housing. It's a curious oversight from Rhino.The Pretenders debut album had it all in spades. Great songwriting, singing, production and a unique mix of a harder rock sound mixed with the melodic bands (The Kinks, The Beatles) that songwriter/singer Chrissie Hynde admired. Hynder's songwriting always struck me as much closer to someone like John Lennon in that there was an emotional directness to all of her songs (and sexuality)that made it feel as if she was connecting with the listener individually. This is a great debut album and certainly one of the top 50 albums of all time. Highly recommended
summary: Debut album sounds terrific in deluxe two CD edition with rarities, b-sides, outtakes and deluxe packaging

reviewText: To all those people who heard INTUITION and labeled Jewel as a sellout...YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU'RE TALKING ABOUT! Just listen to her latest release and you will be pleasantly proved wrong!Jewel explores new styles such as urban grooves, dance, and jazz with sassy grace and witty intelligence. Her lyrics are still the core of her music. To prove her lyrical intelligence take a look at the amazing lyrics to the first verse of STAND-"Walk in a corner shopSee a shop-lifting copSee the old lady with a gunSee the hero try to runNothing's what it seemsI meanIt's not all dirtybut it's not all cleanThere's children paying billsThere's monks buying thrillsThere's pride for sale in magazineThere's pills for rent to make you cleanMarvin Gaye, there's no "brother brother"Woody Guthrie's land can't feed mother"The only difference with this album is: Her amazing lyrics are set to more rythmn-oriented beats and styles! This just increases interest in Jewel's music and expands it.Other great standouts include the irresistable and dark/edgy song SWEET TEMPTATION. Trust me, you won't be able to get that song out of your head.RUN 2 U is the perfect mix of a hypnotic dance beat and classic folk melody.LEAVE THE LIGHTS ON has a killer beat and jazzy influence. (Another very catchy song!)AMERICA-The most controversial track on the album has a Euro-Rock feel to it and very in your face truths about America that we live in. Here's a small snippet of the lyrics from it:"We shed blood in the name of liberty"Uh-huh. Alright.The circus tents are dead but the sideshows doing wellThe Osbournes, Anna Nicole are too freaky to tellUh-huh. Alright.Take the bad with the goodI wanna change it but I wouldn't leave it if I couldWe are trying in AmericaWe're spying in AmericaGetting high in AmericaWe are laughing in AmericaWe're crying in AmericaWe're dying in AmericaThe above songs are just a snippet of what to expect on Jewel's latest effort.In this album, Jewel captures American pop culture perfectly and has lots of witty lyrics and captivating grooves to go along with it. Other resonating themes of the songs are love and finding someone to be with in this world. You also get the overall feeling that she is trying to have fun and test her limits an artist. Jewel speaks for many people and this album is just one of the many ways that she shows that.So don't hesitate to picks this fun and smart piece of work from everyone's favorite girl from Alaska! I feel that Pet Sounds is a listenable and pleasant, but marginal record from a listenable and pleasant, but marginal band. First, the good news: there's nothing as annoying as, say, Little Deuce Coup or Surfin' USA on this album, and the four a-sides (Wouldn't it Be Nice; Sloop John B; God Only Knows; Caroline, No) are easily better than even some of the Beach Boys' stronger hits (Fun, Fun, Fun; In My Room; Don't Worry Baby; even Good Vibrations). Nonetheless, there isn't much to this record outside of the hits and Brian Wilson's egotistical but enjoyable lament I Just Wasn't Made for These Times. The rest sounds silly and dated to my ears: when was the last time you listened to the title track? How about Let's Go Away for A While, I'm Waiting for the Day; Don't Talk (Put Your Head on My Shoulder) or You Still Believe in Me? The group's lack of a good lyricist or instrumentalist hurts even further - the Beach Boys could harmonize, all right, but harmonies can only get you so far. Which is why The Beatles, Simon & Garfunkel, Crosby, Stills & Nash and the Motown acts are all so much better than the Beach Boys - in addition to the harmonies, they also had interesting lyrics, solid instrumentalists, AND great melodies to back the singing up.I understand that this was a big influence on Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band, so it merits careful study for those hooked on '60's rock, as I am. But there are other '60's albums that influenced Sgt. Pepper's (Freak Out!; Blonde on Blonde; Aftermath; The Beatles' own Revolver) that are far better. This sounds distinctively like it was made 40 years ago. Sure, so do all the aforementioned albums, but they all have a timeless quality this one lacks. That leaves Pet Sounds as a good bunch of a-sides accompanied by pure fluff. All of that makes it one of the most overrated records of all time.
summary: Looks like I'm swimming against the tide, but whatever

reviewText: Boz Scaggs' "Silk Degrees" was released in early 1976, & talk about a commercial breakthrough...  All these years later, "Lowdown", "Lido Shuffle", "What Can I Say", "It's Over", & "Georgia" ALL still get a mind-boggling amount of airplay (in my area anyway).  The "Lowdown" single went gold, plus Rita Coolidge did a version of "We're All Alone" that came out the following year & became a big time hit as well.  By all means, "Silk Degrees" is an important album--future Toto members David Paich, David Hungate, & Jeff Porcaro are all part of the core band on "Silk Degrees", and this album had a significant impact on their formation, and that's really nothing to snicker at.  Plus, with its lushness and its funked-up pop-rock/ R&B a la Steely Dan (small wonder than both Paich & Porcaro had played with the Dan), this is simply a great album.  Scaggs' vocals are highly unique--his inflections are quite weird at times, yet there's no denying he sings with arresting passion; he sounds kind of like a mix of Donald Fagen & Van Morrison.  Scaggs & Paich co-wrote half of the tracks here, 4 of which are among the album's staples--of course, there's the uptempo "Lowdown" which, with Porcaro's drumming, the haunting lyrics, & the deathless hooks piled over the 2-chord progression, it grooves along irresistibly; "It's Over" is ultra-catchy, as is "What Can I Say" which has Scaggs cutting loose vocally to irresistible effect; & "Lido Shuffle", with its skittering rhythm & wordless vocal hook on the chorus, is a lot of fun.  Paich gets in one solo composition with "Love Me Tomorrow" which is a funky, infectious gem in its own right.  Scaggs has 3 solo compositions--"Georgia", in characteristic Steely Dan fashion, mixes bright, upbeat music with lyrics of a guy being kept from his woman because he's stuck in jail, and the result is an optimistic hook-fest; the reflective "Harbor Lights" is a gorgeous, dreamy ballad with that 'rainy' intro and a Herb Alpert-style fade; and the album closer "We're All Alone" is a simply masterful composition with a truly beautiful melody (admittedly, he did borrow the chord progression on the chorus from his earlier tune "You Make It So Hard (To Say No)" nearly to a tee)--I think the version here, with its somewhat brittle, echo-y drum sound and excess orchestration, leaves a tad to be desired, but it still soars anyway (Rita Coolidge's hit version is also very good--it's the kind of song that'd take a significant effort to really screw up).  "What Do You Want The Girl To Do", written by Allen Toussaint, is strong and swings along nicely.  There is one major misfire here though with the Paich/ Scaggs composition "Jump Street"--it's an annoyingly tuneless rocker made even more annoying by its false ending/ reprise that pushes the song over the 5-minute mark; it's a textbook example of a 'bad song on a great album'.  And indeed, with the rest of the album being as great as it is, it certainly makes up for it.  You may have heard a majority of the songs here an endless number of times being played all over the place, but there's no denying "Silk Degrees"  deserves to be hailed as a classic.  (If you love "Silk Degrees", you're missing out if you don't check out his superb follow-up album "Down Two Then Left"!)
summary: Boz's 1976 commercial blockbuster... and deservedly so

reviewText: Though it doesnt contain a song like the epic beautiful "nights in white satin" the Moodies second album from 1968 is their most pyschedelic and solid album of their career. This album segues nicely into a track by track tour of what the end of pyschedlia and the beginning of progrock sounded like. There isnt really a song i dislike and this fits in nicely with the best of the post summer of love albums. Lots of flute mellotron sitars and instruments played by the band themselves. Lost chord is a very strong followup to days of future passed and exceeds it in material for me. Great acoustic guitars and truly great singing all mingled in with LSD musical interludes( though apparantly without drugs). A few moments recall early Pink Floyd late Beatles etc but the Moody Blues were a special band for a time-1967-1972 in my humble opinion. Their first three albums are all excellent but this is the one to get. This one seems heavily influenced by George Harrison Ravi Shankar- with most of the album flaoting by a in a mellow transcendental state. Great for evening listens sunday mornings and for contemplation.
summary: almost perfect  moody blues album! 4.75 stars

reviewText: IMO, there are generally 3 types of Tegan and Sara fans:A)The ones who have been around from day one and are still attached to their earlier more acoustic / folky sound but begrudgingly keep up with the newer stuff just because.B)The ones who only recently just caught on to them through such means as MTV "You Hear it First" or maybe their local radio station (as Walking With a Ghost is getting more and more play)C)The ones who were "with them" from the very beginning-(I'm talking about Under Feet Like Ours beginning) and continue to listen to them as they progress. No harsh judgements or calling them sell outs...the people who truly appreciate music and the growth that can take shape, etc.I'm going to say that I fall into category C.  As someone who is quite familiar with their catalog, their background if you will, and has seen them live a few times I'd like to think I know their music fairly well.  So Jealous seems like an extension of If It Was You in a way, only because it's got the more electric elements and leans more towards the poppy-rock.  You definitely notice more maturity in the songwriting, and even just the music in general...I remember seeing them when they were promoting this release and I couldn't help but notice how much better they got at playing and structuring their songs.  The set was practically flawless, as if I just took the cd and popped it in my player.So Jealous has a little bit of everything on there; but mostly it's fun, quirky, and something great to drive around in your car with or show your friends.  If you're looking for songs reminiscent of This Business of Art, you really won't find any.  Think 'If It Was You' with a more polished sound, slightly better lyrics, and more dramatic climaxes.  The fact that these songs are incredibly catchy isn't the only thing that makes them worth listening to.Definitely check out "I Cant Take It", "Downtown", "I Bet It Stung", and "We Didn't Do It"

Recorded the same year as his earllier Masterpiece,Tenor Madness, Rollins hits another one out of the park with this album.The line-up here is completely different from Tenor Madness, with Tommy Flanagan on piano, Doug Watkins on bass and Max Roach on drums. Watkins is a bassist to whom I pay close attention, which makes this album all the more valuable to me. He was Charles Mingus choice to replace himself (so he could play piano) onOh Yeah (US Release), and had Watkins not died at 27 he had the potential to be one of jazz's top bassists.Of course Saint Thomas is the reason most non-jazz aficionados love this album, but my personal favorites are Moritat (also known as Mack the Knife) and Blue 7. However, personal favorites aside, I hold every track on this album to be a masterpiece. Not a bad effort for a 26 year old who had previously that year made a landmark album that would be hard to top.This album (and Tenor Madness) should be in every jazz lovers library, and is so beautifully crafted that any music lover - jazz or otherwise - should enjoy it.

reviewText: I had a review here previously RIGHT when it came out, and gave it 5 stars. Oh have times changed ever since."Antics" seemed amazing at first, but it died quick. It's a short album with 10, tracks, mostly filler. I do believe these guys managed to pull off the dreaded sophomore slump. The GOOD tracks however are in fact good. "Next Exit" "Evil" "Slow Hands" and "Not Even Jail" are stand outs. That's 50% of the album, meaning F. The lyrics have something to do with this, I really have no idea what Paul Banks is talking about in most of the songs, I can't tell whether its about love or losing a friend, or maybe even making grilled cheese. You can be vague with lyrics and still make an awesome song, but sometimes, you can be confusing. If Banks had more of a knowing structure of what his songs were about, maybe the band all together would sound better (good example: "Not Even Jail" every instrument has a purpose and life in this track).You can't deny it though, Interpol has potential (Turn On the Bright Lights?) but stored it for this quick one, I guess. I'm betting their 3rd album will be much more mature, and will travel away from these Franz Ferdinand's, Killers, and Modest Mouse sounds. I at least hope so.

This album was released when John was at the apex of his popularity, and the songs on this album served to continue his ride into the stratosphere. From the wry and yet poignant "I'd Rather Be A Cowboy" to the incredible smash hit "Farewell Andromeda", John Denver showcases his incredible talents here. Denver was instrumental in firmly fixing the younger generation's sights and sensibilities upon the outdoors in general and on environmental issues in particular, and he nearly single-handedly began the outdoor backpacking, hiking, and orienteering movements after popularizing the idea of a more close and intimate human relationship with mother nature. Therefore, more than a few of the young baby-boomers, like John, were more than ready for the kind of unconventional intimacy with nature he sang about so effortlessly and so elegantly. From "Zachary And Jennifer" to an evocative and almost ethereal "Rocky Mountain Suite'", Denver's songs soar in their description of the beauties of a simple and natural life and in being close to the "great wide-open'.Denver also does an unusually good rendition of "Berkeley Woman", written by a friend but usually identified with Denver himself. He shows that even a sugary sweetheart like him can have some "colorful" thoughts about women. Indeed, the simple and well arranged acoustic blast of infectious energy and sweet simplicity that was John Denver is here in spades, whether it be in original songs like "Sweet Misery" or with covers of others' work, the kid who had adopted the majesty of Colorado for his setting and his inspiration sings simply, sentimentally, and superbly about the simple pleasures and undying verities of a homespun and simple life well lived. My special favorites here are "Berkeley Woman" and "I'd Rather be A Cowboy", and I always wondered why they weren't bigger hits for John. Hearing John sing in his youthful enthusiasm about what turns him on is still a rare treat. As with many of his albums, the message outlives the messenger. It has successfully weathered all the seasons since with its energy and beauty intact. I love this album, and I think you will too. Enjoy.

"Someone's Been Telling You Stories" rolls out in a smoky tempo taking the part of a man who's been lied about. There's no doubt this album, "Meantime", was influential to many of today's bands. The band as a whole are very influential, and almost created a whole genre on it's own with their own brand of creative riffing and drumming. Page Hamilton's vocals aren't the greatest, but they definitely suit this brand of music as they're equally as aggressive as the riffs on their angriest songs. On the slower, groovier songs, his vocals can even be surly at times and just relaxed. The riffing is unique in that they're so distinct. When you hear a Helmet riff, you KNOW it's Helmet. This also applies to bands like Meshuggah, Entombed, Strapping Young Lad and Crowbar, just to name a few.This album i think is their second best, behind "Strap It On" which to me is totally flawless. My favourite tracks on this album are "In The Meantime" which they did a video for, "Ironhead", "Unsung", "Better", "You Borrowed", "FBLA II" and the awesome "Role Model". Each track really has a memorable riff in it, and such songs like "Better", "In The Meantime", "Role Model", "FBLA II" and "You Borrowed", are just unforgettable and you'll be coming back to them over and over.This is a 90's Alternative/Hard Rock classic, and is a must for fans of the genre. The songs and lyrics are so catchy, and the riffs are memorable enough to have stuck in your head days after hearing them. Even Page Hamilton's vocals, though not the best, are somewhat creative for how he sings the lyrics. Helmet are full of talent, and have recently rejoined and released a new album titled "Size Matters" which i personally find isn't up to the sort of greatness they found on albums like this and "Strap It On". But it's nice to know they've rejoined, and if you see that they're touring anywhere near your home town, be sure to check them out. It would be a memorable experience.
summary: Helmet's Second Best Release, After "Strap It On"

In the 60's and 70's, the slogan "Black is beautiful" was popular. The subculture celebrated by this statement was certainly reflected in the music of the time. "Soul" music, R&B;, gospel - all the various shades of African-American music - became very pervasive. This sound influenced much of the pop music of the 70's, including Barbra Streisand's 1974 album "ButterFly".The first track, "Love In The Afternoon", is a ballad which has an arrangement colored by a little R&B; groove. It sounds like a typical Streisand pop ballad, but we can hear the soft guitars and rambling bass common to many R&B; ballads. On "Guava Jelly" Barbra gets loose with island music and lyrics which imply some joyful physical intimacy. The Bill Withers song "Grandma's Hands" is dark and bluesy, and Barbra delivers a very strong vocal, hitting some incredible high notes. "Jubilation" is full of gospel fervor ("I'm bettin', I'm bettin' on Jesus/I'm hopin', I'm hopin' Hell freezes"), with another very dynamic vocal. "Since I Don't Have You" is a heartbreak ballad first introduced by the doo-wop group The Skyliners in 1958. On her cover of Ray Charles's hit "Crying Time", Barbra gives the vocal all she's got, and the backup singers, piano and strings all contribute to a very beautiful track. "Let The Good Times Roll" packs a double punch. The first half is sexy and mellow, and the second half is more upbeat and jazzy. Some soulful guitar licks are added to the keyboards and strings."I Won't Last A Day Without You", originally by The Carpenters, is pretty straightforward pop, except I do hear some R&B; bassline. That leaves 2 tracks, and they really have no connection to soul music. "Simple Man" is very pretty, a little soft and tame compared to the other material. And Barbra sings David Bowie's "Life On Mars", certainly an adventurous move, but probably you gotta love Barbra to love this one. And I do!

For those of you who consider yourselves avid music listeners, just look at the tracklisting of Mariah Carey's Greatest Hits album, and you'll know that this 2-disc album is necessary for your collection.  You'll think to yourself, "My, she has had a great career and released a lot of songs!"  When comparing this album to her "# 1's" album, naturally, this one of more complete because, although all of this music didn't reach the top of the charts, it's still the best of Mariah.  This album contains basically everything that Mariah and her camp has ever released to radio, and the finished product is memorable because, regardless your age, there is at least one Mariah song that will recollect some personal, fond memories.  That five octave vocal range is, of course, here, but mostly on the first couple of songs.  This album includes every tempo of music: uptempo songs, midtempo music and, Mariah's strength, the ballads.  With ballads, Mariah is able to really allow her listeners to hear the greatness of her voice (although sometimes she strains her voice because she hits notes incorrectly on occasion.)  In total, there are 28 songs here, so some of the material is better than others.  Honestly, her early material is much better than the music released more recently, but it's all worth listening to.One of Mariah's strongest songs lyrically is the first song she ever released, "Vision of Love."  When I was younger, I was not a fan of this song, but as I grew more mature and actually took the time to listen to the lyrics, I enjoy and appreciate this song; it is undoubtedly one of her best.  Her best uptempo song?  Come on now, that has to go to "Dreamlover."  That song makes you want to get up and dance, sing along, and just recall great junctures in your life.  The production is out of this world!  Mariah's most successful song is "One Sweet Day", which features male quartet Boyz II Men.  This is another track I didn't care for until I was older and took a listen to the lyrics.  This song is about the hope of seeing deceased loved ones again.  In my opinion, it's still not her best song, but great nonetheless.  "Hero" is arguably Mariah's signature song, and there's no need to wonder why.  This song was played or performed at countless graduations and other ceremonies because the message is so important: There is no need to look up to other people, because you are a natural hero, a natural role model.  Mariah isn't afraid to let the world know that she believes in God.  Just take a listen to "Thank God I Found You", "When You Believe", and a song dedicated solely to Him, "Make It Happen."  That vocal range is very present in "Make It Happen." Speaking of which, if one really is really interested in her vocal range, "Emotions" is the song for them to listen to.  Mariah has never showcased her vocal range like she did at the end of that song!  It's one of my personal Mariah favorites.You need this masterpiece in your collection, there is no arguing that fact.  Mariah has sold over 100 million records and is one of the most successful female artists ever.  This greatest hits album enlightens us as to why she has been such a huge success.  She's immensely talented!Mikeisha's Top 5 (Boy, it's difficult picking out just 5)1. "Dreamlover"2. "Love Takes Time"3. "Hero"4. "Emotions"5. "Always Be My Baby"

Lil' Kim - La Bella Mafia (Atlantic, 2003)When we last heard from Lil' Kim, she was recovering from the criticism she received from the commercial sophomore album, Notorious K.I.M. To add insult to injury, almost every magazine was dissing her, saying that she needs psychiatric help. But after hearing the lead-off single, "The Jump Off" (despite sounding exactly like Clipse's "When's the Last Time"), it was clear that Lil' Kim came back to snatch the crown from...um, who had the crown, anyway??I didn't like her last two albums, so why did I get La Bella Mafia? Because I wanted to give her one more chance. Things start off really interesting with the intro, which samples bits and pieces of Biggie giving props to Lil' Kim. Biggie is also featured a few times on this album through Kim's rhymes, so if you've been wishing that Kim would just let him rest in peace, it ain't happening yet. But don't worry, it's not as annoying as it was on her other albums.This album focuses on Kim coming back for revenge, and she has the right beats for it. Havoc takes the "Paul Revere" beat and other old school elements to create the album's best song, "Hold It Now". It'll have you wishing for more Kim/Havoc creations in the future. But this song follows with a radio skit, which is a recurring theme throughout this album, and saying that it's annoying is an understatement. And "Doing it Way Big" has a nice beat but the repetitive chorus makes the song fast-forwardable.Still, there are some more good tracks to be found. "Get in Touch With Us" (featuring Styles) bangs, as well as the aforementioned "Jump Off" single featuring Mr. Cheeks, where her line about making "a Sprite can disappear in my mouth" may gain more male fans than female fans. Why all the guest stars? Because she left Junior M.A.F.I.A. so she has to make up for it, I guess. "Thug Luv" is good also, but mainly because of Twista's usual show-stealing flow.However, as even the most die-hard Lil' Kim fan knows, things can drag for a while. All these songs about being the baddest bee start to wear thin, almost to a point where you wish that she WAS kicking those "rated NC-17" rhymes again. As a result, "Tha Beehive" (featuring a few Lox clones) and the obligatory duet-with-the-artist-of-the-moment, "Magic Stick" with 50 Cent, both fail. "Can't F With Queen Bee" (featuring Full Force, Shelene and Governor) is another casualty made worse by Governor's terrible vocals.Filler flows even more with "Can You Hear Me Now" (with Missy Elliott), "Shake Ya Bum Bum" (with Lil' Shanice from her last album), and "This is a Warning". The latter is an interpolation of R. Kelly's "A Woman's Threat", and though it's humorous to hear Kim sing, I can only listen to it once. The personal "Heavenly Father" saves this album from being another bust from the Queen Bee.Lil' Kim proves that she is back and in focus, with slightly better subject matter and good beats. Like my review title says, La Bella Mafia is better than her last two efforts, but that's not saying much. Lil' Kim is also better than her rivals Trina, Foxy Brown, and Eve (who are all called out on "Came Back for You"), but that's not saying much, either. -EJR
summary: Better than her last two albums, but that's not saying much

reviewText: Maybe it was the cliche video for 'Wait For You' of the band dancing in a junk yard or the Robert Plant-esque vocals of the late Daniel MacMaster that caught my attention, but whatever the reason I truly enjoy Bonham. Like many other bands they were critiqued for sounding like Zep, albeit one might turn the tables considering Plant's later Fate Of Nations album hints of Bonham. This is 80's hard rock that puts away blistering guitars for a more rhythmic & bluesy approach and it works. Singer MacMaster died in 2008 at 39. The reunited Bonham sunk without him -- proof of his draw, so I guess it was him that attracted me to the band, let alone the secret to their success. The problem with this band is it's too much Led Zeppelin as became obvious on the follow-up "Mad Hatter" which I feel a step down as they tried to experiment away from their Zep roots and it has merit for the experiment but not the outcome.
summary: a product of the era, but not bad

reviewText: Pain Is Love is Ja Rule's third and most popish offering yet.  The masses have embraced this cd that came to stores hot while Put It On Me and Living It Up tore up the radios and tv everywhere.  While it is not a terrible cd it is an average piece of work.  He has more success but ironically this is his worst album to date.For one thing most of the beats are not outstanding or even good.  They have a pop sound to them, which can be tolerated from Ja Rule in small doses, but on the cd it almost destroys most songs when he tries to be hard. The second gripe is that the skits are pure filler and serve no purpose at all.  Why not just delete the skits all together?  They do nothing but mess up the flow of the album and it makes the weaker songs clearly evident.  Nonetheless, Ja Rule is king when it comes to choosing songs for singles. Livin It Up is a lush remake of the Stevie Wonder classic Do I Do.  Case sings pretty well on this song and does it justice.  I'm Real feat. Jennifer Lopez is also a banger even though the masses played it till it turned into the natural resource oil. They Played it to death, but it was still a classic song.  The current single Always On Time is also blazin hot.  Down A$$ B!tch is a nice slowed down change of pace song and is pretty tight to me.  However the chorus where Ja says yeah over and over almost ruins it.  Now for the bad news: the Wack songs.  These songs are so horrible I won't waste my time or your time so I will just list them.  Worldwide Gangsta, Smokin & Ridin, X, Lost Little Girl, Pain Is Love.  So Much Pain is a disgrace to Tupac's legacy.  This is not a good tribute or remake of the song.  He steals the flow, parts of the verse, and basically sounds exactly like Pac.  The rating is lowered one star because of this.All in All this is a solid release for Ja Rule fans.  This is nothing that will make you keep listening to it in about two years or so but for right now it is ok.  An average work from a good artist.  I just hope that next time Ja Rule comes correct and drops another classic like Venni Vetti Vecci.
